FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in providing the services of Maintenance and Repairs, Erection, Commissioning & Installation services, Man Power Recruitment/Supply services.

On the ground that during the period from 2003-04 to 2005-06, the assessee had collected the Service Tax from the customers but not paid the same to the Department, proceedings were initiated.

Assessee did not contest the Service Tax liability but, after issue of Show Cause Notice, filed the ST 3 returns claiming CENVAT Credit on capital goods and debited same towards payment of Service Tax and sought to carry forward balance of credit.

The Department allowed credit of capital goods received on or after 10-9-2004, but, denied credit of capital goods received prior thereto.

Commissioner (Appeals) allowed credit of capital goods received prior to 10-9-2004 as well.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee was eligible for credit ?

HELD: Capital goods was not available to service provider prior to 10-9-2004

During the relevant period i.e. prior to 10-9-2004, as per Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, credit could have been taken on the Service Tax paid on input services which fall under the same category of taxable service as that of output service and, therefore, the CENVAT Credit of duty paid on capital goods was not available prior to 10-9-2004. Hence, credit could not be allowed in view of transitional provisions in Rule 11 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. [Paras 4 and 6]

Separate proceedings were not required for denial of credit, as it was a part of assessment :

remained due beyond 30 days i.e., upto June, 2008, Rule 8(3A) was applicable resulting in denial of utilization of Cenvat credit along with interest and penal provisions inasmuch as such goods have to be held as having been cleared without payment of duty - In terms of said rule, assessee was debarred from discharging duty liability by utilizing Cenvat credit [Para 10]

FACT: Facts

The appellant-company had two divisions —

- Paper Division : engaged in the manufacture of paper falling under Chapter 48 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 and

-

Steel Division : engaged in the manufacture of MS ingots falling under Chapter 72 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

The assessee viz. paper division, prior to 1-4-2008, was availing the benefit of Cenvat credit of duty and was paying the excise duty on their final product. However, with effect from 1-4-2008, they opted for Notification No. 4/08 dated 1-3-2008 which granted exemption to their final product.

In terms of transitional provisions of rule 11(2) of the CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, assessee was required to reverse credit relating to inputs lying in stock or in process or contained in Final Product and after making such reversal, a balance of Rs. 5,42,028 as on 31-3-2008 was left, which was to lapse as per said rule.

The assessee claimed that it had cleared certain waste and scrap of ferrous material in the month of March, 2008 to Steel Division but, as proceeds thereof were received in June, 2008, assessee discharged duty thereon in June, 2008, by utilizing said credit balance lying on 31-3-2008 to the extent of Rs. 4,98,260.

The Department argued that —

-

the credit balance of Rs. 5,42,028 had lapsed as on 31-3-2008 under rule 11 ;

-

same could not have been used in June, 2008 ;

-

while selling ferrous waste and scrap, assessee used new series of invoices without the permission of revenue ;

-

though assessee claimed that said clearances of waste and scrap were made in March, 2008, same was never reflected in ER-1 return filed for the month of March, 2008 ; and

-

therefore, assessee had wrongly utilized said credit and was liable to pay the same with interest and Steel Division had wrongly taken credit thereof, which was liable to be reversed with interest and both the divisions were liable to penalty.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld demand.

Issue Involved

Whether lapsed credit balance on 31-3-2008 could be utilized in June 2008 ?

HELD: There cannot be any dispute about legal position that Cenvat credit availed by the assessee and lying with them in their balance in Cenvat credit account lapsed as on 31-3-2008, in terms of provisions of rule 11(2) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

The revenue had alleged that invoices were raised in June itself which were back dated for March, 2008, with a mala fide intention to transfer unutilized and lapsed credit to their sister concern which would take the credit of the same. [Para 7]

The assessee was admittedly clearing their goods on regular invoice book. They have not explained as to why a need for issuing of invoices from a new series arose for clearance of waste and scrap in question. There is no answer to the said question by the assessee, who has simplicitor pleaded lack of knowledge. The assessee, being in existence for the last number of years, cannot be presumed to be not aware of Central Excise laws. To issue the invoices from a pre-authenticated invoice book is the basic and first requirement of Central Excise law. No explanation, worth considering is coming forward from the assessee as to why they used the fresh series invoice, instead of using running invoice book, for the clearance of waste and scrap. This fact lands credence to the Revenues' stand that the goods were cleared in June, 2008 though the invoices show the date of March, 2008. The assessee had not reflected the use of their said credit in their monthly ER 1 return which fact again raises doubt about the actual clearance of goods in the month of March, 2008. [Para 8]

The assessee argued that said capital goods were used for providing taxable roaming facilities, which were provided by it from Bhubaneswar on which service tax was paid.

The Assessing Officer disallowed credit in respect of (a) and (b) above on ground that service tax provisions were not applicable to the State of Jammu & Kashmir and in respect of (c) on ground of improper documents. It also invoked extended period of five years to demand duty and imposed penalty accordingly.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: Cenvat credit is not admissible on capital goods installed in state of Jammu & Kashmir

As per section 69(1), every person liable to pay service tax has to seek registration. Further as per rule 4(2) of the Service Tax Rules, where a person has centralized billing/accounting system, then centralized registration can be obtained. Obtaining centralized registration of Bhubaneswar does not mean that service provider (branch office in the state of Jammu & Kashmir) starts providing services from Bhubaneswar. Further branch office in Jammu & Kashmir was not required to be included by the assessee in the centralized registration from where no taxable service is provided by virtue of section 64(1). There is nothing on record that any special charge was recovered by the assessee from the customers towards the roaming facilities provided in the state of Jammu & Kashmir. Roaming charges are the same whether roaming facilities are provided in Jammu & Kashmir or elsewhere in India as nothing contrary to that aspect has been brought on record by the assessee. In view of the above, all the branch offices of the assessee remain separate service providers even if a centralized registration for discharging service tax liability is obtained by the assessee. Accordingly, when branch office (service provider) in Jammu & Kashmir was not required to discharge service tax, then all the capital goods installed in the state of Jammu & Kashmir have to be considered ineligible for taking credit. [Para 5.1]

It is important to understand the structure of various taxes, duties, cess and fees which have bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation. There are broadly two categories of taxes, duties, cess and fees based on chargeability prevalent in India having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods as under: First category of the taxes, duties, cess and fees having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods are those which are to be absorbed by the enterprise as part of the component of its costs as per prevailing relevant laws, rules and regulations, without any benefit granted by law of adjusting these taxes, duties, cess and fees against the final excise duty payable on the finished goods manufactured by the enterprise. For example, Custom duty payable on import of raw materials broadly has three elements of duties apart from education and secondary education cess viz. (a) Basic Custom Duty (b) Counter veiling Duty (CVD) (c) Special Additional duties(SAD). The basic custom duty paid on import of raw materials for manufacture of finished goods is not allowed as a credit of taxes to be set off against the excise duty payable on the finished goods manufactured by the enterprises under the current value added tax regime known as Cenvat credit scheme and hence is to be absorbed as cost component by the enterprise while in the case of the CVD & SAD component in custom duty paid by the enterprise on import of raw materials for manufacture of finished goods, the same are allowed as Cenvat credit to be set off/utilized for payment of excise duty on the finished goods. Similarly, Central Sales Tax(CST) paid on purchase of raw material from another state, no offset is allowed against the State VAT or CST on finished goods sold by the enterprise as per current schemes pertaining to sales tax and hence is to be absorbed as part of component of cost by the enterprise while State VAT paid on purchase of raw material from supplier within the State is allowed to be set-off against the VAT/CST payable on sale of finished goods to avoid cascading effect of taxes. [Para 16]

The second categories of taxes, duties, cess and fees having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods are known as 'Value Added Taxes'-These Value added taxes were introduced in India in 1986 to avoid cascading effect of taxes with an objective to reduce transaction cost and bring transparency in the system. The scheme allowed setting off of duties paid on procurement of inputs against the duty payable on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise thereby restricting the levy of tax to value addition done by the enterprise in manufacturing the finished goods. The scheme when launched in 1986 was called Modified Value Added tax scheme (popularly known as MODVAT scheme) which allowed credit/set off of duties paid on specified inputs used in manufacture of excisable goods against the excise duty liability of the enterprise on manufacture of goods as per provisions of Excise Laws, rules and regulations. The scheme was expanded and credit of duty paid on capital goods was also brought under the ambit of the scheme MODVAT in the year 1994. The scheme was later renamed CENVAT Credit scheme in the year 2000. The 'Service Tax' was introduced in India from the year 1994 and Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 were introduced in the year 2002 to allow credit on input services used in providing taxable output services. In the year 2004, CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 were unified and new CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 were introduced. The new CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 allowed both manufacturers and service providers to take input credit on goods and services apart from capital goods allowing cross sectorial availment and utilization of credit. The Cenvat Credit Rules permit adjustment of excise duties paid on inputs, CVD/SAD on imports of raw material, excise duties on capital goods and service tax on input services against the excise duty payable on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise without one to one co-relation required by the enterprise to establish before availing the Cenvat credit. The Central Government has now announced its intention to introduce unified Goods and Service Tax, popularly known as 'GST' which is likely to be rolled out shortly which is likely to further unify and merge various indirect taxes both Central and State levies into an unified tax to be known as 'GST' and allow credit of various indirect taxes across goods and services both Central and State levies as per scheme to be notified which will further help in cutting down transaction costs and bring in transparency into the system. [Para 16]

FACT: The assessee, a manufacturer, received taxable services prior to 10-9-2004 (i.e., when Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force). The invoice in respect of said service was issued prior to 10-9-2004 but service tax was paid by service provider after said date. The assessee on basis of above two invoices took credit of service tax under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. Subsequently, when the Central excise records were checked by the Central Excise Audit, they objected to this credit and the credit was reversed on 25-3-2006. However, the assessee on the basis of the legal advice, took re-credit of the same and also informed the department about this. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying said credit on ground that since service had been received prior to 10-9-2004, the assessee was not entitled to credit. The Assistant Commissioner confirmed the demand and imposed penalties under rule 15. Appeal of the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) was dismissed.

On appeal:

HELD: Though sub-rule (7) of rule 4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 provides that the service tax credit to a manufacturer or output service provider would be available on the basis of the invoices issued by the service provider only on or after the day on which the payment is made to the service provider of the value of the input services, rule 3(1) provides that a manufacturer of final products or a provider of taxable services, shall be eligible for the credit of service tax paid under section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994 on any input services received on or after 10-9-2004. The service tax credit in respect of service received prior to 10-9-2004 would be governed only by the transitional provisions of sub-rule (1) of rule 11 and in terms of sub-rule (1) of rule 11, the service tax credit in respect of services received prior to 10-9-2004 would be available only to service provider, as prior to 10-9-2004, a manufacturer was not entitled for credit of service tax paid on any input services. There is no dispute that the services in question had been received prior to 10-9-2004. Therefore, neither in terms of the transitional provisions of rule 11(1) nor in terms of rule 3(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the credit of service tax would be available. In view of this, no infirmity was found in the impugned order upholding the Cenvat credit demand. However, coming to the question of penalty, since it is not disputed that the assessee, after taking the credit second time, had informed the department about this, it cannot be accused of suppression of facts and, hence, the penalty under rule 15(2), read with section 11AC, of the Central Excise Act, 1944 would not be called for. However, since this is a case of taking wrong Cenvat credit, normal penalty under rule 15(1) would be applicable. Accordingly, while the Cenvat credit demand along with interest is upheld, penalty on the assessee was reduced. The impugned order stands modified only to this extent. [Para 3]

These statutory provisions make a few things clear. Facility to avail credit on excise duty paid on capital goods used by the manufacturer in his factory for discharging duty liability on the finished products was made available under rule 57Q of the Central Excise Rules, 1945 with effect from 1-3-1994. This continued even under the CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, subject to conditions. As per clause, sub-rule (2) of rule 4 of the CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, would be restricted to a maximum of 50 per cent of the duty paid on such capital goods in the financial year in which the capital goods were received in the factory of the manufacturer. Remaining 50 per cent could be availed in any financial year subsequent to such year. [Para 14]

In a different format in the GST regime also this facility is continued. As correctly pointed out by the petitioner, the CGST Act does not make a distinction between duty paid on capital goods or inputs for the purpose of granting credits thereof. Sub-section (1) of section 16 allows every registered person, subject to conditions and restrictions as may be prescribed to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him. The term 'input tax' is defined as to mean various taxes charged on any supply of goods or services or both to a registered person. Sub-section (3) of section 16 further clarifies this position when it provides that if the registered person has claimed depreciation of tax component of the cost of capital goods or plant and machinery under the Income Tax Act, 1961, the input tax credit on the such tax component would not be allowed. Similarly, sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 17 which pertain to restriction of the tax credit when the goods or services are utilized partially for business purpose and partially for other purposes or partially for affecting taxable supplies and partially for non-taxable supplies, also makes no distinction between capital goods and inputs. Rule 43 of the CGST Rules makes detailed provision for working out such restriction on eligibility of input tax credit on capital goods to which sub-sections (1) or (2) of section 17 would apply. [Para 15]

However, when it comes to the transition from the central excise to GST regime, the legislature has made slightly different provisions for credit on inputs and capital goods. In this context, section 140 of the CGST Act assumes significance. Sub-section (1) of section 140 enables a registered person other than a person who has opted for payment of tax on composition basis to carry forward CENVAT credit of eligible duties in relation to the period ending with the day immediately preceding the appointed day under the existing law in such manner as may be prescribed. Sub-section (2) of section 140 provides that the registered person other than one opting to pay tax on composition basis shall be entitled to take in his electronic credit ledger credit of unavailed CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods not carried forward in return furnished under the existing law as may be prescribed. These provisions thus, enable an assessee to carry forward and take credit of unutilized CENVAT credit paid on inputs as well as on capital goods, of course in the manner as may be prescribed and subject to conditions contained in the said provision. Sub-section (5) of section 140, however, makes a distinction between the capital goods and inputs. It provides that a registered person shall be entitled to take credit of eligible duties and taxes in respect of inputs or input services received on or after the appointed day but the duty on tax in respect of which has been paid by the supplier under the existing law, subject to the condition that the invoice or any other duty or tax paying document of the same was recorded in the books of account of such person within a period of thirty days from the appointed day. As per the proviso to sub-section (5) such period could be extended by the Commissioner for a further period not exceeding thirty days on sufficient cause being shown. [Para 16]

HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER)

It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Therefore, there is no authority in law for availing Cenvat credit on the quantity of inputs intended or used for the manufacture of exempted goods except in terms of rule 6(2), which allows the manufacturer to avail the Cenvat credit only in respect of that particular quantity of inputs, which is intended to be used in the manufacture of dutiable goods subject to their maintaining separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. But if separate accounts are not maintained, though Cenvat credit is availed, then sub-rule 3 of rule 6 provides for payment of amount equal to Cenvat credit on dutiable inputs for cases covered under sub-rule (3)(a ) and in respect of all other inputs, sub-rule (3)(b) of rule 6 provides for payment of an amount of 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. [Para 15]

If the interpretation put by the majority order is held to be correct, it will render the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) ibid providing for payment of an amount equal to 8 per cent or 10 per cent rather otiose. This militates against an interpretation, which renders it superfluous and is of no significance. [Para 16]

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacturer of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts had to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It cannot be given, as the amount of reversal of credit has to be worked out in a manner prescribed in the Rules. There was no such prescription prior to the amendment. This decision of the majority will make the amendment superfluous. Such interpretation has to be avoided. [Para 23]

In the light of the aforesaid discussions, it was held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. C.B.E. &C. by Circular No. 120/01/2010-S.T., dated 19-1-2010, in the context of the problems faced by the exporter for availing of refund of excess, observed that the major reason causing delay in granting refund as well as rejecting the claim is that as per the wordings of the notification, refund is permitted of duty/tax if only such input/input services which are either used in the manufacture of export goods or used in providing the output services exported. As against this, the phrases used in the Cenvat Credit Rules, permitted credit on service used 'whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final product' or 'for providing output service'. The field formation tend to take the view that for eligibility of refund, the nexus between input or input services and the final product/services has to be close and more direct than that is required for taking credit. It has been clarified that the input services should be directly used in the output service exported. As regards the extent of the nexus between the input/input services and export goods/services, it must be borne in mind that the purpose is to refund the credit that has already been taken by them. There cannot be different yardsticks for establishing the nexus between taking of the credit and for refund of credit. Input service credit could not be denied on ground that it was shown in ER-1 return

As revealed from the adjudication order, input service credit was denied mainly on the basis that the input service credit availed on the input services was shown in ER-1 return instead of ST-3 returns. [Para 11]

C.B.E.& C. vide Circular F. No. 381/23/2010/862, dated 30-3-2000, clarified cross utilisation of credit of input and input service. A manufacturer who is also providing a taxable service obtained registration from the Central Excise authority as well as Service Tax authority and is required to file ER-1 and ST-3 returns separately. In some cases, the Cenvat credit on input, capital goods and input services, which are used in manufacturing of goods or providing output service, is available in a common pool and can be used for payment of excise duty or service tax. Ultimately, the Cenvat credit taken during the period shown in ER-1 or ST-3 return could be same. It is clarified that if these returns are being filed separately the Service Tax Commissionerate, while undertaking service tax audit, the officers should verify the said return also for confirming the correctness of such credit. [Para 12]

Rules permit taking of credit under a common pool and permit the use of the credit from common pool for different purposes and there is no restriction placed to the effect that credit accounts should be maintained for use for manufacture of excisable goods and for use for providing services.

The restriction on utilisation of Cenvat credit stipulated relates only for specific type of duties, i.e., education cess on excisable goods or payment of education cess on output service. There is no restriction for utilisation of common input credit availed on the inputs and also on input service for payment of excise duty or service tax. Hence, there is no reason to deny the input service credit on the ground that it was shown in the ER-1 return. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Rule 2(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Consultancy/Legal Services - Period from 2006-07 to 2009-10 - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on legal services received from a Chartered Accountant relating to sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters - Department denied credit on ground that said services were not taxable prior to 1-3-2011 - HELD : Service provider had discharged service tax liability under 'Chartered Accountant Services' - Since said services were in respect of sales tax matters, banking facilities etc., they were in line of manufacturing of assessee - Classification of services cannot be changed at end of service recipient -Hence, impugned credit was valid [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Legal services received from a Chartered Accountant relating to sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters are eligible for input service credit

FACT: The assessee took Cenvat credit in respect of consultancy and professional fees paid to Chartered Accountants.

The Department denied credit on ground that -

Chartered Accountant who had raised the bills on the assessee had mentioned that it was for legal services in respect of sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters (without identifying the nature of services) ;

such services came in to service tax net with effect from 01.03.2011 ;

while impugned services were rendered during the period 2006-07 to 2009-10.

Assessee filed appeal before Tribunal.

HELD: The said denial of Cenvat credit was totally incorrect for more than one reason —

Firstly, Chartered Accountant who raised the bills on the assessees very clearly discharged the service tax liability under the services 'Chartered Accountant Services' ;

Secondly, the lower authorities have accepted that the services which are rendered by the Chartered Accountants were in respect of sales tax matters, banking facilities etc., which were in the line of manufacturing of the assessee.

It is also a settled-law that the services rendered by the service provider can be classified in the hands of the jurisdictional authorities who are supposed to classify and reclassify the services rendered; the authorities at the recipient's end in this case reclassified the services rendered and denied the cenvat credit. [Para 4]

Hence, impugned order was setaside and credit was allowed. [Para 5]

Rule 2(l),  read with rule 6  of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - General - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was engaged in cargo handling services - Assessee availed input services, which were used for auction of abandoned goods and other non-taxable services - Assessee took credit thereof - Department denied credit in full - Assessee argued that since trading was introduced as 'exempted service' only from 1-4-2011, prior thereto, credit was available - HELD : Input service was exclusively used for non-taxable activity, not commonly for taxable and non-taxable services - Since services were exclusively used for non-taxable activity, hence, assessee was not entitled for CENVAT Credit at first instance, i.e., at time of receipt of service - Even prior to 1-4-2011, since no service tax was payable on auction sale of abandoned cargo and export cargo, credit was not admissible on input service used in such output activity - Hence, credit was denied in full [Para 5] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Services exclusively used for non-taxable activity cannot be regarded as input service and, therefore, no credit can be allowed therefor

Rule 2(e), read with rule 2(l) and rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 35F of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted service - Stay Order - Assessee, a dealer of motor vehicles, took credit of rent paid on premises used for trading purposes - Assessee was also engaged in repair, maintenance and servicing of motor vehicles - In some cases, premises were exclusively used for repair, maintenance and servicing only - Department sought reversal of credit pertaining to trading activity - Tribunal opined, prima facie, that amendment in rule 2(e) with effect from 1-4-2011 covering trading activity as exempted service was clarificatory and retrospective - Tribunal also did not consider aspect of invocation of extended period of limitation and ordered pre-deposit of entire demand with interest - HELD : Adjudicating authority had raised demand based on pro rata credit pertaining to trading activity in ratio of value of trading services as determined as per rule 6 and value of taxable services - One of various issues that was involved was whether said formula was applicable or some other basis could be applied, which was more just, fair or equitable - Keeping in view said position, requirement of pre-deposit was reduced to half of CENVAT credit reversal sought (without interest) [Paras 7 to 10] [Partly in favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : A dealer of motor vehicle is not entitled to credit of rent paid for building used for trading purposes; but, in case of services used for both trading activity and taxable services, reversal of credit may be sought on pro rata basis in ratio of value of two activities or on some other just, fair and equitable basis

Section 66A of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rule  6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Charge of service tax on services rendered from outside India - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it - It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A - Whether as per reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and it had wrongly taken cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 6] [In favour of revenue]Service Tax : Where assessee exported goods manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it and availed credit of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services on manufactured goods and traded goods under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, it was not eligible to avail cenvat of service tax paid on marketing consultancy services for trading of imported goods

Rule 3, read with rule 6, of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Period April, 2004 to March, 2005 - Whether trading activity merely involves purchases and sales and cannot be considered as a service/exempted service - Held, yes - Whether in cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994 and, thus, assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor an excisable goods - Held, yes - Whether, in such a case, once in a quarter or once in a six months, quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities was to be deducted according to standard accounting principles and balance only will be availed for purpose of payment of service tax of output service - Held, yes [Para 8]

II. Rule 6, read with rule 2(1), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Stay Order - Period from November 2006 to March 2011 - Assessee, a manufacturer, was engaged in manufacture as well as trading of goods and took credit of input services used for both, manufacture and trading - Assessee argued that since duty on traded goods was paid by concerned manufacturer, hence, they were entitled to take credit of input services used in trading - HELD : Assessee is not entitled to credit of input services in respect of non-dutiable goods - Hence, since 90 per cent of turnover related to traded goods, proportionate pre-deposit of Rs. 1 crore was upheld as against total demand of Rs. 1.27 crores [Paras 5 to 8] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 3, read with rules 4 and 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - General - Assessee claimed credit of services used for goods exported as such without being used in manufacture - Department denied said credit on ground that no credit could be allowed, as goods were never used in manufacture - HELD : Bought out items exported by assessee were never used in manufacture of finished excisable goods - Components and Services utilised only in activity of trading are not eligible for credit, when they are utilised only for export of such traded items which are not used in stream of manufacture [Para 3] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Components and Services utilised only in activity of trading are not eligible for credit, when they are utilised only for export of such traded items which are not used in stream of manufacture

I. Rule 11 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Transitional Provision - Under erstwhile Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 in force upto 10-9-2004, a service provider was not entitled to credit of duty paid on capital goods - Hence, no credit could be carried forward under Rule 11 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 in respect of capital goods received prior to 10-9-2004 [Paras 4 and 6] [In favour of revenue]ST : I. Service provider is not eligible for credit on capital goods received prior to 10-9-2004  II. In case of assessment of a person who had not paid service tax, issue of availability or otherwise of CENVAT credit is to be considered simultaneously and there is no requirement to issue separate show-cause notice to consider CENVAT Credit  III. Memorandum of cross objections is to be regarded as an appeal filed by party; hence, penalty levied against assessee could be challenged in memorandum of cross objections  IV. Penalty under section 78 is to be waived upto extent of CENVAT credit available to assessee against demand raised on him

Rule 6, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Obligation of manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services - Stay order - Assessee, a constituent of a company, entered into an agreement for sale of telecommunication equipments - Invoice for telecommunication equipments was issued from Corporate Office and invoice for services was issued from assessee-branch office - Assessee took (i) Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in provisions of taxable output services as also (ii) cenvat credit distributed/allotted by Corporate Office i.e., Input service distributor (ISD) - Commissioner took a view that sale of telecommunication equipments from Corporate Office was a trading activity and not a taxable service, hence, exempted within meaning of rule 2(e); Commissioner held that assessee had to avail Cenvat credit only to extent of 20 per cent of amount of service tax payable and, resultantly, excess credit taken by assessee was to be recovered - However, there was no finding that assessee had provided taxable as well as exempted services - Whether, prima facie, trading activity of selling telecommunication equipments did not constitute exempted services for assessee to come within mischief of rule 6(3)(c) and, therefore, demand raised by Commissioner in that regard, prima facie, was not sustainable - Held, yes - Whether further, prima facie, adjudicating authority had no jurisdiction to raise question of admissibility or otherwise of impugned credit allotted by input service distributor and availed of by assessee, as eligibility or otherwise of service tax credit has to be examined at end of ISD only - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, there would be total waiver of pre-deposit requirement - Held, yes [Stay granted]

Rule 2(1), read with rules 2(d), 2(e), and 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Assessee procured contract of Rs. 41.5 crore to supply pre-heaters to DC out of which goods valuing Rs. 5.5 crore were supplied out of own manufacture and balance were supplied out of purchases from market - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on commission in respect of procurement of said contract - Department allowed credit in respect of commission relating to manufacturing activity of Rs. 5.5 crore but denied credit of commission relating to 'trading activity' of Rs. 36 crore - HELD : Assessee availed credit on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products and therefore, assessee is not eligible to avail credit on commission paid on trading goods - Hence, denial of credit relating to Rs. 36 crore was in consonance with rule 2(l) [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods is not eligible for credit because same is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products  Cenvat Credit : Where credit is taken in respect of trading activity and said fact was not disclosed by assessee, same can be denied invoking extended period

Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Invocation of Extended Period of Limitation - Assessee's contention that 'treating trading as exempt service was a bona fide interpretational error' cannot be accepted - Till fiction was introduced from 1-4-2011 that trading is an exempted service, 'trading', being sale of goods covered by sales tax law, could not have been considered as a service (taxable or exempted) - There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect - Extended period is, therefore, invocable [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

II. Rule 2(i) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Position prior to 1-4-2011 - In view of judgment in Ultratech Cement Ltd. 2010 (20) S.T.R. 577 (Bom.), assessee is entitled for input service credit of services availed in course of their business and manufacturing activity - Hence, assessee, a Stock-broker, was entitled to Cenvat credit of Service tax paid towards employees insurance, food charges, subscription/books/periodicals and travelling expenses [Para 5.4] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Goods transport agency's service and telephone service were not covered by list of common services in respect of which credit could be admissible even if they were used for exempted as well as dutiable goods - Hence, assessee was required to maintain separate records for them - Since assessee has failed to maintain separate accounts, credit of said two services was to be disallowed [Para 4] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 2(1), read with Rule 2(d) and Rules 2(e) and 6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Commission Agent's Services - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on commission in respect of procurement of orders in respect of 'manufacturing activity' as well as 'trading activity' - Department allowed credit in respect of commission relating to manufacturing activity but denied credit of commission relating to 'trading activity' on ground that it was ineligible for credit - HELD : Assessee availed credit on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products and therefore, assessee is not eligible to avail credit on commission paid on trading goods - Activities not integrally connected with business of manufacture of final products would not qualify as input service - Hence, credit was rightly denied [Paras 5 to 9] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat Credit : Service tax paid on commission in respect of trading goods, which is not in or in relation to manufacture of final products, is not eligible for input service credit

Rule 11 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Transitional provision - Assessee, a manufacturer, received taxable services prior to 10-9-2004, i.e., date on which Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force - Service tax on said services was paid by service provider after 10-9-2004 - Assessee availed Cenvat credit of above service tax paid - Whether, since in terms of rule 11(1) service tax credit in respect of services received prior to 10-9-2004 would be available only to service provider, assessee was not entitled to credit of service tax paid on input services - Held, yes [Para 3] [In favour of revenue]

Rule 6, read with rule 2(d) and rule 2(e), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Stay Order - Assessee was importing software and selling them : (a) as such or (b) after loading on computer, etc. or (c) using them for providing taxable output services - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on import of software - Department argued that trading in computer, etc. was an 'exempted service'; hence, software used therefor was ineligible for credit and therefore, credit was reversible - Where assessee could not correlate procurement and supply of software as such, assessee reversed credit - HELD : In any case, assessee had paid more service tax on supply of software than what they had taken credit on procurement of software - Hence, assessee was eligible for waiver of pre-deposit [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

I. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2000 to March 2007 - Department denied credit on ground that assessee did not maintain separate accounts for input services used for taxable and exempted services and input service tax credit had been availed/utilised in excess of 20 per cent of credit taken in contravention of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : Cap of 20 per cent was applicable on service tax payable and not on service tax credit actually availed - What was restricted was only utilisation of credit and not taking credit per se; credit taken could be carried forward - When cap was removed on 1-4-2008, assessee was eligible to utilise credit also - Further, utilising credit in excess of limit would attract only interest liability; entire service tax itself could not be denied to assessee - Hence, matter was remanded back to adjudicating authority to re-examine matter in light of CBEC circular dated 21-11-2008 [Para 5.1] [In favour of assessee]ST : Utilising Cenvat credit in excess of limit fixed under rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 would attract only interest liability; entire credit itself cannot be denied to assessee  ST : Break bulk fee and freight rebate are not, prima facie, liable to service tax under Custom House Agent's services and Business Auxiliary Services respectively  ST : Commission and incentive received from airlines for booking of cargo space is, prima facie, liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : CCX fee received from foreign principal for purpose of delivering documents to customers in India, to collect and remit freight charges due to overseas company is liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : Cenvat Credit cannot be denied for procedural violations

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Appellant had entered into a business solutions agreement and another business promotion agreement with Amazon as per which appellant had to store various merchandizes in Amazon warehouse and facilitate dispatch of goods - Service tax was collected from appellant by Amazon for warehousing services provided to appellant - As per business promotion agreement entered with Amazon, appellant had to sell different products at prices fixed by Amazon through various promotion sales - Appellant was engaged not only in trading but also providing taxable service - Appellant utilized input services provided by Amazon for engaging in trading as well as providing taxable service - Appellant availed input tax credit for period commencing from April 2014 and took credit upto October 2015 on service tax collected from it by Amazon on business support service and storage and warehousing services - Since appellant had utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and as credit reversed was in excess of proportionate credit to be reversed, it had filed refund claim being balance of credit wrongly reversed (paid in cash) by it - Original authority rejected refund claim entirely - Commissioner (Appeals) held that appellant had to reverse/pay credit along with interest as per rule 6(3A)(i) at rate of 7 per cent of value of exempted services and, therefore, was eligible for refund of only part of amount - Whether view taken by Commissioner (Appeals) that appellant had to reverse credit as per rule 6(3)(i) was against provisions of law - Held, yes - Whether appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i) - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Amazon was providing BSS and warehousing services to appellant and appellant having utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i)

Rule 6 read with  rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Common input and input service provider providing services taxed on reverse charge basis - Cenvat credit - appellants were aware that supplier of inputs was trader and not manufacturer - invoice issued by trader was not valid for taking credit after omission of Rule 12B of Central Excise Rules, 2002 - credit rightly denied - appeal dismissed (Para 5)

Rule 3 of the  read with Rule 12 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and Ruled 3 and 14 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT credit - Recovery of CENVAT credit wrongly taken respondents were trader and not manufacturer of textiles - on omission of Rule 12B of C.Ex. Rules, 2002 the respondents ceased to be entitled to input credit but continued to pay duty on final product after utilising credit of duty on input stock - since duty paid on final product is more than inadmissible input credit, demand of credit is not sustainable being revenue neutral - Revenue's appeal dismissed (Para 5)

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Common input and inputs services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Cenvat credit - And amending Notification No. 27/2005-CE (NT) dt. 16.5.2005 - Amendment by way of addition of Explanation III to Rule 6 (3) vide notification is effective from 16.5.2005 - Prior to 16.5.2005 a manufacturer producing both dutiable as well as exempted final product and paying 8% or 10% amount on exempted final product, was entitled to take credit on all inputs whether common to both final products or exclusively used in manufacture of exempted goods only (Para 32)

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Catering Services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee took credit of outdoor catering services used to provide food, etc. to its employees - Department denied credit on ground that it had no nexus with manufacture - HELD : Services in question are eligible for input service credit - However, where cost of food is borne by worker, manufacturer cannot take credit of that part of service tax which is borne by consumer - Amendment in rule 2(l) effective from 1-4-2011, could not be applied for earlier periods [Paras 13 to 22] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Rent-a-cab services hired for officials and staff to travel to places in connection with their manufacturing activity, are eligible for credit

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2004 to March 2007 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of cosmetics preparations containing alcohol and also engaged in trading - Assessee took credit of inputs/input services used in said two activities - Department denied such credit and sought reversal under rule 6 - HELD : Cosmetic Preparations containing alcohol were not final product, as they were not excisable goods under Central Excise Act - Hence, inputs/input services used for manufacture of such goods were not eligible for credit - Since assessee was paying 10 per cent of price of such non-excisable goods under rule 6, question of levy of penalty was remanded back to consider whether assessee had any intent to evade payment of duty - Moreover, trading activity is neither an output service nor a final product, hence, assessee was not entitled to avail any Cenvat Credit on inputs/input services used for trading activity - Question as to quantification of reversal to be made in that regard was remanded back to adjudicating authority [Paras 6  7] [In favour of revenue]ST : Goods or services used in manufacture of non-excisable goods and carrying out trading activity are not eligible for Cenvat Credit

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Catering Services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on outdoor catering services provided in factory for employees of factory - Department denied credit on ground that catering/canteen services were not used in or in relation to manufacture - HELD : Impugned credit has been properly availed; however, where cost of food is borne by worker/employee, manufacturer cannot take credit of that part of service tax which is borne by consumer - Substitution of rule 2(l) vide Cenvat Credit (Amendment) Rules, 2011 excluding catering services from scope of input service, would come into effect from 1-4-2011 and cannot be applied for prior period [Paras 6 to 14] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Prior to 1-4-2011, outdoor catering services provided in factory for employees of factory are eligible for input service credit; however, where cost of food is borne by worker/employee, manufacturer cannot take credit of that part of service tax which is borne by consumer

Cenvat credit - Reversal of - Common inputs/input services used for both taxable and exempted final products services - Position prior to 1-4-2016 - Assessee was rendering services to BCCI for organizing IPL T-20 cricket matches under a franchise agreement - Revenue generated from stadium gate receipt/sale of ticket, prize money received from BCCI-IPL and in-stadium sale i.e. stadium revenue could not be considered towards rendering of any services hence no Cenvat credit was required to be reversed - Moreover, prior to amendment to Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2016, there was no requirement to reverse Cenvat credit on input/input services used in an activity that was not a service [Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 5, 5.5 and 5.6] [In favour assessee]

Rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Common imputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Assessment year 2008-09 - During year 2008-09, assessee provided taxable as well as exempted services - Adjudicating Authority having found that assessee had not maintained separate accounts, as required under rule 6(2), confirmed demand as per provisions of rule 6(3)(i) on value of exempted services - Commissioner (Appeals) having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest held that assessee had satisfied conditions in view of retrospective amendment carried out to provisions of rule 6 by Finance Act, 2010 and accordingly set aside impugned order - Against impugned order, revenue filed appeal and assessee filed cross objections - Whether in view of fact that Commissioner (Appeals) had already allowed benefit and further in view of complexity of nature, as a special case, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone for year 2008-09 subject to condition that it would file a letter rectifying deficiencies in letter of option given by it earlier as contemplated in rule 6(3A) - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18][In favour of assessee]CENVAT: Where assessee, during year 2008-09, provided taxable as well as exempted services and Adjudicating Authority having noticed that it had not maintained separate accounts confirmed demand on value of exempted services and further Appellate Authority having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest, set aside impugned order, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone

Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used in dutiable as well as exempted goods - Reversal of proportionate credit - It has been held by CESTAT in Reliance Industries Limited [2019 (28) G.S.T.L. 96 (Tribunal)] that for purpose of calculation of Cenvat credit reversal, "Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods -CESTAT further held that Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods - Substitution of sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6 ibid by Notification No. 13/2016-C.E. (N.T.) clarificatory and therefore retrospective in nature - Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 4.3] Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used in dutiable as well as exempted goods - Reversal of proportionate credit by Input Service Distributor (ISD) - Services used for Central depot and reversal made by Input Service Distributor unit - Assessee at ISD level in-fact reversed excess CENVAT credit as certified by independent chartered accountant - That being so, demand of reversal again from recipient manufacturing units of assessee cannot be justified, for the reason no inadmissible credit distributed by ISD - Rule 3 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Paras 4.5  4.6]

Rule 2(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Consultancy/Legal Services - Period from 2006-07 to 2009-10 - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on legal services received from a Chartered Accountant relating to sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters - Department denied credit on ground that said services were not taxable prior to 1-3-2011 - HELD : Service provider had discharged service tax liability under 'Chartered Accountant Services' - Since said services were in respect of sales tax matters, banking facilities etc., they were in line of manufacturing of assessee - Classification of services cannot be changed at end of service recipient -Hence, impugned credit was valid [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Legal services received from a Chartered Accountant relating to sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters are eligible for input service credit

Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used in dutiable as well as exempted goods - Reversal of proportionate credit - It has been held by CESTAT in Reliance Industries Limited [2019 (28) G.S.T.L. 96 (Tribunal)] that for purpose of calculation of Cenvat credit reversal, "Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods -CESTAT further held that Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods - Substitution of sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6 ibid by Notification No. 13/2016-C.E. (N.T.) clarificatory and therefore retrospective in nature - Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 4.3]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods; Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods   EXCISE/ST/VAT : When assessee at ISD level in-fact reversed excess CENVAT credit as certified by independent chartered accountant, demand of reversal again from recipient manufacturing units of assessee cannot be justified, for the reason no inadmissible credit distributed by ISD

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Periods 2008-09 to 2009-10 - Assessee provided dutiable and exempted services and also availed Cenvat credit on certain common input services - It opted for payment at prescribed percentage on value of exempted services and also paid amounts for earlier periods - Revenue held that assessee could not exercise option retrospectively for earlier period and hence credit taken was improper - Whether there is no bar for making payments as per prescribed percentages for prior period as it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input service credit pertaining to dutiable and exempted services and, therefore, assessee's actions of paying amounts for past period was justified - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]CENVAT: There is no bar for making as per prescribed percentage payment on value of exempted services for prior period where it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input services pertaining to dutiable  exempted services

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Travelling services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was providing Management Consultancy and Insurance Auxiliary Services - Assessee took input service credit of Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent Service - Department denied credit on ground that both these services are used for employees' benefit - Assessee argued that : (a) Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for present case relating to period prior to 1-4-2011, credit is allowed; (b) air travel agent's services were availed for travel of employees for business purposes - HELD : Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent services, though used by employees, are for performance of assessee's business - Hence, both services are input service - Further, expenses towards both services was booked as expenditure in profit and loss account - Rent-a-cab service was not excluded from definition of input service; hence, prior to 1-4-2011, credit was admissible [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for period prior to 1-4-2011, said service availed for employees for business purposes, is eligible for credit; similarly, air travel agent's services availed for travel of employees for business purposes is also eligible for credit

I. Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 64(1) of the Finance Act, 1994 - CENVAT Credit - Period April 2007 to September 2011 - Assessee, a telecom service provider, having centralized registration at Bhubaneswar, availed CENVAT credit on capital goods installed in state of Jammu  Kashmir - Whether obtaining centralized registration of Bhubaneswar did not mean that service provider (branch office) in Jammu  Kashmir started providing services from Bhubaneswar and further branch office in Jammu  Kashmir was not required to be included by assessee in centralized registration from where no taxable service was provided by virtue of section 64(1) of Finance Act, 1994 - Held, yes - Whether since branch office in Jammu  Kashmir was not required to discharge service tax by virtue of section 64(1), all capital goods installed there had to be considered ineligible for taking credit - Held, yes [Para 5.1] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat: When assessee's branch office in Jammu  Kashmir was not required to discharge service tax by virtue of section 64(1) of Finance Act, 1994, all capital goods installed there were ineligible for taking credit  Cenvat: Cenvat Credit Rules do not apply on cenvat credit of service tax in state of Jammu  Kashmir and, therefore, credit taken with respect to services availed in state of Jammu  Kashmir has to be denied  Cenvat: Where details prescribed in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are available in a document, it will be a proper document for availing cenvat credit  Service Tax: Where assessee availed cenvat credit on capital goods/services installed/availed in Jammu  Kashmir by including premises of JK in centralized registration though no taxable services were provided in state of JK, by virtue of section 64(1) of Finance Act, 1994, extended period was applicable to demand duty tax

Rule 3, read with rule 11, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Period from 1-7-2003 to 10-9-2004 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of Power Distribution Transformers and HV/LV coils - It availed Cenvat credit on input service - Revenue issued a show-cause notice raising a demand alleging that service tax credit lying in Cenvat account as on 10-9-2004 was wrongly utilized for payment of central excise duty instead of payment of service tax as provided under rule 11 - Whether since as per transitional provision under rule 11, credit can be utilized in accordance with rule 3(4) for payment of any duty of excise on any final product, allegation made in show-cause notice was not correct - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, denial of credit was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 6] Circulars and Notifications : Notification No. 23/2004-CE (NT), dated 10-9-2004

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Travelling Services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee took credit of rent-a-cab services hired for their officials and staff to travel to places in connection with their manufacturing activity - Department denied said credit on ground that it was not eligible as input service - HELD : Said activity was necessary for manufacturing purposes and could not be considered as welfare measure - Hence, same was eligible for input service credit - Amendment in rule 2(l) effective from 1-4-2011, could not be applied for earlier periods [Paras 19 to 22] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Manner of Distribution of Credit by Input Service Distributor - Assessee availed consultancy services for its Vadodara and Silvassa units - Since majority of services were used for Vadodara unit, assessee took entire credit at Vadodara - Department denied proportionate credit to Vadodara unit - Assessee argued that procedure for proportionate credit under Input Service Distributor, was brought only from 2012; hence, prior thereto, credit could not be denied - HELD: Prior to 17-03-2012, there was no restriction on distribution of credit and hence, assessee was eligible to take credit on entire amount in one unit [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]

II. Rule  3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - General - Period from 2005-06 to 2011-12 - Assessee had wrongly availed cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs and input services and availed abatement under notification no. 1/06 ST dated 1-3-2006 in respect of mandap keeper service simultaneously - However, they reversed whole disputed cenvat credit along with interest - Whether in view of total reversal credit availed alongwith interest, their claim for abatement under notification no. 1/06 ST could not have been denied and thus they would be eligible for abated rate of duty - Held, yes [Para 10][In favour of assessee]

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Stock Broker's Services - Position prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was a manufacturer of telecom equipments and was also engaged in providing services in relation to installation, commissioning, maintenance and repair, manpower supply, etc. in respect of its products and also renting of immovable property - Assessee had invested in another telecom company and, later, sold shares of such company and took credit of service tax paid on stock-broker's services used for sale of shares - Assessee argued that sale of shares was an 'activity in relation to business', which provided money to assessee, which was used for various business purposes and, therefore, impugned credit was available - Department denied said credit on ground that said services had no relation with business of manufacture or provision of output service - HELD : On perusal of Memorandum of Association of assessee-company, it was clear that assessee was carrying not only its main objects but was also carrying out objects incidental or ancillary to attainment of main objects - But, it was found by lower authorities that incidental object of investing and dealing in shares did not, in any way, relate to and form part of main business of assessee - In fact, said incidental business was not being actually carried on as a 'business' - Therefore, claim for input service credit was not against any liability arising out of business activity of assessee and was not relatable to business activity of assessee - Accordingly, claim of input service credit was denied [Paras 16 to 20] [In favour of revenue]CENVAT : Where assessee, a manufacturer of telecom equipments, had invested in another telecom company and, later, sold shares therein by availing stock-broker's services, service tax paid on such services could not be allowed as input service credit even prior to 1-4-2011 because such services did not relate to any business activity of assessee

Rule 2(d), read with rule  6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted Goods - Exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty - Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods - Imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 would not apply thereto [Para 5.2] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Exempted goods have to be excisable goods; hence, imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 of CENVAT Credit rules, 2004 would not apply thereto

Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 2(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Eligibility and conditions for taking credit - Whether cenvat credit of service tax paid on outdoor catering service is not admissible post 1-4-2011 - Held, yes [Para 7.2] [Partly in favour of assessee]GST/EXCISE/ST/VAT : Service Tax paid on outdoor catering service is not eligible for cenvat credit post amendment dated 1-4-2011

Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Period prior to 16-6-2005 - Whether Cenvat credit of service tax paid by an assessee on ‘Goods transport agency services’ through TR-6 challan, can be availed for period prior to 16-6-2005 - Held, yes [Para 5]

facts.text:
Assessee was manufacturing TV, washing machines, AC, etc. and was also importing said goods for resale.

Assessee took credit of input services pro rata based on turnover ratio attributable to manufacturing business.

Department argued that since 'imported goods' were 'exempted goods', assessee was liable to pay 10 per cent 5 per cent 6 per cent of value of said exempted goods. Department issued notice dated 7-10-2011 invoking extended period to seek demand.

Assessee argued that —

since he was not taking credit relating to 'trading business', rule 6(2) or rule 6(3) were inapplicable ;

since credit as per formula under Rule 6(3A) was merely Rs. 16 lakh, which was not taken; demand of Rs. 297 crore was invalid ;

its procedure of taking credit only on dutiable goods based on turnover ratio was known to department when audit was conducted in 2008 and furthermore, for earlier period, proceedings on same ground had been initiated and were pending before Tribunal; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3).

Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

The appellant was engaged in providing maintenance and repair services and commissioning and installation service of RO systems. It was observed that the appellants were availing the credit on advertising, security, courier, telephone and banking services which were not entirely used in providing ‘maintenance and repair’ services, but also used in trading activity and, therefore, credit of input services which were entirely used in trading activity was not available to the appellants for payment of service tax. The amounts of service tax payable for two half-yearly period were Rs. 34,143 and Rs. 27,315. Total Cenvat credit available to the appellants was Rs. 6,828, i.e., 20 per cent of Rs. 34,143 as per rule 6(3) and Rs. 8,877, i.e., 35 per cent of Rs. 25,363 as per rule 3(5). The balance amount was to be paid by the appellants in cash only.

The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and wrongly availed Cenvat credit of Rs. 43,801.

The lower authorities claimed that appellant should have maintained separate accounts in respect of input services used for trading activity which were liable to service tax and the Cenvat credit availed by the appellant was demanded.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. During the year 2011-12, it had exported final products manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on import of services received from one 'C' under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A.

The Adjudicating Authority having discovered that the assessee had availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy services for traded goods (exempted goods) rendered by 'C' opined that the assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and the cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods was erroneous and recoverable in terms of rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Thereupon the assessee reversed the cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading of imported goods and also paid interest. It asserted that it was eligible for the cenvat credit in respect of market consultancy services.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of service tax and interest and also imposed equal penalty on the assessee under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original.

On second appeal:

The assessee was registered with the Department for providing taxable services falling under the categories of Consulting Engineer, Maintenance or Repair Services and, Erection, Commissioning and Installation Services. It had entered into a contract with ‘B’ for supply and installation of BTS, Microcell and other Microwave equipments for telecommunication network. The invoice for the supply of telecommunication equipment was issued from its corporate office and the invoice for service portion was issued from its branches. The assessee was taking the Cenvat credit of tax paid on the input services used in the provision of taxable output services as well as the Cenvat credit distributed by its Corporate Office (i.e., input service distributor). It was noticed that the Cenvat credit distributed by the corporate office also pertaining to the input services used exclusively for the procurement of telecommunication equipments. The revenue took a view that the assessee was engaged in the sale of telecommunication equipments from its Corporate Office which was a trading activity and a non-taxable service outside the scope of the Act. Therefore, the trading activity fell within the meaning of exempted services as defined under rule 2(e). According to the revenue as the assessee had not maintained separate records at its Corporate Office for the input services commonly used in the taxable output services provided from the branches or in the exempted services provided from the Corporate Office, it was liable to utilize the Cenvat credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty per cent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services in terms of rule 6(3)(c). However, the assessee had utilized the entire Cenvat credit available with it towards the discharge of service tax liability on the taxable output services. Thus, the Commissioner confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had utilized excess Cenvat credit which was liable to be recovered from it. Besides that, the Commissioner also confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had wrongly availed of the Cenvat credit on insurance service, foreign consultancy service, etc., which were used exclusively in the provision of exempted services and, were utilized towards payment of service tax. The Commissioner also confirmed the demand disallowing the Cenvat credit on the services, viz., flower arrangements, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate agent’s services for residential accommodation of its employees distributed by its Corporate Office on the ground that same could not be termed as input services defined under rule 2(l).

On application :

Facts

The assessee is a trader in personal computers, photocopiers, telecom products and mobile phones etc. and had provided taxable services like Maintenance and Repair; Commissioning and Installation; Leased Circuit; Online Information and Data Processing and Business Auxiliary Services.

Assessee -

availed credit on service tax paid on input services utilized for its trading activities;

utilized credit to an extent not exceeding 35 per cent up to 09-09-2004 and to an extent of 20 per cent thereafter, of the Service tax payable on its taxable output services,

in terms of Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004,

treating trading as an exempted service.

The show-cause notice dated 11-10-2006 alleged that as trading of goods is not a service, this cannot be considered as an exempted service and provisions of the Act and rules thereunder do not apply to trading activities.

The assessee reversed credit availed on service tax incurred by the assessee on sales commission, brokerage, travel agent service, warehouse charges, freight and courier charges, being input services for its trading activities.

The assessee neither responded to the show-cause notice nor attended personal hearing. Hence, the impugned order was passed ex parte.

Revenue's Arguments

Services utilized for trading of computers etc. would not amount to services utilized/consumed in the rendition of output services, since output services were provided after culmination of trading activities i.e. sale and delivery of computers etc. to customers. Input services in respect of which cenvat credit was taken stood utilized prior to delivery of computers and cannot be said to have been consumed/used in relation to rendition of output services;

Since trading is neither a service nor amounts to an exempted service, cenvat credit earned on an input services of trading-cannot be considered as credit earned on exempted service;

Consequently, cenvat credit taken in respect of input services of trading is liable to be reversed in toto and the inadmissible cenvat credit utilized for payment of service tax on taxable output services liable to be recovered, along with interest and penalty;

Since the assessee deliberately availed to disclose availment of cenvat credit on services which were not an input services for its output services, assessee contravened Rules 3 and 4 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, with an intent to evade payment of Service tax and therefore the extended period is invocable and interest and penalty also leviable.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee submitted that -

all taxable services were provided by the assessee only in relation to computers, photocopiers etc. sold to various customers;

commissioning, installation, maintenance and repair services etc. were also services provided in relation to these traded goods;
