Rule 2(b) of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 defines 'Input Services' as any service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service;

transportation of goods and the other services utilized for despatching goods to customers premises, is integral to the post-trading rendition of taxable services such as installation, commissioning, repair, maintenance etc.; and

thus, credit taken is unexceptionable.

The assessee alternatively claimed that since credit was utilized only to the extent of 35 per cent or 20 per cent of the payable service tax, as the case may be, interest should be calculated only on amount of credit actually utilized; that there is a distinction between taking of credit and utilization of credit and it is utilization alone that results in lesser remittance of tax in cash to Government and not taking of credit in assessee's books. Therefore, interest should be calculated only on the amount actually utilized, if wrongly utilized, but not on the gross credit wrongly availed.

No penalty should be imposed since availment of credit on the assumption that trading is an exempted activity was on account of interpretation and penalty is leviable only for wilful and deliberate conduct and not where availment of credit is on the basis of a mistaken but plausible interpretation of relevant provisions.

Issue Involved

Whether credit was rightly claimed and reversed ?

The assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on 'courier services' for the period after 1-4-2011.

It also availed cenvat credit of service tax on 'rent-a-cab service'.

The Adjudicating Authority held that the assessee was not eligible to cenvat credit of service tax paid on 'courier services' for the period after 1-4-2011.

He also held that the assessee was not eligible to cenvat credit of service tax paid on 'rent-a-cab service'.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of cement and clinker. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on gardening services and hiring of tractors for watering the gardens during the period from 2009-10 to 2014-15.

The Adjudicating Authority disallowed the credit on the subject services and confirmed the demand against the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was eligible to avail cenvat credit of service tax paid on gardening services and hiring of tractors prior to 1-4-2011.

On second appeal:

Facts

Assessee, a firm of Chartered Accountants, was providing both taxable as well as exempted services.

Assessee did not maintain separate accounts for services used in providing taxable and exempted services as required under rule 6(2) and also did not opt for pro rata reversal of the Cenvat Credit under rule 6(3A). Hence, department raised demand of 8 per cent/6 per cent of value of exempted services.

It was also noticed that they had availed and utilised Cenvat credit on input services of insurance and maintenance of motor vehicles which were not in the name of the firm.

Assessee's Arguments

They had paid proportionate of Cenvat credit as required under rule 6(3)(ii) before the issue of show cause notice. Further, the provisions of rule 6(3A) are technical in nature and there is no time limit prescribed for giving option to avail rule 6(3A).

Rule 6(3A) was amended from 1-4-2008 and he was ignorant about these provisions and continued to follow the old provision which restricted utilisation of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent.

Input services of insurance and car are used for business and expenses are reflected in the profit & loss account of the firm.

Order-in-Original and Order-in-Appeal travelled beyond the show-cause notice to the extent that the show-cause notice only sought to deny credit on the bills which were not in the name of the firm.

Extended period of limitation cannot be invoked in the absence of mens rea.

The revenue issued on the assessee a show cause notice alleging that it was utilizing the input service for providing output taxable service of clearing and forwarding agent service as well as for trading and proposed to raise demand upon it.

The Adjudicating Authority dropped the demand proposed in the show cause notice. He held that to be an exempted service, it must be a taxable service under the Finance Act, 1994. He further held that the trading activity was a non-taxable service. Therefore, it could not be an exempted service.

The Revisional Authority opined that as per rule 2(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 'exempted services' means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon, and includes services on which no service tax is leviable under section 66 of the Finance Act. Therefore, service on which no service tax was leviable under section 66 could be termed as 'exempted service'.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee, a service provider, had three departments. The department 'A' provided taxable service. The department 'B' provided exempted service. The department 'C' received the input service.

The assessee allocated the cenvat credit of service tax paid on input service availed by the department 'C' to the department 'A' to the extent of Rs. 1.11 crores and the department 'B' to the extent of Rs. 6.66 lakhs on the ratio of the turnover.

The Adjudicating Authority disallowed the entire cenvat credit allocated to the department 'A' on the ground that the department 'B', which provided exempted service, availed part of the cenvat credit.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal the revenue submitted that when the manufacturer or the service provider provides taxable service as well as exempted service, he comes under rule 6(2) to maintain record for verification by revenue. Once the assessee comes under rule 6(2), in that circumstance, application of rule 6(2) and rule 6(3) simultaneously is not possible. The assessee failed to comply with the condition prescribed by rule 6(3) read with rule 6(3A). Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has rightly denied the entire cenvat credit of Rs. 1.11 crores allocated to the department 'A'.

The assessee had centralized service tax registration for providing various taxable services. It was also involved in activity of sale of parts relating to gas turbines. On verification of its records, the revenue noticed that (i) the assessee was availing Cenvat credit on the service tax paid on the input services, i.e., telephones, courier, rent-a-cab, clearing services, outdoor catering, Chartered Accountant services, business support services, manpower supply and recruitment service, etc., (ii) that these were all common inputs which had been used by it for taxable output service as well as sale of parts relating to gas turbines. The revenue, accordingly, issued a show cause alleging that the assessee was not maintaining separate records for the input services commonly used in the taxable services as well as in the sale of gas turbines and, hence, it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of the service tax payable from the Cenvat Credit and having not done so, and having utilized the Cenvat credit in excess of 20 per cent it had violated the provisions of rule 6(3)(c) and, accordingly, raised demand. The adjudicating authority confirmed the demand. The assessee filed instant application seeking waiver of a part of pre-deposit amount contending that the amount of the Cenvat credit taken on the common inputs attributable to the services of sale of parts of gas turbines had already been reversed by it and, as such, there was no need for any confirmation of the demand.

The assessee was engaged in providing various output services. The Commissioner confirmed service tax demand for relevant period on the assessee on the ground that it had availed Cenvat credit in respect of services which were used for providing services in J&K State and SEZ which were exempted during relevant time, and while paying the service tax, it was required to utilize only 20 per cent of the credit available for payment of service tax on the input service in accordance with the provisions of rule 6(3)(c ). On appeal, the assessee contended that rule 6(3)(c) was not applicable to instant case since it had not at all taken the credit in respect of ten common services which were utilized by it. The assessee also contended that once it had not taken credit on the common services, question of maintenance of separate records also did not arise.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. It also imported finished goods on payment of duty. During the course of the business, it availed a number of services which were used in relation to the manufacture of final products as well as in relation to selling and marketing of final products, etc. As the assessee was having its head office situated in Mumbai which was registered as ‘Input service distributor’, the assessee received various services which it distributed to various factories as an input service distributor by issue of invoice in terms of rule 4A(2). The credit so distributed and availed by the assessee at various factories was utilized to discharge the excise duty liability of various factories on various final products manufactured by them. The revenue, however, denied said input service credit taken by the assessee on ground that said credit was availed for duty paid final products as well as exempted final products and, hence, it was not entitled to input service credit as per rule 6(2), as it was not maintaining separate account of input service for dutiable as well as exempted goods. Accordingly, demand was confirmed on assessee along with penalties.

On appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Polystyrene. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on the services received from two railway agents in respect of transportation of goods by rail from July, 2007 to June, 2012.

It also availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on information technology software services.

It further availed cenvat credit of service tax paid for the demurrage charges in respect of goods imported by Air.

The Adjudicating Authority held that the assessee was not eligible for credit of service tax paid.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee, a telecom service provider, having centralized registration at Bhubaneswar availed cenvat credit on (a) capital goods installed in the state of Jammu & Kashmir; (b) input services availed in Jammu & Kashmir; and (c) managerial services. The assessee argued that said capital goods were used for providing taxable roaming facilities, which were provided by it from Bhubaneswar on which service tax was paid.

The Assessing Officer disallowed credit in respect of (a) and (b) above on ground that service tax provisions were not applicable to the State of Jammu & Kashmir and in respect of (c) on ground of improper documents. It also invoked extended period of five years to demand duty and imposed penalty accordingly.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

• The assessee had written off certain inputs on 31-3-2007 for income tax purposes.

• The Department sought reversal of credit thereon.

• The assessee took credit of service tax paid on the services/activities viz. pest control, annual maintenance contract (AMC) for ST plant for sewage disposal, AMC for air conditioners for instrumentation room, canteen facility and AMC for computers.

• The Department sought reversal of credit on inputs written off and input services.

Assessee's arguments

• They were not liable to reverse the CENVAT credit on such inputs inasmuch as the requirement for such reversal of credit was introduced for the first time in the CENVAT Credit Rules by the Central Government by way of insertion of sub-rule (5B) in rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 11-5-2007

• They were eligible for credit of service tax paid on services aforesaid, as they were input services.

Revenue's arguments

• Credit could not be allowed in inputs written off.

• Further, since number of employees employed by assessee was less than 250, hence, outdoor catering could not be input service.

• CENVAT Credit on other services was admissible, as they had no relation to manufacture.

Issue involved

• Whether the assessee was entitled to credit as claimed ?

The assessee had availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on certain services, namely, rent-a-cab service, courier service, air travel agent’s service, maintenance and repair service and telephone service. However, Cenvat credit was denied on the ground that the assessee had not submitted any evidence to show that the said services were used for the manufacture of final product. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the input service credit had been taken in or in relation to the handling of marketing of goods after place of removal on which no Cenvat credit was permissible.

The assessee had availed Cenvat credit on mobile phone services. The revenue was of the view that as per CBEC Circular No. 59/8 of 2003, dated 20-6-2003, credit of service tax paid on mobile phone services should not be allowed as input service credit and issued a show-cause notice to the assessee for contravention of rule 2(l). The adjudicating authority on finding that the mobile phones had been used both for personal and business purposes, denied credit. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the adjudication order.

On appeal :

Food supply/catering service was being done in the premises of the appellants factory by the service providers/contractors as mandated in the Factories Act.

The authorities below disallowed the credit availed on outdoor catering services stating that these services are for personal consumption and excluded as per definition of 'input service' as per rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2011

Hence, the issue to be decided is whether credit is eligible on outdoor catering services post 1-4-2011

The Cenvat Credit was denied on the premise that as the production in the appellant's factory started on 4-2-2010 and input service distributor (ISD) distributed the Cenvat Credit to the appellant prior to start of its production and said credit stood utilized for payment of duty for the month of March, 2010. The Revenue's case was that the appellant was not entitled to take credit on service tax on Cargo handling service which had been distributed to them by its Head office prior to start of its production.

The appellant submitted that there was no restriction under rule 3 for availing Cenvat Credit prior to start of manufacture and for its utilization.

On second appeal before the Tribunal:

♦ The assessee was a manufacturer of transmission towers and was also providing services of erection, commissioning & installation, management, maintenance or repair, testing, inspection of such towers.

♦ For their activity of manufacturing and providing the above services, the assessee availed CENVAT credit on inputs, capital goods and input services.

♦ The department was of the view that since the assessee appellants are not maintaining a separate account in respect of input/input services utilized in the manufacture of final product and used in providing the output services therefore, they were not entitled for input service credit availed by them.

ISSUE INVOLED

♦ Whether separate CENVAT Credit account is required to be maintained for input/input services utilized in the manufacture of final product and used in providing the output services ?

The assessee was engaged in providing banking service and was registered under banking and other financial services and business auxiliary service.

The department issued a show-cause notice on basis of scrutiny of ST-3 returns for the half year ending March, 2005 and September 2005 alleging that:

(a)

The assessee short paid service tax during the period October, 2004 to September, 2005 in respect of banking and other financial services and business auxiliary services. As the assessee paid the service tax after a delay, therefore interest was liable to be paid and

(b)

The assessee had availed the Cenvat credit on the strength of ineligible/improper documents wherein details of input service providers were not available or kept blank. Hence, the Cenvat credit was sought to be recovered.

The Commissioner confirmed the aforesaid demand and Cenvat credit was ordered to be recovered.

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that there was excess payments of service tax in the months of May, June and September, 2005 in respect of banking and financial services and business auxiliary services. There had also been short payments during the month of Nov, 2004, February, 2005 to April, 2005, July, 2005, and August, 2005. He submitted that the excess amounts paid had been adjusted towards short paid service tax in the respective ST-3 returns. Regarding the irregular availment of Cenvat credit, the assessee submitted that the relevant invoices was in possession based on which the Cenvat credit had been taken. However, since the input documents were scattered among a large number of branches it was practically not possible to produce copies of such bills. However, the adjudicating authority had travelled beyond the show-cause notice and confirmed the demand for service tax on altogether different grounds saying that many of the services were not input services.

The revenue contended that the facility of adjustment of excess and short paid amounts was extended only with effect from 16-6-2005, with introduction of rule 6(4A) of the Cenvat Credit Rules. Hence, such adjustment could be allowed for the period prior to this date. Consequently, the demand deserves to be upheld.

The assessee was a South Korea based company having an office in India. It was providing the service of operation and maintenance of captive power plant owned by ‘H’ Ltd. Though the agreement of the assessee with ‘H’ specified separate charges for the services relating to operation and services relating to maintenance, the department had treated its entire services including plant operation as ‘Repair and maintenance services’ and charged service tax on the gross amount being received by the assessee from ‘H’. The assessee took Cenvat credit of duty paid on the goods and input services which was utilized towards payment of service tax on output service. The department, however, denied Cenvat credit in respect of input services on ground that same pertained only to operation and not to maintenance. On that basis, the original authorities confirmed the Cenvat credit demand. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the input credit in respect of abovementioned service only to some extent.

On appeal :

• The assessee was engaged in business of manufacture and trading of yarn and fibre.

• It was paying higher rate of excise duty on the raw material purchased by it as against the rate of excise duty applicable on the manufactured items and, consequently, credit of excise duty was available with it.

• The said excise duty paid from year to year was not claimed as an expenditure but was carried forward from year to year to be adjusted against the excise duty payable by the assessee on its manufactured items.

• During the year, the assessee had closed its manufacturing unit and the said credit remained unadjusted in absence of excisable finished goods.

• The assessee wrote off said CENVAT credit and claimed same as business expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it did not fall as an expense under section 36 or 37. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

• On second appeal:

The assessee availed cenvat credit in respect of distribution of credit by the Head Office, an input service distributor [ISD], which was distributed by the Head Office before obtaining registration. The assessee also availed credit of service tax paid on rent-a-cab service and security service.

The Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit in respect of distribution of credit by the Head Office on the plea that the credit was distributed by the Head Office before obtaining registration and the assessee had taken credit not on basis valid invoice but on basis the allocation chart. He also denied cenvat credit of tax paid on rent-a-cab service and security service on the plea that the services were provided at job worker's place, where the job worker was carrying out cutting process of paper on behalf of the assessee.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the original order.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of automobile parts. It registered itself with Central Excise Department on 28-11-2006 for manufacture of automobile components. The assessee set up its new factory by awarding the contract of construction thereof to a contractor. During the period from January 2007-08, the assessee availed cenvat credit on service tax paid on the construction services on the strength of 12 invoices issued by the contractor. Out of 12 invoices, invoices involving cenvat credit were issued prior to 28-11-2006 and remaining were issued after 28-11-2006, i.e. the date on which the assessee was registered with the Central Department. The Commissioner allowed the credit relating to the invoices which were issued subsequent to 28-11-2006, however, disallowed the credit in relation to the invoices which were issued prior to 28-11-2006 on the ground that the assessee was not registered with the Department at the time of issuance of those invoices and secondly, on the ground that the invoices were issued in the earlier name of assessee and not in the current name of the assessee.

On appeal:

The appellant was engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. The appellant obtained centralized registration with the service tax department under the category "Business Ancillary Services".

Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the department. The audit carried out revealed that the appellant had been claiming credit of service tax on various common input services which were used both for its trading activity and its business of commission agent.

As far as the commission agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. Thus, the audit party came to the conclusion that excess credit of service tax had been claimed by the assessee.

The stand taken by the appellant was that during relevant period trading activity was not amenable to service tax. It was alleged that due to an incorrect audit objection to the alleged utilization of cenvat credit qua the exempted services, the appellant had paid up the purportedly excess amount, which was, otherwise not payable.

The Adjudicating Authority, however, was not impressed with the stand taken by the appellant and, therefore, proceeded to reject its claim for refund.

The Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order passed by Adjudicating Authority.

On appeal to the High Court:

The assessee was engaged in maintenance and repair services of computers and peripherals.

Following an adjudication order dated 23-1-2006 passed by the Commissioner, the assessee had paid service tax through cash and cenvat credit along with interest.

Later the assessee made an application stating that it had paid service tax in excess and claimed for refund of same.

The revenue issued on the assessee a show cause notice stating that the Circular No. 59/8/2003, dated 20-6-2003 provided that the cost of goods and material would not form part of the value for service tax if evidence like sale invoices, bills showed that these goods were sold. No such bifurcation regarding the value of sale of components and labour had been made in the invoices issued by the assessee. Therefore, the refund claim of the assessee deserved to be rejected in terms of the Circular dated 20-6-2003.

The Adjudicating Authority processed the show cause notice and rejected the refund claim taking the plea that the assessee did not maintain separate records as per rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 for the relevant period and there was no separate statement in respect of taxable and exempted services and the assessee was unable to specifically identify the invoices, bills against which credit was taken.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting the refund claim while holding that the assessee had only made an attempt to prove that there was excess payment of service tax by adjusting the cenvat credit which was not available to it during the relevant months towards payment of service tax.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee-firm had availed of the Cenvat credit in terms of rule 3. The credit was disallowed by the Commissioner on the ground that the payment of service tax made by assessee under TR-6 challan could not be treated as evidence and same could not be considered as a prescribed document for the purpose of taking the Cenvat credit.

On appeal :

The assessee, a manufacturer, received taxable services prior to 10-9-2004 (i.e., when Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force). The invoice in respect of said service was issued prior to 10-9-2004 but service tax was paid by service provider after said date. The assessee on basis of above two invoices took credit of service tax under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. Subsequently, when the Central excise records were checked by the Central Excise Audit, they objected to this credit and the credit was reversed on 25-3-2006. However, the assessee on the basis of the legal advice, took re-credit of the same and also informed the department about this. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee denying said credit on ground that since service had been received prior to 10-9-2004, the assessee was not entitled to credit. The Assistant Commissioner confirmed the demand and imposed penalties under rule 15. Appeal of the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) was dismissed.

On appeal:

The assessee, an asset management company, paid brokerage charges to the broker/distributor under reverse charge mechanism. It availed cenvat credit on service tax paid on such charges.

The adjudicating authority denied cenvat credit on such brokerage charges on ground that it was ineligible input service credit. It also held that the document on which credit was availed, i.e. T.R. 6 challan, was not an eligible document prescribed under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

Assessee was providing dutiable and exempted services and also availed Cenvat credit on certain common input services. It opted for payments at prescribed percentage on the value of exempted services under rule 6(3) and also paid amounts for the earlier periods 2008-09 and 2009-10.

According to revenue assessee could not exercise option retrospectively for the earlier period and hence credit taken was improper.

The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the appellant's appeal.

On second appeal:

The assessee was awarded a contract by the State Government under the Sujalam Sufalam Spreading Canal Pipe Line Project for laying pipelines. The assessee by considering the said service as falling under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’ paid the service tax on the same after availing the benefit of Modvat credit and filed due service tax returns with the department. Based upon the enquiries conducted and investigations made, the revenue entertained a view that the above laying down of pipelines did not amount to providing services under the category of ‘Commercial or industrial construction services’, and the service being non-taxable, the assessee was not entitled to avail the Cenvat credit. A show-cause notice was issued to the assessee raising demand by invoking the provisions of rule 6(3)(c), which provide for restriction for utilizing of Cenvat credit to the extent of 20 per cent only, in the event of non-maintenance of separate accounts for inputs and input services used for both exempted and taxable services. On adjudication, the Commissioner held that inasmuch the services of laying down pipelines had been held to be a non-taxable service, the same could not be equated with exempted services and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) could not be invoked. He further held that as the assessee had maintained separate Cenvat credit accounts project wise, the allegation of maintenance of a common credit account was incorrect and, as such, rule 6(3)(c) had no applicability. He, accordingly, dropped the demand. Though in the instant appeal the assessee did not dispute service tax liability, yet challenged impugned order on ground of limitation.

The assessee had started functioning from its business premises from 11-4-2006 and had obtained registration on 22-8-2006.

It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid in the interregnum.

The Adjudicating Authority held that registration was pre-requisite for availment of cenvat credit. He accordingly disallowed the cenvat credit availed by the assessee.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee-manufacturer availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid in respect of four services, viz., xerox machine maintenance and repairs service, air travel agent service, tourist taxi service and photography service. The lower appellate authority denied the credit on the ground that the assessee had not been able to provide evidence to show that above services had a bearing on the production or on manufacture.

On appeal :

The assessee, a hundred per cent export oriented undertaking, was engaged in the manufacturing of ship. It was also rendering output service insofar as repair and refit of ship.

The Adjudicating Authority denied cenvat credit to the assessee on input, input service and capital goods used in the manufacture of excisable goods and outward service.

On appeal to Tribunal, the assessee submitted that on the identical issue, the Tribunal in its own case by Final Order A/10460/2015, dated 30-4-2015 allowed the appeal for the subsequent period from October, 2010 to February, 2011.

The assessee availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on mobile phone service and utilized same for payment of duty on its final products. The revenue denied said credit to the assessee on the ground that mobile phones were not shown to have been used for providing output service or used in or in relation to manufacture of finished goods. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), following decision of the Tribunal in Indian Rayon Industries Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 6 STT 328 (Mum. - CESTAT), allowed said credit to the assessee.

On appeal :

The respondents were manufacturing excisable goods like motor vehicle parts, drugs, fabrics, papers, cement, ignition coil, solenoid switch, etc. They availed outdoor catering service. The canteen service providers used to bring prepared food into the factory and served to the labourers and staff. The canteen service providers charged service tax in the bills. Service tax so paid was taken as credit by the respondents and adjusted towards payment of excise duty on the manufactured goods. Show-cause notices were issued to the respondents. The revenue denied credit on the grounds that food was supplied for the labourers and staff only and that no goods were manufactured utilizing the impugned catering service. The catering services were not even remotely related to the manufacture of the final product. It was further contended that the catering services are also not specifically mentioned in the inclusive part of the definition of ‘Input service’ under rule 2(l).

However, the lower appellate authorities allowed credit in favour of the respondents applying the decision of the Larger Bench in the case of CCE v. GTC Industries Ltd. [2008] 17 STT 63 (Mum. - CESTAT).

On the revenue’s appeals :

During the period June, 2011 to March, 2012, the assessee paid service tax on 'construction service' involving modernization, renovation and repair work within the factory so as to meet USA, FDA guidelines for manufacture of their products.

It availed cenvat credit of the service tax paid.

The revenue issued on the assessee a show cause notice stating that after amendment to definition of 'input service' with effect from 1-4-2011 'construction service' being placed on the exclusion clause, therefore, credit availed by the assessee was irregular. Consequently, it demanded the cenvat credit availed by the assessee.

The Adjudicating Authority reduced the demand to some extent.

The Commissioner (Appeals) further reduced the demand.

On appeal to Tribunal:

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of Power Distribution Transformers and HV/LV coils. It was also registered with the service tax authority for providing maintenance and repair services, commissioning and installation services and technical testing service. It availed Cenvat credit on input service. The revenue issued a show-cause notice raising a demand on allegation that credit of service tax amount lying unutilised was wrongly utilized for payment of central excise duty instead of payment of service tax as provided under rule 11. The original authority confirmed demand and imposed penalty along with interest. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the adjudication order on the ground that by virtue of provisions of rule 3(1) of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 the assessee wrongly availed and utilized the credit.

On appeal :

The respondent-assessee was engaged in the business of manufacture of cotton fabrics. It used grey cotton, dyes, chemicals, packing material, etc., as inputs for manufacture of cotton fabrics. Prior to February, 2005, the respondent was clearing goods on payment of applicable duty under Notification No. 29/2004-C.E., dated 9-7-2004. It was noticed that the respondent had started availing benefit of both Notifications Nos. 29/2004 and 30/2004 simultaneously from February, 2005. However, the respondent was not maintaining separate accounts for receipt of inputs being used in the manufacture of fabrics subsequently cleared without payment of duty by availing of the benefit of second Notification No. 30/2004-C.E., dated 9-7-2004. According to the revenue, maintenance of such accounts was a mandatory condition. The assessee contended that if the manufacturer reverse credit before clearance, it must be taken that the credit was never availed of, and that neither the Board’s circular nor the clarification issued in the RAC meeting required the manufacturer to maintain separate accounts with regard to the inputs, rather they were required to maintain separate books of account only for the final goods. However, the Commissioner took the view that the respondent had contravened the provisions of the notification read with the clarification issued rendering it liable for penal action under section 11AC. On appeal, following the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 1996 (81) ELT 3 wherein it is held that the reversal of credit of duty originally availed of would amount to the effect as if no credit has been availed, the Tribunal held that the credit availed and reversed would amount to the situation as if the same was not availed, thus, satisfying the condition of Notification No. 30/04-C.E.

On revenue’s appeal :

The Assessee was registered under Indian Port Act, 1908 and it has been providing services in relation to Port.

The Assessee operate Port and its services encompass entire arrangement of activities right from the berthing of ships to the storing of the goods and subsequent dispatch to customers.

During April 2005 to September, 2011, the Assessee availed CENVAT Credit on inputs, capital goods and input services used in various output services, as follows :

(A)

Inputs Cement and Steels used in construction of jetty and other building in the Port area

(B)

Other inputs used for repair and maintenance of the capital goods and Capital Goods. CENVAT credit is available on Tower parts, without which the Service in the form of Passive Telecom Infrastructure could not have been provided.

(C)

Input services.

The Department denied said credit. Credit of input services was denied on ground of lack of documents.

The assessee engaged in the export of services falling under heading Information Technology Software Services as defined under section 65(105)(zzzze) had obtained registration in October 2010.

The Assessing Officer noticed that assessee had availed the CENVAT credit for the period prior to taking registration, which was not permissible and thereby having short paid the service tax for the period from March 2009 to March 2011. The assessee had also wrongly paid CENVAT credit for the services provided from outside India and received in India by them on reverse charge basis in terms of section 68(2). Thus, a show-cause notice was issued proposing to recover irregular CENVAT credit along with interest and penalties. The show-cause notice was confirmed by the original authorities.

The assessee submitted that credit availed by it was proper and correct inasmuch as it was eligible to avail credit for the period prior to registration as per CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which did not impose any time limit nor make registration a pre-condition for availment of CENVAT credit and further that the services which were exported could not be termed as exempted services to deny the CENVAT credit. Assessee also raised the ground that there were no restriction under the statute for utilization of CENVAT credit towards payment of service tax on import of services and further the demand of service tax was more than the amount proposed in the show-cause notice, which was illegal.

On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order-in-original.

On appeal:

w.e.f. 1-3-2008, and just because in course of processing of the raw menthol for manufacture of menthol crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP, some residual oil is obtained which on further processing is converted into flavouring materials which are dutiable, it cannot be said that the provisions of rule 11(3) read with rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would not be applicable. Assessee's argument that materials in the instant case were not exclusively and solely used in the manufacture of exempt goods and therefore, the provisions of rule 11 (3) would not apply, is unfounded, fallacious and patently wrong as sub-rule (3) (ii) of rule 11 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not make any exception in respect of export goods as is evident from the words "whether cleared for home consumption or for export" in this sub-rule.

In view of section 5A(1A), exemption was mandatory. A harmonious construction of section 5A (1A) of Central Excise Act, 1944 with rule 6 (6) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be that the term "excisable goods" in this sub-rule should be read as "dutiable goods".

Notification No. 24/10-CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from duty, other than the goods cleared by 100% EOU, is not allowed under bond should be treated as retrospective amendment.

As per proviso to rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 no refund shall be allowed if the manufacturer inter alia claims rebate in respect of such duty. In the instant case, no segregation of duty paid on inputs was made in reference to the final products and the refund and rebate were claimed from a common basket of input credit.

Menthol falling under heading 29061100 of the Central Excise Tariff happened to be both input as also the export product in the subject case involving no manufacturing process in between. As per rule 3 (5) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 to which when Cenvat credit availed inputs or capital goods are cleared as such, an amount equal to the credit availed in respect of such inputs or capital goods shall be payable under the cover of invoices.

It was open to the assessee to claim rebate of duty of the un-utilised input credit under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules read with Notification No. 21/04-CE (NT) instead of seeking refund under rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. It is inexplicable as to why the assessee avoided such obvious legitimate course for tax neutralization in respect of their exempted products which were exported.

The inputs in this case had been received from four Jammu units availing of exemption under Notification No. 56/02-CE, namely. Subsequent investigations revealed that these from Jammu suppliers of inputs had made only paper transactions with the assessee to generate Cenvat credit based on bogus invoices without any manufacture.

Assessee's Arguments

While the Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP, became fully exempt from duty w.e.f. 1-3-2008 under Notification No. 4/08-CE, the other final products remained dutiable. However, all the final products whether exempted or dutiable were being exported out of India. While Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP were being exported under bond without payment of duty under rule 19 of Central Excise Rules, 2002, the other final products flavouring agents were being cleared on payment of duty and were being exported under rebate claim.

When inputs are used in manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted final products and the exempted final products are exported out of India, the provisions of rule 6 (6) (V) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be applicable and the bar of rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules and the liability created under rule 6 (3) (b) would not be attracted.

The words "excisable goods" in rule 6 (6) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 are wide enough to include both dutiable as well as exempted goods.

Amendment to Notification No. 42/01- CE (NT) dated 26-6-2001 by Notification No. 24/10 - CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from payment of duty, other than the goods cleared by a 100% EOU, shall not be allowed under this notification cannot be given retrospective effect, as this amendment restricts the benefits.

Rule 11 (3) (ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not apply when a manufacturer manufacturers dutiable as well as exempted final products out of common Cenvat credit availed inputs.

Facts

The assessee was engaged in providing the services of Maintenance and Repairs, Erection, Commissioning & Installation services, Man Power Recruitment/Supply services.

On the ground that during the period from 2003-04 to 2005-06, the assessee had collected the Service Tax from the customers but not paid the same to the Department, proceedings were initiated.

Assessee did not contest the Service Tax liability but, after issue of Show Cause Notice, filed the ST 3 returns claiming CENVAT Credit on capital goods and debited same towards payment of Service Tax and sought to carry forward balance of credit.

The Department allowed credit of capital goods received on or after 10-9-2004, but, denied credit of capital goods received prior thereto.

Commissioner (Appeals) allowed credit of capital goods received prior to 10-9-2004 as well.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee was eligible for credit ?

During the period April 2008 to March 2011 the appellant/assessee received services from 'C' Ltd. The assessee made alterations in the invoices with respect to the quantity of service availed and the rate per unit of the service. This was done to reconcile the total amount of work done in their records. However, the amounts of service tax paid on those invoices were not altered.

The assessee's claim for Cenvat credit on such invoices containing alterations was rejected by revenue authorities.

On appeal:

The assessee was registered with the service tax department for providing services under the category of 'Port services', 'Goods Transport Services', 'Management Consultancy', 'Consulting Engineering Services', 'Sponsorship services' and 'Storage & warehousing services'. As the assessee was paying service tax on all the above services, it was availing the benefit of Cenvat credit of service tax paid on various inputs and input services utilized by it for providing output services. The Cenvat credit of duty paid on various input services are also being availed by it. The revenue held that since as per provisions of rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 in force up to 31-3-2008 assessee was entitled to avail credit up to 20 per cent, excess credit was not allowable. After reversing said credit, the revenue also imposed penalty on the assessee. The Commissioner however dropped penalty proceeding observing that since entire credit stands paid back by assessee much before issuance of show-cause notice and inasmuch as interest on the said amount was neither contemplated nor paid at stage, no penalty should be imposed upon assessee in view of the provisions of section 80.

On revenue's appeal:

Facts

•

Assessee was engaged in providing Construction of Complex Services, Commercial or Industrial Construction Service and Works Contract Services.

•

Under works contract services, assessee was paying service tax on full value and availing CENVAT credit benefit.

•

But, it was paying tax on abated value under Notification No. 1/2006-ST on two construction services on condition of non-availment of credit.

•

Assessee utilized CENVAT credit account for discharging service tax on two construction services on abated value.

•

Department argued that tax on two construction services could not be paid out of utilization of centralized CENVAT credit balance.

•

Department also alleged that assessee was not maintaining separate account of input/input service received by them in respect of services on which abatement had been claimed.

Issue Involved

•

Whether CENVAT credit balance could be utilized to pay service tax on abatement value of two construction services ?

held.text:
I. Trading an exempted service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5]

Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9]

The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9] From the provisions of both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35 per cent or 20 per cent, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided.

The Explanation added in 2011 though stated to be clarificatory in character can have only a prospective effect since the Finance Act does not authorize rules to be made with retrospective effect. Therefore, trading would be comprehended within the scope of an exempted service only with effect from 01.04.2011, the date of coming into force of the Explanation added to rule 2 of the 2004 Credit Rules. [Para 10]

The assessee not only availed cenvat credit of input services used/ consumed for its trading, by debiting in its cenvat credit account to that extent but had also utilized the credit for discharging its service tax liability for having provided taxable services, to the extent of 35 per cent up to 10-09-2004 and 20 per cent thereafter of the service tax payable on such taxable services, clearly contrary to the provisions of the 2002 Credit Rules and the 2004 Credit Rules, as the case may be. [Para 11]

II. Invocation of extended period valid :

Show-cause notices in both cases were issued invoking the extended period of limitation on the ground that the assessee had deliberately failed to disclose availment of cenvat credit utilized for trading which clearly does not amount to input service used for providing taxable or exempted services; and since trading would not in any event be considered an exempted service. The assessee's contention that 'this is a bona fide interpretational error on the part of the assessee and therefore invocation of the extended period is not justifiable' does not merit acceptance. Till the fiction was introduced that trading is an exempted service, by the Explanation introduced with effect from 01-04-2011 in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, trading which is a sale of goods could not have been considered as a service, a taxable service or an exempted service. The input services (on which cenvat credit was earned by the assessee) were consumed for its trading activities and could not have been availed or taken for discharging service tax on the services provided by the assessee, after the trading activity. There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect. Invocation of the extended period is therefore without error. Trading is purchase and sale of goods, covered by sales tax law and cannot be considered a service or an exempted service. [Para 13]

III. Option to pay penalty at 25 per cent of duty/tax granted, as said option was not granted by lower authorities

An Adjudication Authority should explicitly specify the option available to the assessee under section 11AC of the Act (which is similar to the option available under Section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994). In view of Board Circular dated 22-5-2008, all cases where penalty under section 11AC of the Central Excise Act is imposed, provisions contained in the first and second proviso of this Section should be mandatorily mentioned in the adjudication order. [Para 14]

Hence, the assessee was required to be provided an option to remit 25 per cent of the penalties imposed under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994, within thirty days from the date of the adjudication order, along with interest and the amount of cenvat credit disallowed, after taking credit for the service tax and interest if any already remitted. It requires to be noted that the total amount of disallowed cenvat credit was already remitted by the assessee in respect of both the adjudication orders impugned in these appeals, even prior to issue of the respective show-cause notices. If no such option was indicated in an adjudication order, the Tribunal must provide such option from the date of its order. [Para 15]

IV. Interest not leviable, if credit availed not utilized

Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit

In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. [Para 8]

[Para 11]

The next question for consideration would arise as to whether the assessee was also required to reverse proportionate credit, out of the valid input service credits availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., availing during the time when whole of output service of construction of residential complex was taxable. [Para 12]

While the law does not intend to allow any undue benefit to a service provider in terms of cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in providing non-taxable output activity, cenvat credit is a vested right. Once it is legally and validly availed, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific provisions exist for the same. [Para 13]

It has been a consistent judicial view that credit entitlement is on the date of receipt of inputs when the output activity was wholly dutiable. Merely because the finished goods eventually became exempt later on, the credit availed on inputs which were contained in semi-finished/finished goods form was held as not deniable. [Para 14]

In fact, in order to overcome such legal position, transitional provisions were introduced in the Cenvat Credit Rules. Rule 11, as it existed during the material period, provides that where any inputs are contained in semi-finished or finished goods form, as on date when the finished goods become exempt or output services become exempt, such credit will have to be reversed. As clarified vide Clarification No.334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-2-2007 and also taken note of by the Madras High Court in the case of Tractor And Farm Equipment Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 54 taxmann.com 122/50 GST 68 and eventually upheld by the Apex Court, such embargo applies only to inputs and not to input services at all. Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15]

This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

The Income Tax Act,1961 cannot work in vaccum in isolation but has to progress along-with the rapid development taking place in the economy as it is a living Act and harmonization of various laws is the need of the hour to reduce complexities and bring in the ease of doing business, of course, without compromising/sacrificing with the basic intent and mandate of the Act, to collect correct taxes as per provisions of the Act. During the last few decades, things have radically and drastically changed in the economy the way businesses are conducted as now e-commerce and international transactions have taken primacy in the economy which are now the key areas of challenge under the Income Tax Laws. It is for the Parliament to frame and amend laws to keep pace with the fast changing environment in the economy. Section 145A was brought into statute in 1998 when MODVAT scheme was prevalent which allowed credit/set off on specified inputs used in manufacture of excisable goods apart from capital goods but now with Cenvat Scheme in operation which allows both manufacturers and service providers to take input credits on goods and services apart from capital goods across cross sectors without any one to one correlation, there is a need to align section 145A with the present regime of indirect taxation which Parliament alone in its wisdom can do to keep pace with the developments taking place in economy. Separate proceedings were not required for denial of credit, as it was a part of assessment :

From the Board’s Circular No. 137/203/2007-CX-4, dated 1-10-2007, there was no doubt that the intention of the Government is not to restrict the utilization of the credit of 17 services specified in sub-rule (5) of rule 6 to the 20 per cent limit specified in rule 6(3)(c) and this will apply with equal force to capital goods Cenvat credit for which a similar provision has been made in sub-rule (4) of rule 6 and which are also part of fixed assets that cannot be apportioned for maintaining separate records. Therefore, the word ‘credit’ in the expression - ‘the provider of output service shall utilize credit only to the extent of...’ in sub-rule (3)(c) of rule 6 does not include the ‘capital goods credit’ and the ‘service tax credit in respect of 17 services referred to in sub-rule (5)’ and, accordingly, the ceiling of ‘20 per cent of the service tax payable’ on utilization of credit for payment of service tax, as prescribed in rule 6(3)(c), has to be compared not with the total credit utilization, but with the utilization of the credit, other than the capital goods credit and service tax credit in respect of the 17 input services mentioned in rule 6(5) and only the utilization of the credit, other than the ‘capital goods Cenvat credit and service tax credit in respect of 17 services specified on rule 6(5)’, which is in excess of 20 per cent of the service tax payable, would not be permissible. [Para 4.1-1]

The assessee had pleaded that if the 20 per cent ceiling on utilization was applied only to credit of services other than the services covered by rule 6(5) and credit of input goods other than capital goods, utilization of credit for payment of service tax, in excess of the ceiling had taken place only in January, 2005, March, 2005 and May, 2005 and this excess utilized credit could not be demanded as rule 6(3)(c ) was silent with regard to the period during which the 20 per cent credit shall be utilized. The Tribunal in case of Vijayanand Roadlines Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 15 STT 417 (Bang. - Cestat) had held that the utilization is not restricted to monthly or quarterly basis and that it can be utilized at any time. Applying the ratio of said case to instant case, if during certain months, the credit utilization for payment of service tax was less than the 20 per cent ceiling specified in rule 6(3)(c), then the unutilized credit of those months had to be adjusted against utilization in excess of the 20 per cent ceiling in other months. [Para 4.2]

The demand for excess utilized credit was, therefore, required to be quantified as per above findings. [Para 4.3]

In the instant case, neither the circumstances indicate ‘suppression of facts’, mis-statement, fraud, etc., nor any evidence in this regard had been produced. Therefore, neither the demand beyond the normal limitation period of one year was sustainable nor penalty under rule 15(4), read with section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994 was attracted. [Para 5.1]

In view of the above discussion, it was to be held that while the provisions of rule 6(3)(c) were attracted and wrongly utilized credit, if any, was recoverable with interest, the demands were sustainable only for the normal limitation period of one year and had to be quantified and no penalty was imposable under rule 15(4), read with section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994. The impugned orders were to be set aside and the matters were to be remanded to the Commissioner for de novo adjudication. [Para 6]

Under the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944, rule 57Q was inserted vide notification dated 1-3-1994. Sub-rule (1) of rule 57Q essentially provided the benefit of duty paid on capital goods used by the manufacturer in his factory for payment of duty of excise leviable on its final product subject to conditions contained therein. Term capital goods is defined in the definition below sub-rule (1). Sub-rule (2) of rule 57Q provided that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1), no credit of the specified duty paid on capital goods shall be allowed if such duty has been paid on such capital goods before first day of March 1994. Thus, this rule for the first time granted the facility of utilizing the specified duty paid on capital goods used by the manufacturer in the factory discharging its duty liability but restricted the application thereof to the duty which was paid on such capital goods after 1-3-1994. [Para 7]

CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, also granted similar benefits. Term 'capital goods' was defined in rule 2A. Rule 3 of the CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, pertains to CENVAT credit. Sub-rule (1) of rule 3 provided that a manufacturer or producer of final products or a provider of output service shall be allowed to take credit to be called CENVAT credit of the various duties specified in clauses (i) to (xi) contained therein paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of final product or by the provider of output services on or after 10-9-2004 and any input service received by the manufacturer of the final product or by the provider of output service on or after the said date. Rule 4 of CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, prescribed conditions for allowing CENVAT Credit and essentially provided that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received by the provider of output services or the manufacturer of final products can claim the credit of duty paid on such capital goods for an amount not exceeding 50 per cent of such duty in the same financial year and the balance credit may be taken in any financial year subsequent to the financial year in which the capital goods were received in the factory of the manufacturer or the premises of the goods of output services. [Para 8]

Section 2(19) of the CGST Act defines the term 'capital goods' as to mean the goods, the value of which is capitalized in the books of account of the person claiming the input tax credit and which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business. Term 'input' is defined in section 2(59) as to mean any goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used by a supplier in the course or furtherance of a business. Section 2(62) defines the term 'input tax' in relation to a registered person as to mean the Central tax, State tax, integrated tax or Union territory tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both made to him and would include several taxes specified in clauses (a) to (e) contained therein. Term 'input tax credit' is defined under section 2(63) as to mean the credit of input tax. [Para 9]

Section 16 of the CGST Act pertains to eligibility and conditions for taking input tax credit. Sub-section (1) of section 16 provides that every registered person shall subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in section 49, be entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course of furtherance of his business and said amount shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger of such person. Sub-section (3) of section 16 provides that where the registered person has claimed depreciation on the tax component of the cost of capital goods and plant and machinery under the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the input tax credit on the said tax component shall not be allowed. [Para 10]

Section 17 of CGST Act pertains to apportionment of credit and blocked credits. Sub-section (1) of section 17 provides that where the goods or services or both are utilized by the registered person partially for the purpose of any business and partially for other purposes, the amount of credit shall be restricted to so much of the input tax as is attributable to the purposes of his business. Likewise, sub-section (2) of section 17 provides that where the goods or services or both are used by the registered person partially for affecting taxable supplies including zero rated supplies and partially for exempt supplies, the amount of credit shall be restricted to so much of the input tax as is attributable to the said taxable supplies including zero rated supplies. [Para 11]

Coming to the issue of rejected export turnover, it is seen that a part of turnover has been rejected by original authority which decision has been upheld by the lower appellate authority in the impugned order. [Para 9.2]

Discernably, original authority has reduced the export turnover for the reason that said amount relates to FIRCs though received in the relevant quarter, however, export invoices thereof have been raised before 21-6-2012 and hence are beyond the period of one year stipulated under section 11B of the Central Excise Act, since claim has been filed by appellant only on 21-6-2013. [Para 9.4]

There is merit in the contention of assessee that there is a distinction between the definition of Export Turnover of Goods and that of Export Turnover of Services, in rule 5 of the CCR 2004. [Para 9.6]

From the perusal of rule 5, what emerges is that for considering the export turnover of goods, value of final products and intermediate products cleared and exported during the relevant period alone can be taken. However, for calculating export turnover of services, while advances received for export services where provision of service has not been completed during the relevant quarter, will not be taken into account, nonetheless, two other types of turnover will be definitely taken into account as follows :

(i)

Exported services for which advance payment had been received in earlier quarters, but actual export thereof has been effected only during the relevant quarter.

(ii)

Payment received during the relevant quarter for export of services. There is no condition indicated that such payment will be related only for services exported during the relevant quarter. By implication, there is no bar to inclusion of payment received during the relevant period for export of services which have been effected in an earlier quarter. [Para 9.7]

Thus, relevant quarter/period for which refund has been claimed under rule 5 ibid can very well also relate to export of services effected earlier. From a combined reading of the various portions of the definition of 'export services' in rule 5(D), the only requirement is that both receipt of payment and provision of export services should have been completed by, or within the quarter for which the refund claims under rule 5 are being made. That is, if payments had been received earlier and actual export effected only in the relevant period, claim of corresponding credit refund can only be made during the relevant period. So also, if any export of services has been effected earlier but inward remittances/FIRCs have been received only during the relevant quarter for which claim is made, refund of credit amount corresponding to the payments received can only be made during the relevant quarter. In this way, the Government is ensuring that not only services are exported but also payments thereof are received at the point when the refund claim under rule 5 is made. [Para 9.8]

No doubt, the provisions of section 11B have been made applicable to service tax vide section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994. Nonetheless, by the rule of implied exception, the specific provisions of rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, will definitely take precedence following the maxim Generalia Specialibus non derogant according to which when a matter falls under a specific provision, then it must be governed by that provision and not by the general provision.
