6.15 The most significant amendment effected by the Finance Act, 2008 is with respect to the availment of credit on common input goods and services used in taxable and exempt output goods and services. As per the amended provisions where a manufacturer of final product or a provider of output service uses common inputs for manufacture of exempted and taxable goods or for providing exempt and taxable services, and opts not to maintain separate books of account, there are two options for the utilisation of the common CENVAT credits.

u First; the manufacturer can avail of common Cenvat credit and pay excise duty equivalent to 10% of the value of exempted goods. Similarly, the provider of output service can avail of common Cenvat credit and pay service tax equivalent to 8% of the value of exempted services.

u Second; the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service can avail common Cenvat credit and pay an amount equivalent to Cenvat credit attributable to input goods and services consumed in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or the provision of exempted services, as per conditions specified in sub-rule 3A of Rule 6.

The option to choose either of the above options has to be exercised and intimated to the department at the beginning of the year and once the option is exercised, it would be in force throughout the relevant financial year. But the question is-whether when credit attributable to inputs in exempted product is taken wrongly by the assessee but the same is reversed, whether demand can still be made against the assessee?

In one case the assessee was manufacturer of cartons and printed paper labels. The cartons were dutiable whereas the paper labels were exempted. The manufacturer maintained separate accounts of receipt, consumption and inventory in respect of common inputs utilized for the manufacture of the above products. However, such accounts were not maintained in respect of input services. After due process of law, the Commissioner demanded an amount of Rs. 1,29,09,031 being 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods cleared during the period from September 2004 to February 2006; appropriate interest and equivalent amount of penalty, even though the assessee had reversed the entire input service credit availed by it. The Commissioner confirmed the demand by invoking rule 6(3) for having contravened the provisions of rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

The Tribunal held that in a catena of decisions, it has been held that once the credit availed on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods is reversed, no demand can be made under Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944/Rule 26 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. So the Tribunal held that when credit attributable to inputs of exempted product is reversed by assessee, demand cannot be made against the assessee.

Tax credit illusory

6. It appears that cross settlement of input tax credit between the services and the goods is more on paper than real. Often the input tax credit for goods consumed in the service sector is obtained from dealers who cannot provide cenvatable invoices. The supply of goods is widespread among various dealers not all of whom provide cenvatable bills or cater to the requirements of the end-user who is a taxable service provider.

Similarly goods used in service contracts are not necessarily purchased from the first stage or second stage dealer or from the manufacturer directly. The input credit for goods consumed in service contracts is largely illusory as the output service provider purchases inputs from available sources of supply and on such terms as to credit and quantity which suit his business needs. The input credit for goods is thus not available as the cenvatable invoice essential for claiming the input credit is not there but only an ordinary purchase invoice to support the purchase of goods. Goods which are purchased under cenvatable invoices and undergoing further process not amounting to manufacture lose their cenvatable advantage when they are sold again in the processed stage; the processor is not a manufacturer of any new goods and the CENVAT chain is broken at his level and cannot be continued further into the hands of the next consumer.

Certain identified issues in Rule 6(3) and 6(3A):

6. Though the issues are numerous which still need clarity since the statute is still in its nascent stage, some of the identified issues are as under :

(i) Rule 6(3), Opt in - your choice, Opt out - no choice during the financial year

The sub-rule clarifies that an option would be exercisable both in the case of goods and services as manufactured or provided by the assessee. He cannot opt for Option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Also, exercise of such option cannot be withdrawn at any point of time during the financial year. He may change his option from the next year onwards. Thus, though the choice of opting in for the non-maintenance of separate books of account is open during the financial year, yet the option to opt out of it is unavailable to the manufacturer of service provider for that financial year.

(ii) Meaning of the term - ‘exempt’

The sub-rule does not define the term ‘exempt’ for the purpose of this sub-rule. Technically speaking, exempted goods/services are a sub-set of taxable goods/services. Exempted goods/services are specified by a notification by the Central Government and, accordingly, no duty/tax is leviable on them. However, there are other goods or services which are non-taxable and cannot be called ‘exempt’ technically. For example services of an advocate.

Having said this, the interpretation of the term ‘exempt’ is important for the calculation of duty/tax in respect of the Cenvat credit attributable towards exempted goods/services. Thus, extension of the term ‘exempt’ on non-taxable goods/services or otherwise would change the entire computation. For example when a provider of taxable services is providing exempt services and also is engaged in trading of goods (non-taxable), whether he needs to pay an amount equal to Cenvat credit attributable towards trading activity also, as he has to do in the case of exempt services. The answer is in affirmative when we equate trading to an exempt service and not otherwise.

Further, a larger question would be whether in case of an assessee engaged in the provision of taxable service and non-taxable service, would the computation under rule 6(3A) be applicable on him ? The question would be answered as ‘YES’ when non-taxable is equated as ‘exempt’ otherwise the answer is ‘NO’.

The more logical calculation would be to take out the Cenvat credit attributable towards non-taxable activities and then apply rule 6(3) on the balance Cenvat credit. Thus, the assessee should avail only the credit excluding that which is attributable towards non-taxable activities.

(iii) Choice of option - whether premises-wise or assessee-wise

Further, another point worth mentioning here is that the term used by the statute for availment of choice is manufacturer/service provider and not premises of manufacturer (factory) or service provider. Even the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under central excise uses the word ‘person’ and not ‘factory’. Accordingly, one school of thought might interpret that the availment of the options above should be same throughout all locations across India and the option cannot be availed of differently for different premises.

Expressing it with an example, Mr. X is a service provider having offices in Delhi, Mumbai and Pune, all three offices being separately registered with service tax department. Mr. X is providing taxable services under the category of ‘chartered accountant services’ and also availing the exemption provided thereunder. Thus, he is the provider of both taxable as well as exempt services. Now, the question is whether he can opt for option I for his Delhi and Mumbai offices and option II for Pune or will he have to opt for a single option for all his offices since the sub-rule uses the words ‘service provider’ when offering the choice.

ALLOWABILITY OF INPUT CREDIT FOR TAXABLE AND EXEMPT SERVICES - OPTIONS, CONTRADICTION AND CONFUSION GALORE

Despite having various positive aspects, levying tax on the basis of value addition has its own set of problems. In cases where tax cannot be charged for various reasons, generally an issue arises, that is, how to deal with Input Credit (IC). Determination of IC attributable to taxable services is much simpler than in case of exempt services. Budget 2008 made drastic changes in this area by making amendment in rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In the opinion of the author, this contains lot of confusion and contradictions as the terminology used is confusing and some of the provisions are contradictory to other provisions. An attempt has been made in this comprehensive article to explain the provisions of rule 6 and the terminology associated with it in detailed manner.

Introduction

1. Despite having various positive aspects, levying tax on the basis of value addition has its own set of problems. The tax structure has to take cognizance of certain special cases wherein tax cannot be charged for various reasons. An issue that arises in such cases is, how to deal with Input Credit (IC) availed in respect of such services. Since the Government is not deriving any revenue, it will be reluctant to permit IC on it. If the services dealt with are the only taxable item for the assessee, the things would have been much simpler. However, the issue arises in the case where both, i.e., taxable and exempt, services are dealt with. Determination of IC attributable to exempt services raises various issues. Ideally the assessee can be asked to maintain separate records in respect of IC as applicable to taxable and exempt services and claim IC as applicable to taxable services only. To some extent it may be possible in the case of tangible goods. However, it may not be so in the case of services which are intangible. Apart from that, in real life, it may not be possible to maintain so much of detailed records. Even if one tries to do so the cost may outweigh the benefits derived.

Scenario before Budget 2008

2. Prior to 2008 the assessees were given two options, viz., to maintain separate records with respect to inputs and Input Services (IS) for receipt and consumption, etc., and for Exempt Services (ExS). Rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 (‘the Rules’) made detailed provisions in this respect. Another option as provided under rule 6(3)(i ) was to keep the IC restricted to 20 per cent of the ST payable. Under this arrangement, the assessee, despite having substantial IC entitlement, was required to pay ST. In the case of Service Providers (SP), having substantial volume of taxable services and low volume of ExS, this was turning out to be a losing proposition as it involved cash-outflow. To some extent it was not logical in the sense that the assessee was required to pay tax while large amount of IC was forced to remain unutilised.

Post-Budget Scenario

3. Budget 2008 made drastic changes in this area. The assessee has been provided with more options. Without disturbing the provisions of rule 6(2), i.e., permitting the assessee to maintain detailed records for IC for ExS and ExG, erstwhile rule 6(3) has been replaced with new rule giving two more options to the assessee. Initially, while reading the Finance Minister’s Budget Speech one was led to believe about pragmatic approach of the revenue to the problems of the assessee. However, as it happens in the life wherein things can never be so simple, there is no reason for taxation to be the exception to the said rule. Even a cursory glance at the provisions of rule 6(3) will make the reader uncomfortable as it involves the terminology which looks the same every where. Secondly, the formula for computation which should have been put in mathematical format has been described in text format.

Understanding the basic terms

4. Before trying to understand the provisions of rule 6, it will be appropriate to have basic understanding of certain terms used most frequently. They are ‘exempt goods’, ‘exempt services’, ‘export of goods’ services’, ‘services not liable to tax’, ‘availment of Cenvat credit’ and ‘utilisation of Cenvat credit’.

100% Cenvat credit is available in case of capital goods and input services used exclusively for providing output (taxable) services.

In case of common input services, on the basis of Constitutional deeming provision, it can be argued that only difference between sale price and purchase price should be taken as the value of exempted services and then rule 6 should be applied. INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

A manufacturing company manufactures twisted and texturising yarn. It pays excise duty on such yarn. It is also appointed dealer of POY/PFY of a Ltd. Co. The same company also manufactures machines for own use and for public sale. Excise duty is paid on manufacturing of final machines. It pays service tax on job charges paid in manufacture of making machines and also on repairs and maintenance on machines. The company is registered under excise and service tax provisions. Query - (a) Whether service tax paid on (input services) relating to job work and R and M can be set-off against service tax payable by company on output service tax on yarn commission? (b) It is said that with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, across the board sectorial credit can be enjoyed by manufacturer-cum-service provider? (c) What are restrictions for a manufacturer-cum-service tax provider in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004?

Basically, Cenvat provisions do not require one to one relationship. Cenvat is a common pool of credit of all duties as specified in rule 3(1). This credit can be utilised for payment of any duty or tax, as specified in rule 3(4), subject to restrictions as specified in rule 3(7). Thus, except restrictions under rule 3(7), the credit is completely inter-changeable.

Moreover, definition of input service is very wide. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’. Any relation with manufacture or provision of service is not required. Hence, in my view, Cenvat credit of any input service is available for payment of service tax on any output service.

Of course, department may not easily agree to this but I think legal position is quite clear.

Analysis of Law

2. Sub-rule (7) of rule 4 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 is applicable to the present question. The said sub-rule is analysed herein :

2.1 Statutory Provisions as amended on or after 1-9-2014 - Relevant portion of said rule is reproduced for the ready reference—

"(7) The CENVAT credit in respect of input service shall be allowed, on or after the day on which the invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9 is received:

Provided that in respect of input service where whole of the service tax is liable to be paid by the recipient of service, credit shall be allowed after the service tax is paid:

Provided further that in respect of an input service, where the service recipient is liable to pay a part of service tax and the service provider is liable to pay the remaining part, the CENVAT credit in respect of such input service shall be allowed on or after the day on which payment is made of the value of input service and the service tax paid or payable as indicated in invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9:

Provided also that in case the payment of the value of input service and the service tax paid or payable as indicated in the invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9, except in respect of input service where the whole of the service tax is liable to be paid by the recipient of service, is not made within three months of the date of the invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan, the manufacturer or the service provider who has taken credit on such input service, shall pay an amount equal to the CENVAT credit availed on such input service and in case the said payment is made, the manufacturer or output service provider, as the case may be, shall be entitled to take the credit of the amount equivalent to the CENVAT credit paid earlier subject to the other provisions of these rules:

Provided also that CENVAT credit in respect of an invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9, issued before the 1st day of April, 2011 shall be allowed, on or after the day on which payment is made of the value of input service and the service tax paid or payable as indicated in invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9:

Provided also that the manufacturer or the provider of output service shall not take CENVAT credit after six months of the date of issue of any of the documents specified in sub-rule (1) of rule 9."

It also provides that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed on that part of its value, which the assessee includes in the value of the capital goods for the purpose of claiming depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. In Roots Cast (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2007 (216) ELT 448 (Chennai - CESTAT)], it has been held that depreciation of unavailed credit under the Act can be claimed in the year of receipt of goods.

(vi) Transfer of Credit - Rule 10 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (‘Rules’ for short) deals with the transfer of credit. It provides that if a manufacturer of the final product shifts his factory to another site or the factory is transferred on account of change in ownership or on account of sale, merger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the factory to a joint venture with the specific provision for transfer of liabilities of such factory, then the manufacturer shall be allowed to transfer the CENVAT credit lying unutilized in his accounts to such transferred, sold, merged, leased or amalgamated factory.

If a provider of output service shifts or transfers his business on account of change in ownership or on account of sale, merger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the business to a joint venture with the specific provision for transfer of liabilities of such business, then the provider of output service shall be allowed to transfer the CENVAT credit lying unutilized in his account to such transferred, sold, merged, leased or amalgamated business.

The transfer of CENVAT credit shall be allowed only if the stock of inputs as such or in process, or the capital goods, is also transferred with the factory or business premises to the new site or ownership and the inputs, or capital goods, on which credit has been availed of are duly accounted for to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise or as the case may be, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise.

Case study - CCE v. SmithKline Beecham Consumer Health Care Ltd. - [(2008) (CESTAT - Chennai)] - The inputs, on which credit has been availed, had been duly accounted for the satisfaction of the Commissioner having jurisdiction over the old unit and, therefore, the requirement of physical transfer of stock of inputs from the old unit to the new one stood fulfilled. The department cannot any longer object to the utilization of the credit by the new unit.

Hindustan Lever Ltd. v. CCE - [(2007) - (Mum. - CESTAT] - The goods manufactured earlier remained the same even after change in management. The appellants sought the permission from the authorities well in advance and after having waited for two years, they effected transfer of credit again informing the authorities. The procedure in seeking permission was rightly followed. There being no communication from the authorities concerned either granting or refusing the permission, it shall be deemed to have been granted after a lapse of reasonable length of time.

(vii) Can credit be availed on receipt of services from abroad - Yes. Where the services received qualify as input services within the meaning of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, the same would qualify for credit availment once the payment of service tax on such services received from abroad, has been made. In a case where these payments are substantial, the payment may be made in the last week of the month to enable early credit availment.

(viii) Can a trader avail input service tax credit? - Where the manufacturer of excisable goods has no exempted final product but has trading activity, it is worthwhile to note that rule 6 does not cover such cases specifically. The credits in respect of inputs used for manufacture can be claimed as there is manufacturing involved. Further, sub-rule (3)(c) of the above said rules reads as under : "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service opting not to maintain separate accounts shall follow either of the following conditions as applicable to him, namely :

The provider of output service shall utilize the credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services."

From the above-said provision, it is clear that where an output service provider is availing credit on inputs and input services and providing taxable as well as exempted services without opting to maintain separate account of inputs and input services received and used for the exempted services and refrains to avail Cenvat Credit on such inputs/input services, he has no other option but to use Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on the output services. Therefore, the intention of the law is, the assessee shall either maintain separate account of input and input services for exempted output services and not to avail Cenvat Credit thereon or to utilize Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the service tax payable on output services. Therefore, if the assessee decides to avail Cenvat Credit directly related to the taxable output services and utilizes the same fully for payment of service tax on output services and simultaneously avails Cenvat Credit on common inputs and input services without maintaining separate account and utilizing such credit only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable, it will defeat the intention of the legal provision which is explained in the example given below :

Let the input service credit availed on input services used exclusively for taxable output service is Rs. 10,000.

Common input services which are used partly for taxable and partly for exempted services, credit availed fully of Rs. 20,000.

Let service tax payable on the taxable output service be Rs. 50,000.

The correct way to utilize the Cenvat Credit for the above said situation would be 20% of Rs. 50,000, i.e., Rs. 10,000 which can be utilized out of the total credit of Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 10,000 related to the taxable output services and Rs. 20,000 credit on common input services used for taxable as well as exempted output service). Therefore, the balance amount, i.e., Rs. 50,000 minus Rs. 10,000 Cenvat Credit utilized = Rs. 40,000 has to be used as to be paid through TR-6 challan.

Had Cenvat Credit been utilized as explained in the query, the assessee can utilize the credit of Rs. 10,000 which is directly related to taxable output service plus another Rs. 10,000 i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 service tax payable on output service = Rs. 20,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 30,000 would have been paid through TR-6 challan.

However, it may be noted that the provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, do not provide for more than one set of Cenvat Credit record for input service credit i.e. one for the input service credit related to taxable output service and second common input services credit account which are partly used for taxable output service and party for exempted services nor this sort of arrangement is prohibited, but considering the practice followed under Central Excise, I am of the opinion, that under above stated example, the assessee can avail total credit on Rs. 30,000 (10,000 + 20,000), but utilization will be restricted to 10% of service tax payable i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 10,000 and balance amount of Cenvat Credit unutilized (Rs. 30,000 total Cenvat Credit minus Rs. 10,000 credit utilized = Rs. 20,000) will be carried forward to the next month. It is further clarified that the law does not restrict the assessee to take Cenvat Credit on common input service only to the extent of 20% of service tax paid.

In the above said example the common input service credit of entire Rs. 20,000 can be availed and it is not restricted for availment of credit upto 20% of Rs. 20,000 i.e. Rs. 4,000.

Opinion : In short, if the assessee does not opt for separate account as envisaged under Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, he can avail the credit on the common inputs services fully but he can utilize the total credit available at the end of the month not exceeding 20% of service tax payable.

New Cenvat credit rule 6(3) (to be effective from April 1, 2008) is correct so far as Cenvat principles are concerned. However, in practice the calculations as provided in rule 6(3) and 6(3A) are so complicated that even with help of professional chartered/cost accountant, the calculation of amount of Cenvat credit is going to be a big problem. Many issues remain unanswered in the rule and it is bound to open Pandora’s Box. In this article, the provisions of new rule are discussed and difficulties analyzed. As drafted, the new rule is incomplete and does not provide for many situations. There are some drafting mistakes also.

No Cenvat credit if final product/service exempt

1. As per the basic principle of VAT, credit of duty or tax can be availed of only for payment of duty on final product or output services. As a natural corollary, if no duty is payable on final product or output services, credit of duty/tax paid on inputs or input services cannot be availed. This principle has been embodied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

As per rule 6(1) of the Rules, Cenvat credit is not admissible on such quantity of inputs or input service which is used in manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services [The words ‘provision of’ are inserted with effect from April 1, 2008, but this is only clarificatory amendment]. Thus, if inputs and input services are partly used in exempted final product/output service, Cenvat credit of that portion of inputs/input service will not be available.

(a) Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services - Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/taxable services and partly for exempted goods/services.

In such cases, the earlier rule 6 provided two options - (a) Forget about Cenvat credit of common inputs and input services (b) Pay 10 per cent ‘amount’ on exempted goods and/or restrict Cenvat credit to 20 per cent of service tax on output services.

Now, under new rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider has following three options with effect from April 1, 2008 -

(i) Maintain separate accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services and take Cenvat credit only of inputs and input services used in dutiable goods and taxable output services - Rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules - same as earlier rule.

(ii) Pay amount equal to 10 per cent of value of exempted goods (if he is ‘manufacturer’) and/or 8 per cent of value of exempted services (if he is service provider), if he does not maintain separate accounts of inputs and input services - Rule 6(3)(i) with effect from April 1, 2008.

(iii) Pay an ‘amount’ equal to proportionate Cenvat credit attributable to exempted final product/exempted output services, if he does not maintain separate accounts of inputs and input services - Rule 6(3)(ii) with effect from April 1, 2008.

(b) Cenvat credit on capital goods - If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and partly for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products - rule 6(4).

(c) Some services eligible even if partly used for manufacture of exempted goods/output services - Rule 6(5) provides that in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. Rule 6(5) has been given overriding effect over rules 6(1), 6(2) and 6(3).

In case of these services, reversal of Cenvat or payment of ‘amount’ is not required, if these services are even partly used for providing output service or manufacture of dutiable final product. Cenvat credit will be disallowed only when these services are used exclusively in manufacture of exempted final product or exempted output service.

EXPERTS’ OPINION : CENVAT CREDIT

Thus Spake Experts

An assessee is pro-viding both taxable and exempt services. He utilises various input services for providing his output services. In respect of some of the input services, he is in a position to establish direct correlation between his input service and taxable output service. In respect of general (common input services like telephone, courier, manpower supply, bank services etc., he is not able to establish direct relation with either exempt output service or taxable output service. He is utilising full Cenvat credit in respect of input services where he is able to establish direct relation between input service and output taxable service, as per rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules. In addition, in respect of common input services where he is not able to establish any direct relation with output service, he is availing Cenvat credit to the extent of 20% of amount of service tax payable on taxable output service, as provided in rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

For example, service tax payable by him is Rs. 100. Service tax paid on his common input services is Rs. 25. Service tax paid on services where he can directly establish relation with his taxable output service is Rs. 10. He is availing Cenvat credit of Rs.10 [rule 6(2)] plus Rs. 20 [rule 6(3)(c)]. Is it legally correct? In short, whether rules 6(2) and 6(3)(c) are mutually exclusive or they can be used simultaneously.

V.S. DATEY

The issue will arise in due course and it appears to be a borderline case. There is no specific prohibition in simultaneous availment of credit under rules 6(2) and 6(3). Hence, it can be argued that what is not prohibited is deemed to have been permitted and hence simultaneous availment of rules 6(2) and 6(3) is permissible. This is also justifiable on the principle that ambiguity in taxation provision should be resolved in favour of tax payer.

Counter View - Rule 6(3) starts with the words ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rules 6(1) and 6(2)’. Thus, rule 6(3) overrides provisions of rules 6(1) and 6(2). From this, it appears that assessee has to follow either rule 6(2) [which allows full credit if he can maintain separate accounts of input service] or rule 6(3)(c) [which allows use of common input services for providing dutiable as well as exempted/excluded taxable services].

In other words, if he is not able to maintain separate accounts even in respect of some of the input services, he has to either completely forego input credit on those services and go under rule 6(2) for services where he can identify separately, or avail rule 6(3)(c ) in respect of all input services and take credit to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on output services.

However, there is no clear provision that these are mutually exclusive and assessee cannot avail partially rule 6(2) and partially rule 6(3)(c).

Hence, if assessee is slightly risk taking type, he may avail simultaneously rules 6(2) and 6(3), as one never knows which view will ultimately prevail in such borderline cases.

CCE [2012] 37 STT 584/27 taxmann.com 67 (Delhi - CESTAT), it was held that an SSI unit could take the Cenvat credit of capital goods received when he was not registered. He could utilise the credit when he was registered and started payment of excise duty. Mr. A is proprietor of two business concerns. He has one dry cleaning shop and one orchestra group. Both the services are rendered from single premises. Being a proprietor he has common PAN number. However, Mr. A has obtained separate service tax registration numbers for the two businesses. There is excess Cenvat credit of additional customs duty ('CVD') due to huge imports of dry clearing equipment in dry cleaning business while orchestra group has to pay service tax in cash. Can A transfer the surplus Cenvat credit of dry cleaning business to its orchestra business?

The Credit Rules do not provide for any mechanism for transfer of credits accumulated under one service tax registration to another, where the credits are not relatable to such other business. In the given case, dry cleaning equipments are in no way related to orchestra business. Therefore, Mr. A will not be eligible to transfer the surplus credit of CVD on import of equipments for payment of service tax on orchestra services. Had the two businesses been covered under a single service tax registration, the CVD credit in question could have been utilized for payment of service tax on orchestra services.

A Ltd. has imported tools from outside India. It filed the Bill of Entry after payment of applicable customs duty. However, A Ltd. has lost original as well as the duplicate copy of the bill of entry. Whether A Ltd. can claim Cenvat credit of eligible duties on the strength of triplicate copy of the bill of entry?

As per rule 9(1) of the Credit Rules, the provider of output services can claim Cenvat credit on the strength of the bill of entry. The rule does not specify the original/duplicate/triplicate copy for availing of the Cenvat credit. Thus, in the absence of any specific mention of original or duplicate copy, A Ltd. can claim Cenvat credit on the strength of the triplicate copy of the bill of entry.

A Ltd. is engaged in the business of manufacture of chemicals. In terms of the guidelines issued by the pollution control department, A Ltd. has installed plants in 33% of the areas and engaged B Ltd. for gardening/maintenance services of plants. Whether A Ltd. is eligible to claim Cenvat credit on such maintenance fee paid to B Ltd.?

In case of certain businesses which are potentially hazardous, the manufacturing activity cannot be legally undertaken without having the requisite gardening and maintenance of greenery in the precincts of the factory in terms of applicable environmental laws. The question relates such a situation. In such a case, gardening activity will be considered as an integral part of the manufacturing process and, hence, the service tax charged by B Ltd. on maintenance/garden services will be available to A Ltd. Reference may be had to following case laws:

In Brakes India v. CCE [2010] 29 STT 50 (CESTAT-Bang.) service tax paid on maintenance of garden was held as an input service, since maintenance of garden was statutorily required as per consent given by the State Pollution Control Board.

In CCE v. Nirma Ltd. 2012 (277) ELT 207 (Tri. - Ahd.) it was found that the respondent's factory, being a chemical factory, was covered under the Pollution Control norms. Accordingly, the maintenance of garden, being a mandatory activity under section 25 of Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution), 1981 of the Gujarat Pollution Control Board, was held as an input service.

In JBM Auto System (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Final Order No. 763/2011, Appeal No. E/647/2010, dated 18-7-2011] it was held that the manpower service used for garden maintenance was required for infrastructure for manufacture and clearance of final products and that credit was admissible.

In CCE v Voith Turbo (P.) Ltd. [Final Order Nos. 1149 & 1150/2010, dated 27-8-2010] it was held that when it was on record that the assessee had given its consent for the manufacturing of the goods in the factory premises subject to discharge of industrial and domestic effluents within the factory premises and was directed to maintain a green belt, then the service was utilized by the assessee from the experts for maintaining the garden of such type and credit could not be denied on the service tax paid on such services.

Ultratech Cement Ltd., In re [Appeal Nos. P11/PAP/102-103/2009, dated 23-4-2009] it was held that services such as cleaning/maintenance of garden/trees, plantation, etc., were used to control the pollution created by the industry and, thus, the same could be considered as input services which were used in relation to the manufacture of final product, viz., cement.

General rate of service tax

| Period | Rate of service tax | Availability of credit for tax/duty paid in respect of input goods or services against payable in respect of output goods or services |
| --- | --- | --- |

| Sl. No. | Issue | Clarification |

| 1. | Can credit of capital goods be availed of when used in manufacture of dutiable goods on which benefit under Notification No. 1/2011-CE is availed or in provision of a service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services is taken? | As per rule 6(4) no credit can be availed on capital goods used exclusively in manufacture of exempted goods or in providing exempted service. Goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 is availed are exempted goods [Rule 2(d)]. | 2. | Is the credit of only specified goods and services listed in the definition of inputs and input services not allowed such as goods used in a club, outdoor catering etc., or is the list only illustrative? | The list is only illustrative. | 3. | How is the "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final product" to be determined? | Credit of all goods used in the factory is allowed except insofar as it is specifically denied. The expression "no relationship whatsoever with the manufacture of a final pro-duct" must be interpreted and applied strictly and not loosely. The expression does not include any goods used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final product or not. Only credit of goods used in the factory but having absolutely no relationship with the manufacture of final product is not allowed. Goods such as furniture and stationery used in an office within the factory are goods used in the factory and are used in relation to the manufacturing business and hence the credit of same is allowed. |
| 4. | Is the credit of input services used for repair or renovation of factory or office available? | Credit of input services used for repair or renovation of factory or office is allowed. | 5. | Is the credit of Business Auxiliary Service (BAS) on account of sales commission now disallowed after the deletion of expression "activities related to business"? | The definition of input services allows all credit on services used for clearance of final products upto the place of removal. Moreover activity of sale promotion is specifically allowed and on many occasions the remuneration for same is linked to actual sale. Reading the provisions harmoniously it is clarified that credit is admissible on the services of sale of dutiable goods on commission basis. |
| 6. | Can the credit of input or input services used exclusively in trading, be availed? | Trading is an exempted service. Hence the credit of any inputs or input services used exclusively in trading cannot be availed. |
| 7. | What shall be the treatment of credit of input and input services used in trading before 1-4-2008? | Trading is an exempted service. | 8. | While calculating the value of trading what principle to follow- FIFO, LIFO or one to one correlation? | The method normally followed by the concern for its accounting purpose as per generally accepted accounting principles should be used. |
| 9. | Are the taxes and year end discounts to be included in the sale price and cost of goods sold while calculating the value of trading? | Generally accepted accounting principles need to be followed in this regard. | 10. | Does the expression "in or in relation" used in Rule 6 override the definition of "input" under Rule 2(k) for determining the eligibility of Cenvat credit? | The definition of "input" is given in Rule 2(k) and Rule 6 only intends to segregate the credits of inputs used towards dutiable goods and exempted goods. Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

10.1-3 Manner of distribution of Cenvat Credit w.e.f. 1-4-2016

Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules has been revamped w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

As per revised rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2016, the distribution should be as follows —

(a)

Credit distributed should not be more than credit of input service tax available.

(b)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly by a unit shall be distributed only to that unit.

(c)

Credit of service tax attributable to services used by more than one unit (but not to all units) shall be distributed pro-rata on the basis of turnover of such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of such units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(d)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used by all the units shall be distributed pro-rata on the basis of turnover of all such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of all the units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(e)

The Cenvat credit can be distributed to 'outsourced manufacturing unit'. Such 'outsourced manufacturing unit' can utilize the Cenvat credit only for purpose of payment of duty on goods manufactured for such input service distributor.

(f)

Credit of Cenvat credit as on 31-3-2016 shall not be distributed to outsourced manufacturing unit.

(g)

Provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules applies to units manufacturing excisable goods or provider of output service. It shall not apply to input service distributor. Thus, ISD should distribute on basis of total turnover of goods and services (exempted as well as taxable).

Meaning of 'unit' - 'Unit' includes premises of provider of output service and the premises of a manufacturer, including the factory, whether registered or otherwise or the premises of outsourced manufacturing unit - Explanation 1 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Meaning of total turnover - Total turnover will be calculates per provisions of rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules. Turnover of outsourced manufacturing unit will be only of goods manufactured by the outsourced manufacturing unit for the Input Service Distributor - Explanation 2 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Meaning of 'relevant period' - 'Relevant Period' means (a) if the assessee has turnover in the 'financial year' preceding to the year during which credit is to be distributed for the month or quarter, as the case may be, the said financial year or (b) If the assessee does not have turnover for some or all the units in the preceding financial year, the last quarter for which details of turnover of all the units are available, previous to the month or quarter for which credit is to be distributed - Explanation 3 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Thus, if Cenvat Credit for July 2016 is to be distributed and if all the units of assessee were working in financial year 2015-16, then distribution should be on basis of turnover of each unit during 2016-17. However, if some of the units started operations after April 2016, then turnover for April 2016 - June 2016 will have to be considered for distributing the Cenvat credit to various units.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

Does the provision apply to invoices issued prior to 1-9-2014? - The provision of taking Cenvat credit is really only a procedural amendment and not a substantive provision. Hence, it should apply to all Cenvat Credit taken on or after 1-9-2014.

There was similar amendment made in 1995.

In Osram Surya v. CCE 2002 (142) ELT 5 = 2002 taxmann.com 1238 = 122 Taxman 583 (SC), rules were amended fixing time limit of 6 months for taking Cenvat credit. It was held that the time limit applies even to credit accrued prior to amendment. The amendment does not take away a vested right but merely introduces a time limit. The amendment is not retrospective - followed in Ashok Leyland v. CCE (2015) 315 ELT 292 (CESTAT SMB).

Procedural amendments generally have retrospective effect unless such (retrospective) construction is textually impossible - Jose Da Costa v. Bascora Sadashiva Sinai Narcornin - AIR 1975 SC 1843 = (1976) 2 SCC 917.

Procedural amendment to a law, in absence of anything to contrary, operates retrospectively in the limited sense that they apply to all actions after the date they come into force even though the claim on which the action is based may be of an anterior date. - Memon Abdul Karim Haji v. Dy. Custodian General, New Delhi - AIR 1964 SC 1256 as also in National Woollen Mills v. CCE - 1991 (56) ELT 613. - similar views in Narhari v. Pannalal AIR 1977 SC 164.

Substantive laws are generally not retrospective unless specified contrary by legislature. Procedural laws may be retrospective unless shown to the contrary - Rochiram and Sons v. UOI (2008) 226 ELT 20 (SC).

Can the provision be challenged? - Really, taking Cenvat credit is only a procedural aspect. It is not a substantive provision. The time limit of six months is confiscatory and not regulatory. Rule making authority can only make regulatory provisions and not confiscatory provisions.

In Osram Surya v. CCE 2002 (142) ELT 5 = 2002 AIR SCW 2292 = 122 Taxman 583 (SC), it was specifically noted by Supreme Court that the validity of rule of six months limit has not been challenged and hence Supreme Court did not express its views.

In Century Laminating Com v. CCE (2015) 320 ELT 406 (All HC DB), it was held that the time limit for taking Cenvat credit is procedural in nature. It did not dis-entitle assessee from claiming Cenvat credit on bona fide transactions. - same view in Bharat Heavy Electricals v. CCE (2016) 332 ELT 411 (MP HC DB).

There is ample case law that a substantive benefit cannot be lost on account of procedural lapses. All provisions in law are not automatically mandatory. Further, rule cannot be penal, unless there is specific provision in Act to provide for penal provision.

In Baroda Rayon Corporation v. UOI (2014) 306 ELT 551 (Guj HC DB), it was held that right conferred under rule 57A of Cenvat Credit Rules cannot be curtailed by prescribing a time limit [Though the decision was in different context, the principle can apply here also].

However, in USA Agencies v. CTO (2014) 305 ELT 404 (Mad HC DB), time limit prescribed for taking input tax credit was held as valid.

1.3

Cenvat Scheme, 2004

Section 37 of Central Excise Act gives powers to Central Government to make rules to : (a) provide for the credit of duty paid or deemed to have been paid on goods used in or in relation to manufacture of excisable goods. [Clause (xvia)] (b) provide for giving of credit of sums of money with respect to raw materials used in manufacture of excisable goods. [Clause (xvib)] (c) provide for credit of service tax leviable under Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994, paid or payable on taxable services used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of excisable goods.

In exercise of these powers, MODVAT credit scheme was introduced in 1986 vide rules 57A to 57U. Since rules can be amended easily by Central Government, the scheme remains flexible and hence can be modified quickly as per changing requirements. Cenvat was introduced in place of Modvat w.e.f. 1.4.2000, vide new set of rules 57AA to 57AK. Later, separate Cenvat Credit Rules were introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2001. These were replaced by Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002. These are now replaced by Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f. 10-9-2004. Cenvat credit of excise and service tax has been integrated w.e.f. 10-9-2004.

Section 94(2) of Finance Act, 1994 empowers Central Government to make rules for – (i) credit of service tax paid on services consumed for providing a taxable service in case where the services consumed and the service provided fall in the same category [clause (ee)] (ii) credit of service tax paid on the services consumed or duties paid or deemed to have been paid on goods used for providing taxable service [clause (eee)] (iii) provisions for determining export of taxable services [clause (f)] (iv) Rebate of service tax paid or payable on taxable services consumed or duties paid or deemed to have been paid on goods used for providing taxable services which are exported out of India [clause (h)].

Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 were issued effective from 16-8-2002, which are now merged with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 w.e.f. 10-9-2004.

Merging of Cenvat and Service Tax Rules - Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 have been issued by superseding Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 and Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. The new rules are effective from 10-9-2004.

Rule 16(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 states that any reference in any notification, circular, trade notice, rules etc. to Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 or Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, shall be construed as reference to Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

6.7

Other Issues relating to availment of Cenvat Credit

Other issues relating to availment of Cenvat credit are discussed below.

6.7-1 One to one correlation not necessary in Cenvat

Rule 3(4)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that Cenvat credit may be utilised for payment of any duty of excise on any final product or service tax on output service. Thus, there is no requirement of establishing relation between inputs/input services and final product/output services. One to one relation is not required.

There is no corelation of the raw material and the final product; that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product that is manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related - CCE v. Dai Ichi Karkaria Ltd. 112 ELT 353 = AIR 1999 SC 3234 = 1999 AIR SCW 3205 = (1999) 7 SCC 448 (SC 3 member bench) - quoted with approval in CCE v. Bombay Dyeing (2007) 10 STT 286 (SC).

Cenvat rules do not provide for 'one to one' co-relation between input and output. - Kisan Products Ltd. v. CCE - (1996) 88 ELT 440 (CEGAT) * Bajaj Sevashram Ltd. v. CCE - (1996) 87 ELT 726 (CEGAT) * Nisha Conductors v. Collector and Rama Cables and Wires Ltd. v. Collector - 1993 (68) ELT 256 (CEGAT) * Pratap Steels Ltd. v. CCE 1997(95) ELT 584 (CEGAT) * Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CCE 2000 (117) ELT 423 (CEGAT) * HMT v. CCE (2009) 18 STT 8 = 232 ELT 217 (CESTAT 3 member bench) * CCE v. Motherson Sumi Electric Wires (2010) 252 ELT 543 (CESTAT) * Shri Dnyaneshwar SSK v. CCE (2014) 310 ELT 770 (CESTAT).

There is no one to one co-relation in Cenvat scheme - PSL Corrosion Control v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 495 (CESTAT).

One to one corelation between credit availed on inputs and its utilisation of final products is not required under Cenvat. The rules do not provide for segregated credits, depending upon inputs and final products made from the inputs - Indian Aluminium v. CCE (2001) 137 ELT 1092 (CEGAT).

No one to one correlation is required for taking Cenvat credit - CCE v. National Trading Co. - (1996) 83 ELT 636 (CEGAT) - both members agreed on this point, though they differed on other points.

In CCE v. Bajaj Tempo Ltd. 2005 (1) STT 242 (CESTAT), it was held that credit of duty paid on inputs meant for 'matador' vehicle can be used for payment of duty on other motor vehicle 'tempo-traveller'.

CBE&C, vide para 2(viii) of circular No. 33/33/94-CX dated 4-5-1994 has confirmed that there is no 1:1 correlation between input and final product under the Cenvat scheme for utilisation of credit.

Credit by assessee who is manufacturer as well as service provider - Cenvat credit of manufacturing activity can be utilised for payment of service tax since there is no such restriction in Cenvat Credit Rules or CBEC manual - CCE v. Nahar Industrial Enterprises Ltd. (2007) 10 STT 117 (CESTAT SMB) - followed in CCE v. Vardhman Spinning (2008) 14 STT 503 (CESTAT SMB).

Cenvat credit of input service tax can be utilized for payment of excise duty - S S Engineers v. CCE (2015) 317 ELT 597 (CESTAT).

There is no provision in Cenvat credit rules for segregation of input services, which are utilised in manufacture or to provide output service - Forbes Marshall v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 571 (CESTAT SMB).

Meaning of 'exempted services'

27.4 Rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules defines exempted service as follows :

"Exempted service" means a —

(1)

taxable service which is exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon; or

(2)

service, on which no service tax is leviable under section 66B of the Finance Act; or

(3)

taxable service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken;

but shall not include a service

(a)

which is exported in terms of rule 6A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 or

(b)

by way of transportation of goods by a vessel from customs station of clearance in India to a place outside India [The words in italics are inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2016]

Services on which no tax is payable are also 'exempt services' - For purpose of the definition of 'exempted services', services on which no service tax is leviable are also 'exempted services'. Thus, if a particular service is not taxable under present provisions of Finance Act, 1994, it will be 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

It has been clarified that export of service will not be treated as exempted service for rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules - para 6 of CBE&C Circular No. 868/6/2008-CX dated 9-5-2008.

Activity which is not 'service' is also 'exempted service' - 'Exempted service' shall include an activity which has been defined as 'not service' under section 65(44) of Finance Act, 1994, if such activity has used inputs or input services - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016 and amended w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

Meaning of 'if such activity has used inputs or input services' - In my view, activities like interest, dividend, deposits, loans etc. do not use inputs or input services in real sense of the term. Hence, these should not be treated as 'exempted service'.

Thus, trading of goods, transactions in immovable property, transaction in money and services provided by employee to employer will be 'exempted service' [The provision that service provided by employee to employer is 'exempted service' for rule 6(1) does not seem to make sense, as really in that case, assessee (employer) is service receiver and not service provider at all] - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such activity shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 4 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Trading of goods or securities is 'exempted service'

27.4-1 A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods or immovable property. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods or immovable property. The sale may be within India or outside.

For example, authorised service station of automobiles is also selling spare parts. A brand name owner manufactures some goods and also gets similar goods manufactured from ancillary units.

A Builder/Developer may also be trading in land or other immovable property.

Obviously, there will be many common input services.

As per section 66D(e) of Finance Act, 1994, trading of goods has been specified as service in negative list.

Thus, trading of goods is 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

In case of traded goods, the value of exempt service shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards the purchases) or ten percent of the cost of goods sold, whichever is more [Explanation I(c) after rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2011].

Thus, if the sale price is Rs. 100 and the purchase cost is Rs. 60, the difference of Rs. 40 will be considered as value of 'exempted service'. If purchase price is Rs. 95, value of exempted service will be Rs. 10 (difference or 10% whichever is more).

Rule 6(3) did not apply to Input Service Distributor? - As per para 5 of CBE&C circular No. 868/6/2008-CX dated 9-5-2008, ISD does not provide any service and is like a trader. Hence, question of availing either of option [of rule 6(3)(i) or rule 6(3)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules] does not arise.

However, in Colgate Palmolive v. CCE (2011) 31 STT 214 = 10 taxmann.com 168 (CESTAT), it has been held that if assessee is manufacturing both exempted goods as well as taxable goods, assessee is required to reverse Cenvat credit on proportionate basis while distributing Cenvat credit.

In any case, this case law is not relevant in respect of Cenvat credit availed on or after 1-4-2012.

10.1-6 Responsibilities of Input Service Distributor

The input service distributor has to submit half yearly return within one month from close of the half year, in prescribed form ST-3 [rule 9(10)]

Penalty can be imposed on the input service distributor under rule 15 for taking wrong credit. Credit wrongly taken can be recovered under rule 14.

Even if the capital goods are received during the period when his turnover was less than Rs. 150 lakhs, he can utilise credit only after his turnover crosses Rs. 150 lakhs (He should make suitable entries in Cenvat credit on capital goods account, but actually start debiting the account only after turnover crosses Rs. 150 lakhs) - confirmed in - Bell Packaging (India) P Ltd. Turnover of both units to be considered parallely to calculate limit of 150 lakhs - In CCE v. Mahavir Textiles (2012) 285 ELT 215 (CESTAT), assessee had two units. SSI exemption limit has to be calculated only from beginning of the year

32.3-1 SSI exemption notifications clearly use the words 'first clearances on or after 1st April in any financial year'. Hence, in Ramakrishna Engineering Works v. CCE - (1996) 83 ELT 346 (CEGAT 3 member bench), it has been held that all clearance from 1st April in chronological order have to be considered for purpose of calculation of exemption limit of Rs. 150 lakhs. However in CCE v. Neo Era Agro Engg 2000(124) ELT 665 (CEGAT), it was held that decision in Ramakrishna Engineering Works in no more a good law as decision in another contrary case i.e. El. P. Em. Industries v. CCE 1989(43) ELT 559 (CEGAT) was upheld by Supreme Court - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC - (2001) 127 ELT A47. - same view in CCE v. Mech Engineers 2001(127) ELT 145 (CEGAT). the ISD. It shall be subject to Rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 and depending upon the option exercised under the Rule 6 due reversals will be required to be effected - Para 10.3.4 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012. [In my view, such reversal should be done at the factory level or place where separate service tax registration has been obtained]. What to do if assessee has more than one offices registered as ISD - If assessee has many offices registered as ISD, calculating such ratio for every office would be very cumbersome. My suggestion for distribution - In my view, such month/quarter wise calculations are not very easy. Hence, for the month/quarter of March (or any year end month or quarter), the distribution should be kept pending and should be done only after the balance sheet is finalised.

Meaning of 'unit' -'Unit' includes premises of provider of output service and the premises of a manufacturer, including the factory, whether registered or otherwise.

Meaning of total turnover - Total turnover means sum of value of (a) all excisable goods cleared during the relevant period including exempted goods, dutiable goods and excisable goods exported (b) export turnover of services and value of all other services during relevant period and (c) all inputs removed as such under rule 3(5) against an invoice during relevant period.

Export turnover of services = payments received during the relevant period for export service + export services whose provision has been completed for which payment has been received in advance in any period prior to the relevant period - advances received for export of services for which the provision of service has not been completed during the relevant period.

[In short, value of services actually provided for which payment has been actually received] [Definitions under rule 5 made applicable to rule 7 also]

10.1-5 Manner of distribution of credit by ISD upto 1-4-2012

The 'Input Service Distributor' may distribute Cenvat Credit in respect of service tax, among its manufacturing units or providing output service. The credit distributed should not be more than the service tax paid. If an input service is attributable to service use in a unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services, the credit of such credit of service tax shall not be distributed [rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 1-4-2012].

Entire service tax credit could be utilised in one factory - Even if assessee had various factories, in my view, it was perfectly legal to utilise entire credit of service tax in only one of the factories, for the following reasons - (a) Definition of 'input service' was very wide. Any service in relation to business of assessee is eligible 'input service'. Any relation with 'manufacture' or 'provision of output service' was not required (b) Cenvat Rules do not require one-to-one relationship between input goods/service and final product/output services (c) Even provisions relating to 'Input Service Distributor' do not require distribution/allocation of credit in any particular ratio (d) Entire credit could be 'distributed' from HO to main factory itself, as law does not require distribution in any specific ratio. (e) In the worst possible situation, it can be considered a procedural lapse for which penalty may be imposable. It could not result in loss of substantial benefit of Cenvat credit, if basic eligibility of Cenvat credit is not in doubt. (f) The entire exercise would be revenue neutral.

CCE (2009) 23 STT 381 = 33 VST 754 (CESTAT), it has been confirmed that Input Service Distributor can distribute entire credit to only one of its unit, even if services are for both the units - followed in Asian Paints v. CCE (2010) 28 STT 367 (CESTAT SMB) - quoted with approval in Anglo French Drugs v. CCE (2011) 267 ELT 113 (CESTAT), while granting stay.

Contrary decisions - In P V Singhvi v. CCE (2004) 171 ELT 24 (CESTAT), disallowance of Cenvat credit was held valid. In CCE v. Inductotherm (2013) 39 STT 141 = 29 taxmann.com 281 = 283 ELT 359 (Guj HC DB), assessee paid excise duty on activity which was not manufacture, through Cenvat credit (presumably to utilise Cenvat credit which was otherwise not utilisable). It was held that duty collected from purchaser is payable under section 11D of CEA and Cenvat credit is not available (double whammy).

No Cenvat credit to assessee or the customer if assessee pays duty on unconditionally exempted goods - It has been clarified that if assessee still pays duty on goods which are unconditionally exempted, the amount paid is not 'duty'. Hence, the buyer will not be eligible for Cenvat credit of such amount. Further, the person paying excise duty will not be eligible for Cenvat Credit of duty paid on inputs. Further, the assessee is required to deposit the duty charged with Central Government, in view section 11D of Central Excise Act - CBE&C circular No. 940/01/2011-CX dated 14-1-2011

Entire Cenvat credit even if duty payable on final product lower than input credit available

24.1-9A In CCE v. Camphor Allied Products (2015) 51 GST 259 = 57 taxmann.com 154 (All HC DB), it was held that entire Cenvat credit on inputs is available even if excise duty payable on final product was lower than input Cenvat credit available.

Registration and eligibility of Cenvat credit are independent issues

24.1-10 Cenvat Credit rules nowhere state registration as a condition for availing Cenvat credit.

In J R Herbal Care v. CCE (2010) 253 ELT 321 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that there is no provision in law that Cenvat credit is not available to unregistered manufacturer.

There is no provision in Cenvat Credit Rules that Cenvat credit is not available prior to registration and hence assessee is eligible even in respect of period prior to registration - I Knowledge Factory v. CCE (2011) 30 STT 177 = 42 VST 477 (CESTAT SMB) * Imagination Technologies v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 227 (Mag) = 11 taxmann.com 410 (CESTAT) * Well Known Polyesters v.
