Rule 6, read with rule 2(d) and rule 2(e), of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Stay Order - Assessee was importing software and selling them : (a) as such or (b) after loading on computer, etc. or (c) using them for providing taxable output services - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on import of software - Department argued that trading in computer, etc. was an 'exempted service'; hence, software used therefor was ineligible for credit and therefore, credit was reversible - Where assessee could not correlate procurement and supply of software as such, assessee reversed credit - HELD : In any case, assessee had paid more service tax on supply of software than what they had taken credit on procurement of software - Hence, assessee was eligible for waiver of pre-deposit [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

I. Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2000 to March 2007 - Department denied credit on ground that assessee did not maintain separate accounts for input services used for taxable and exempted services and input service tax credit had been availed/utilised in excess of 20 per cent of credit taken in contravention of rule 6(3)(c) - HELD : Cap of 20 per cent was applicable on service tax payable and not on service tax credit actually availed - What was restricted was only utilisation of credit and not taking credit per se; credit taken could be carried forward - When cap was removed on 1-4-2008, assessee was eligible to utilise credit also - Further, utilising credit in excess of limit would attract only interest liability; entire service tax itself could not be denied to assessee - Hence, matter was remanded back to adjudicating authority to re-examine matter in light of CBEC circular dated 21-11-2008 [Para 5.1] [In favour of assessee]ST : Utilising Cenvat credit in excess of limit fixed under rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 would attract only interest liability; entire credit itself cannot be denied to assessee  ST : Break bulk fee and freight rebate are not, prima facie, liable to service tax under Custom House Agent's services and Business Auxiliary Services respectively  ST : Commission and incentive received from airlines for booking of cargo space is, prima facie, liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : CCX fee received from foreign principal for purpose of delivering documents to customers in India, to collect and remit freight charges due to overseas company is liable to service tax under Business Auxiliary services  ST : Cenvat Credit cannot be denied for procedural violations

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Appellant had entered into a business solutions agreement and another business promotion agreement with Amazon as per which appellant had to store various merchandizes in Amazon warehouse and facilitate dispatch of goods - Service tax was collected from appellant by Amazon for warehousing services provided to appellant - As per business promotion agreement entered with Amazon, appellant had to sell different products at prices fixed by Amazon through various promotion sales - Appellant was engaged not only in trading but also providing taxable service - Appellant utilized input services provided by Amazon for engaging in trading as well as providing taxable service - Appellant availed input tax credit for period commencing from April 2014 and took credit upto October 2015 on service tax collected from it by Amazon on business support service and storage and warehousing services - Since appellant had utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 and as credit reversed was in excess of proportionate credit to be reversed, it had filed refund claim being balance of credit wrongly reversed (paid in cash) by it - Original authority rejected refund claim entirely - Commissioner (Appeals) held that appellant had to reverse/pay credit along with interest as per rule 6(3A)(i) at rate of 7 per cent of value of exempted services and, therefore, was eligible for refund of only part of amount - Whether view taken by Commissioner (Appeals) that appellant had to reverse credit as per rule 6(3)(i) was against provisions of law - Held, yes - Whether appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i) - Held, yes [Para 5]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Amazon was providing BSS and warehousing services to appellant and appellant having utilized input services for trading (exempted services) as well as taxable output services, it opted for reversal of proportionate credit as provided under rule 6(3A)(ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, appellant would be eligible for refund after reversal/paying of proportionate credit on exempted services by applying rule 6(3)(i)

Rule 6 read with  rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Common input and input service provider providing services taxed on reverse charge basis - Cenvat credit - appellants were aware that supplier of inputs was trader and not manufacturer - invoice issued by trader was not valid for taking credit after omission of Rule 12B of Central Excise Rules, 2002 - credit rightly denied - appeal dismissed (Para 5)

Rule 3 of the  read with Rule 12 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2002 and Ruled 3 and 14 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT credit - Recovery of CENVAT credit wrongly taken respondents were trader and not manufacturer of textiles - on omission of Rule 12B of C.Ex. Rules, 2002 the respondents ceased to be entitled to input credit but continued to pay duty on final product after utilising credit of duty on input stock - since duty paid on final product is more than inadmissible input credit, demand of credit is not sustainable being revenue neutral - Revenue's appeal dismissed (Para 5)

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Common input and inputs services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Cenvat credit - And amending Notification No. 27/2005-CE (NT) dt. 16.5.2005 - Amendment by way of addition of Explanation III to Rule 6 (3) vide notification is effective from 16.5.2005 - Prior to 16.5.2005 a manufacturer producing both dutiable as well as exempted final product and paying 8% or 10% amount on exempted final product, was entitled to take credit on all inputs whether common to both final products or exclusively used in manufacture of exempted goods only (Para 32)

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Catering Services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee took credit of outdoor catering services used to provide food, etc. to its employees - Department denied credit on ground that it had no nexus with manufacture - HELD : Services in question are eligible for input service credit - However, where cost of food is borne by worker, manufacturer cannot take credit of that part of service tax which is borne by consumer - Amendment in rule 2(l) effective from 1-4-2011, could not be applied for earlier periods [Paras 13 to 22] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Rent-a-cab services hired for officials and staff to travel to places in connection with their manufacturing activity, are eligible for credit

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Obligation of a manufacturer or producer of final products and a provider of output service - Period from April 2004 to March 2007 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of cosmetics preparations containing alcohol and also engaged in trading - Assessee took credit of inputs/input services used in said two activities - Department denied such credit and sought reversal under rule 6 - HELD : Cosmetic Preparations containing alcohol were not final product, as they were not excisable goods under Central Excise Act - Hence, inputs/input services used for manufacture of such goods were not eligible for credit - Since assessee was paying 10 per cent of price of such non-excisable goods under rule 6, question of levy of penalty was remanded back to consider whether assessee had any intent to evade payment of duty - Moreover, trading activity is neither an output service nor a final product, hence, assessee was not entitled to avail any Cenvat Credit on inputs/input services used for trading activity - Question as to quantification of reversal to be made in that regard was remanded back to adjudicating authority [Paras 6  7] [In favour of revenue]ST : Goods or services used in manufacture of non-excisable goods and carrying out trading activity are not eligible for Cenvat Credit

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Catering Services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on outdoor catering services provided in factory for employees of factory - Department denied credit on ground that catering/canteen services were not used in or in relation to manufacture - HELD : Impugned credit has been properly availed; however, where cost of food is borne by worker/employee, manufacturer cannot take credit of that part of service tax which is borne by consumer - Substitution of rule 2(l) vide Cenvat Credit (Amendment) Rules, 2011 excluding catering services from scope of input service, would come into effect from 1-4-2011 and cannot be applied for prior period [Paras 6 to 14] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Prior to 1-4-2011, outdoor catering services provided in factory for employees of factory are eligible for input service credit; however, where cost of food is borne by worker/employee, manufacturer cannot take credit of that part of service tax which is borne by consumer

Cenvat credit - Reversal of - Common inputs/input services used for both taxable and exempted final products services - Position prior to 1-4-2016 - Assessee was rendering services to BCCI for organizing IPL T-20 cricket matches under a franchise agreement - Revenue generated from stadium gate receipt/sale of ticket, prize money received from BCCI-IPL and in-stadium sale i.e. stadium revenue could not be considered towards rendering of any services hence no Cenvat credit was required to be reversed - Moreover, prior to amendment to Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2016, there was no requirement to reverse Cenvat credit on input/input services used in an activity that was not a service [Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004] [Paras 5, 5.5 and 5.6] [In favour assessee]

Rule 6  of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Common imputs and input services for taxable and exempt final products and services - Assessment year 2008-09 - During year 2008-09, assessee provided taxable as well as exempted services - Adjudicating Authority having found that assessee had not maintained separate accounts, as required under rule 6(2), confirmed demand as per provisions of rule 6(3)(i) on value of exempted services - Commissioner (Appeals) having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest held that assessee had satisfied conditions in view of retrospective amendment carried out to provisions of rule 6 by Finance Act, 2010 and accordingly set aside impugned order - Against impugned order, revenue filed appeal and assessee filed cross objections - Whether in view of fact that Commissioner (Appeals) had already allowed benefit and further in view of complexity of nature, as a special case, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone for year 2008-09 subject to condition that it would file a letter rectifying deficiencies in letter of option given by it earlier as contemplated in rule 6(3A) - Held, yes [Paras 17 and 18][In favour of assessee]CENVAT: Where assessee, during year 2008-09, provided taxable as well as exempted services and Adjudicating Authority having noticed that it had not maintained separate accounts confirmed demand on value of exempted services and further Appellate Authority having noticed that assessee had reversed proportionate credit on value of exempted services subsequently with interest, set aside impugned order, assessee would be eligible to reverse proportionate credit attributable to clearances to Jammu  Kashmir State alone

Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used in dutiable as well as exempted goods - Reversal of proportionate credit - It has been held by CESTAT in Reliance Industries Limited [2019 (28) G.S.T.L. 96 (Tribunal)] that for purpose of calculation of Cenvat credit reversal, "Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods -CESTAT further held that Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods - Substitution of sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6 ibid by Notification No. 13/2016-C.E. (N.T.) clarificatory and therefore retrospective in nature - Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 4.3] Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used in dutiable as well as exempted goods - Reversal of proportionate credit by Input Service Distributor (ISD) - Services used for Central depot and reversal made by Input Service Distributor unit - Assessee at ISD level in-fact reversed excess CENVAT credit as certified by independent chartered accountant - That being so, demand of reversal again from recipient manufacturing units of assessee cannot be justified, for the reason no inadmissible credit distributed by ISD - Rule 3 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Paras 4.5  4.6]

Rule 2(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Consultancy/Legal Services - Period from 2006-07 to 2009-10 - Assessee took credit of service tax paid on legal services received from a Chartered Accountant relating to sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters - Department denied credit on ground that said services were not taxable prior to 1-3-2011 - HELD : Service provider had discharged service tax liability under 'Chartered Accountant Services' - Since said services were in respect of sales tax matters, banking facilities etc., they were in line of manufacturing of assessee - Classification of services cannot be changed at end of service recipient -Hence, impugned credit was valid [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Legal services received from a Chartered Accountant relating to sales tax matters, banking facilities and other legal consultation in various matters are eligible for input service credit

Cenvat Credit -  Common inputs used in dutiable as well as exempted goods - Reversal of proportionate credit - It has been held by CESTAT in Reliance Industries Limited [2019 (28) G.S.T.L. 96 (Tribunal)] that for purpose of calculation of Cenvat credit reversal, "Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods -CESTAT further held that Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods - Substitution of sub-rule (3A) of Rule 6 ibid by Notification No. 13/2016-C.E. (N.T.) clarificatory and therefore retrospective in nature - Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. [Para 4.3]EXCISE/ST/VAT : Total Cenvat Credit" for purpose of formula under Rule 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 is only total Cenvat credit of common input services and not Cenvat credit on input/input service exclusively used for manufacture of dutiable goods; Government had no intention to deny Cenvat credit on input/input service even though used in dutiable goods   EXCISE/ST/VAT : When assessee at ISD level in-fact reversed excess CENVAT credit as certified by independent chartered accountant, demand of reversal again from recipient manufacturing units of assessee cannot be justified, for the reason no inadmissible credit distributed by ISD

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted and dutiable goods or exempted and taxable services, obligation of assessee - Periods 2008-09 to 2009-10 - Assessee provided dutiable and exempted services and also availed Cenvat credit on certain common input services - It opted for payment at prescribed percentage on value of exempted services and also paid amounts for earlier periods - Revenue held that assessee could not exercise option retrospectively for earlier period and hence credit taken was improper - Whether there is no bar for making payments as per prescribed percentages for prior period as it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input service credit pertaining to dutiable and exempted services and, therefore, assessee's actions of paying amounts for past period was justified - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]CENVAT: There is no bar for making as per prescribed percentage payment on value of exempted services for prior period where it may not be feasible to segregate quantum of input services pertaining to dutiable  exempted services

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Input service - Travelling services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was providing Management Consultancy and Insurance Auxiliary Services - Assessee took input service credit of Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent Service - Department denied credit on ground that both these services are used for employees' benefit - Assessee argued that : (a) Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for present case relating to period prior to 1-4-2011, credit is allowed; (b) air travel agent's services were availed for travel of employees for business purposes - HELD : Rent-a-cab and Air Travel Agent services, though used by employees, are for performance of assessee's business - Hence, both services are input service - Further, expenses towards both services was booked as expenditure in profit and loss account - Rent-a-cab service was not excluded from definition of input service; hence, prior to 1-4-2011, credit was admissible [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Rent-a-cab service is expressly excluded from input service from 1-4-2011, but, for period prior to 1-4-2011, said service availed for employees for business purposes, is eligible for credit; similarly, air travel agent's services availed for travel of employees for business purposes is also eligible for credit

I. Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 64(1) of the Finance Act, 1994 - CENVAT Credit - Period April 2007 to September 2011 - Assessee, a telecom service provider, having centralized registration at Bhubaneswar, availed CENVAT credit on capital goods installed in state of Jammu  Kashmir - Whether obtaining centralized registration of Bhubaneswar did not mean that service provider (branch office) in Jammu  Kashmir started providing services from Bhubaneswar and further branch office in Jammu  Kashmir was not required to be included by assessee in centralized registration from where no taxable service was provided by virtue of section 64(1) of Finance Act, 1994 - Held, yes - Whether since branch office in Jammu  Kashmir was not required to discharge service tax by virtue of section 64(1), all capital goods installed there had to be considered ineligible for taking credit - Held, yes [Para 5.1] [In favour of revenue]Cenvat: When assessee's branch office in Jammu  Kashmir was not required to discharge service tax by virtue of section 64(1) of Finance Act, 1994, all capital goods installed there were ineligible for taking credit  Cenvat: Cenvat Credit Rules do not apply on cenvat credit of service tax in state of Jammu  Kashmir and, therefore, credit taken with respect to services availed in state of Jammu  Kashmir has to be denied  Cenvat: Where details prescribed in rule 4A(1) of Service Tax Rules are available in a document, it will be a proper document for availing cenvat credit  Service Tax: Where assessee availed cenvat credit on capital goods/services installed/availed in Jammu  Kashmir by including premises of JK in centralized registration though no taxable services were provided in state of JK, by virtue of section 64(1) of Finance Act, 1994, extended period was applicable to demand duty tax

Rule 3, read with rule 11, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - General - Period from 1-7-2003 to 10-9-2004 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of Power Distribution Transformers and HV/LV coils - It availed Cenvat credit on input service - Revenue issued a show-cause notice raising a demand alleging that service tax credit lying in Cenvat account as on 10-9-2004 was wrongly utilized for payment of central excise duty instead of payment of service tax as provided under rule 11 - Whether since as per transitional provision under rule 11, credit can be utilized in accordance with rule 3(4) for payment of any duty of excise on any final product, allegation made in show-cause notice was not correct - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, denial of credit was not sustainable - Held, yes [Para 6] Circulars and Notifications : Notification No. 23/2004-CE (NT), dated 10-9-2004

Rule 2(l) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Travelling Services - Period prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee took credit of rent-a-cab services hired for their officials and staff to travel to places in connection with their manufacturing activity - Department denied said credit on ground that it was not eligible as input service - HELD : Said activity was necessary for manufacturing purposes and could not be considered as welfare measure - Hence, same was eligible for input service credit - Amendment in rule 2(l) effective from 1-4-2011, could not be applied for earlier periods [Paras 19 to 22] [In favour of assessee]

Rule 7 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Manner of Distribution of Credit by Input Service Distributor - Assessee availed consultancy services for its Vadodara and Silvassa units - Since majority of services were used for Vadodara unit, assessee took entire credit at Vadodara - Department denied proportionate credit to Vadodara unit - Assessee argued that procedure for proportionate credit under Input Service Distributor, was brought only from 2012; hence, prior thereto, credit could not be denied - HELD: Prior to 17-03-2012, there was no restriction on distribution of credit and hence, assessee was eligible to take credit on entire amount in one unit [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]

II. Rule  3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - General - Period from 2005-06 to 2011-12 - Assessee had wrongly availed cenvat credit of duty paid on inputs and input services and availed abatement under notification no. 1/06 ST dated 1-3-2006 in respect of mandap keeper service simultaneously - However, they reversed whole disputed cenvat credit along with interest - Whether in view of total reversal credit availed alongwith interest, their claim for abatement under notification no. 1/06 ST could not have been denied and thus they would be eligible for abated rate of duty - Held, yes [Para 10][In favour of assessee]

Rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - CENVAT Credit - Input service - Stock Broker's Services - Position prior to 1-4-2011 - Assessee was a manufacturer of telecom equipments and was also engaged in providing services in relation to installation, commissioning, maintenance and repair, manpower supply, etc. in respect of its products and also renting of immovable property - Assessee had invested in another telecom company and, later, sold shares of such company and took credit of service tax paid on stock-broker's services used for sale of shares - Assessee argued that sale of shares was an 'activity in relation to business', which provided money to assessee, which was used for various business purposes and, therefore, impugned credit was available - Department denied said credit on ground that said services had no relation with business of manufacture or provision of output service - HELD : On perusal of Memorandum of Association of assessee-company, it was clear that assessee was carrying not only its main objects but was also carrying out objects incidental or ancillary to attainment of main objects - But, it was found by lower authorities that incidental object of investing and dealing in shares did not, in any way, relate to and form part of main business of assessee - In fact, said incidental business was not being actually carried on as a 'business' - Therefore, claim for input service credit was not against any liability arising out of business activity of assessee and was not relatable to business activity of assessee - Accordingly, claim of input service credit was denied [Paras 16 to 20] [In favour of revenue]CENVAT : Where assessee, a manufacturer of telecom equipments, had invested in another telecom company and, later, sold shares therein by availing stock-broker's services, service tax paid on such services could not be allowed as input service credit even prior to 1-4-2011 because such services did not relate to any business activity of assessee

Rule 2(d), read with rule  6, of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat Credit - Exempted Goods - Exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty - Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods - Imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 would not apply thereto [Para 5.2] [In favour of assessee]Cenvat Credit : Exempted goods have to be excisable goods; hence, imported goods, which are traded, cannot be considered as exempted goods and rule 6 of CENVAT Credit rules, 2004 would not apply thereto

Section 16 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 2(1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Input tax credit - Eligibility and conditions for taking credit - Whether cenvat credit of service tax paid on outdoor catering service is not admissible post 1-4-2011 - Held, yes [Para 7.2] [Partly in favour of assessee]GST/EXCISE/ST/VAT : Service Tax paid on outdoor catering service is not eligible for cenvat credit post amendment dated 1-4-2011

Rule 9 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Documents and accounts - Period prior to 16-6-2005 - Whether Cenvat credit of service tax paid by an assessee on ‘Goods transport agency services’ through TR-6 challan, can be availed for period prior to 16-6-2005 - Held, yes [Para 5]

facts.text:
Assessee was manufacturing TV, washing machines, AC, etc. and was also importing said goods for resale.

Assessee took credit of input services pro rata based on turnover ratio attributable to manufacturing business.

Department argued that since 'imported goods' were 'exempted goods', assessee was liable to pay 10 per cent 5 per cent 6 per cent of value of said exempted goods. Department issued notice dated 7-10-2011 invoking extended period to seek demand.

Assessee argued that —

since he was not taking credit relating to 'trading business', rule 6(2) or rule 6(3) were inapplicable ;

since credit as per formula under Rule 6(3A) was merely Rs. 16 lakh, which was not taken; demand of Rs. 297 crore was invalid ;

its procedure of taking credit only on dutiable goods based on turnover ratio was known to department when audit was conducted in 2008 and furthermore, for earlier period, proceedings on same ground had been initiated and were pending before Tribunal; therefore, allegation of suppression was invalid.

Revenue argued that activity of trading could be considered as services and since during material time, it was not a taxable service, it should be construed as 'exempted service'. Since assessee has not maintained any separate account in respect of the dutiable/taxable goods/services and exempted goods/services, payment at 10 per cent/ 5 per cent of the value of the exempted services was to be made under rule 6(3).

Assessee argued that trading was deemed as exempted service only from 1-4-2011; hence, demand for period prior thereto cannot be made on that count.

The appellant was engaged in providing maintenance and repair services and commissioning and installation service of RO systems. It was observed that the appellants were availing the credit on advertising, security, courier, telephone and banking services which were not entirely used in providing ‘maintenance and repair’ services, but also used in trading activity and, therefore, credit of input services which were entirely used in trading activity was not available to the appellants for payment of service tax. The amounts of service tax payable for two half-yearly period were Rs. 34,143 and Rs. 27,315. Total Cenvat credit available to the appellants was Rs. 6,828, i.e., 20 per cent of Rs. 34,143 as per rule 6(3) and Rs. 8,877, i.e., 35 per cent of Rs. 25,363 as per rule 3(5). The balance amount was to be paid by the appellants in cash only.

The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and wrongly availed Cenvat credit of Rs. 43,801.

The lower authorities claimed that appellant should have maintained separate accounts in respect of input services used for trading activity which were liable to service tax and the Cenvat credit availed by the appellant was demanded.

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. During the year 2011-12, it had exported final products manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on import of services received from one 'C' under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A.

The Adjudicating Authority having discovered that the assessee had availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy services for traded goods (exempted goods) rendered by 'C' opined that the assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and the cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods was erroneous and recoverable in terms of rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Thereupon the assessee reversed the cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading of imported goods and also paid interest. It asserted that it was eligible for the cenvat credit in respect of market consultancy services.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of service tax and interest and also imposed equal penalty on the assessee under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original.

On second appeal:

The assessee was registered with the Department for providing taxable services falling under the categories of Consulting Engineer, Maintenance or Repair Services and, Erection, Commissioning and Installation Services. It had entered into a contract with ‘B’ for supply and installation of BTS, Microcell and other Microwave equipments for telecommunication network. The invoice for the supply of telecommunication equipment was issued from its corporate office and the invoice for service portion was issued from its branches. The assessee was taking the Cenvat credit of tax paid on the input services used in the provision of taxable output services as well as the Cenvat credit distributed by its Corporate Office (i.e., input service distributor). It was noticed that the Cenvat credit distributed by the corporate office also pertaining to the input services used exclusively for the procurement of telecommunication equipments. The revenue took a view that the assessee was engaged in the sale of telecommunication equipments from its Corporate Office which was a trading activity and a non-taxable service outside the scope of the Act. Therefore, the trading activity fell within the meaning of exempted services as defined under rule 2(e). According to the revenue as the assessee had not maintained separate records at its Corporate Office for the input services commonly used in the taxable output services provided from the branches or in the exempted services provided from the Corporate Office, it was liable to utilize the Cenvat credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding twenty per cent of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services in terms of rule 6(3)(c). However, the assessee had utilized the entire Cenvat credit available with it towards the discharge of service tax liability on the taxable output services. Thus, the Commissioner confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had utilized excess Cenvat credit which was liable to be recovered from it. Besides that, the Commissioner also confirmed the demand on the ground that the assessee had wrongly availed of the Cenvat credit on insurance service, foreign consultancy service, etc., which were used exclusively in the provision of exempted services and, were utilized towards payment of service tax. The Commissioner also confirmed the demand disallowing the Cenvat credit on the services, viz., flower arrangements, garden maintenance, outdoor catering, real estate agent’s services for residential accommodation of its employees distributed by its Corporate Office on the ground that same could not be termed as input services defined under rule 2(l).

On application :

Facts

The assessee is a trader in personal computers, photocopiers, telecom products and mobile phones etc. and had provided taxable services like Maintenance and Repair; Commissioning and Installation; Leased Circuit; Online Information and Data Processing and Business Auxiliary Services.

Assessee -

availed credit on service tax paid on input services utilized for its trading activities;

utilized credit to an extent not exceeding 35 per cent up to 09-09-2004 and to an extent of 20 per cent thereafter, of the Service tax payable on its taxable output services,

in terms of Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004,

treating trading as an exempted service.

The show-cause notice dated 11-10-2006 alleged that as trading of goods is not a service, this cannot be considered as an exempted service and provisions of the Act and rules thereunder do not apply to trading activities.

The assessee reversed credit availed on service tax incurred by the assessee on sales commission, brokerage, travel agent service, warehouse charges, freight and courier charges, being input services for its trading activities.

The assessee neither responded to the show-cause notice nor attended personal hearing. Hence, the impugned order was passed ex parte.

Revenue's Arguments

Services utilized for trading of computers etc. would not amount to services utilized/consumed in the rendition of output services, since output services were provided after culmination of trading activities i.e. sale and delivery of computers etc. to customers. Input services in respect of which cenvat credit was taken stood utilized prior to delivery of computers and cannot be said to have been consumed/used in relation to rendition of output services;

Since trading is neither a service nor amounts to an exempted service, cenvat credit earned on an input services of trading-cannot be considered as credit earned on exempted service;

Consequently, cenvat credit taken in respect of input services of trading is liable to be reversed in toto and the inadmissible cenvat credit utilized for payment of service tax on taxable output services liable to be recovered, along with interest and penalty;

Since the assessee deliberately availed to disclose availment of cenvat credit on services which were not an input services for its output services, assessee contravened Rules 3 and 4 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 and the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, with an intent to evade payment of Service tax and therefore the extended period is invocable and interest and penalty also leviable.

Assessee's Arguments

The assessee submitted that -

all taxable services were provided by the assessee only in relation to computers, photocopiers etc. sold to various customers;

commissioning, installation, maintenance and repair services etc. were also services provided in relation to these traded goods;

Rule 2(b) of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 defines 'Input Services' as any service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service;

transportation of goods and the other services utilized for despatching goods to customers premises, is integral to the post-trading rendition of taxable services such as installation, commissioning, repair, maintenance etc.; and

thus, credit taken is unexceptionable.

The assessee alternatively claimed that since credit was utilized only to the extent of 35 per cent or 20 per cent of the payable service tax, as the case may be, interest should be calculated only on amount of credit actually utilized; that there is a distinction between taking of credit and utilization of credit and it is utilization alone that results in lesser remittance of tax in cash to Government and not taking of credit in assessee's books. Therefore, interest should be calculated only on the amount actually utilized, if wrongly utilized, but not on the gross credit wrongly availed.

No penalty should be imposed since availment of credit on the assumption that trading is an exempted activity was on account of interpretation and penalty is leviable only for wilful and deliberate conduct and not where availment of credit is on the basis of a mistaken but plausible interpretation of relevant provisions.

Issue Involved

Whether credit was rightly claimed and reversed ?

It also availed cenvat credit of service tax on 'rent-a-cab service'.

He also held that the assessee was not eligible to cenvat credit of service tax paid on 'rent-a-cab service'.

Thus, a show-cause notice was issued proposing to recover irregular CENVAT credit along with interest and penalties. The show-cause notice was confirmed by the original authorities.

The assessee submitted that credit availed by it was proper and correct inasmuch as it was eligible to avail credit for the period prior to registration as per CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 which did not impose any time limit nor make registration a pre-condition for availment of CENVAT credit and further that the services which were exported could not be termed as exempted services to deny the CENVAT credit. Assessee also raised the ground that there were no restriction under the statute for utilization of CENVAT credit towards payment of service tax on import of services and further the demand of service tax was more than the amount proposed in the show-cause notice, which was illegal.

On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the order-in-original.

On appeal:

w.e.f. 1-3-2008, and just because in course of processing of the raw menthol for manufacture of menthol crystals BP/USP and Menthol BP/USP, some residual oil is obtained which on further processing is converted into flavouring materials which are dutiable, it cannot be said that the provisions of rule 11(3) read with rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would not be applicable. Assessee's argument that materials in the instant case were not exclusively and solely used in the manufacture of exempt goods and therefore, the provisions of rule 11 (3) would not apply, is unfounded, fallacious and patently wrong as sub-rule (3) (ii) of rule 11 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not make any exception in respect of export goods as is evident from the words "whether cleared for home consumption or for export" in this sub-rule.

In view of section 5A(1A), exemption was mandatory. A harmonious construction of section 5A (1A) of Central Excise Act, 1944 with rule 6 (6) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be that the term "excisable goods" in this sub-rule should be read as "dutiable goods".

Notification No. 24/10-CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from duty, other than the goods cleared by 100% EOU, is not allowed under bond should be treated as retrospective amendment.

As per proviso to rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 no refund shall be allowed if the manufacturer inter alia claims rebate in respect of such duty. In the instant case, no segregation of duty paid on inputs was made in reference to the final products and the refund and rebate were claimed from a common basket of input credit.

Menthol falling under heading 29061100 of the Central Excise Tariff happened to be both input as also the export product in the subject case involving no manufacturing process in between. As per rule 3 (5) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 to which when Cenvat credit availed inputs or capital goods are cleared as such, an amount equal to the credit availed in respect of such inputs or capital goods shall be payable under the cover of invoices.

It was open to the assessee to claim rebate of duty of the un-utilised input credit under rule 18 of the Central Excise Rules read with Notification No. 21/04-CE (NT) instead of seeking refund under rule 5 of the Cenvat Credit Rules. It is inexplicable as to why the assessee avoided such obvious legitimate course for tax neutralization in respect of their exempted products which were exported.

The inputs in this case had been received from four Jammu units availing of exemption under Notification No. 56/02-CE, namely. Subsequent investigations revealed that these from Jammu suppliers of inputs had made only paper transactions with the assessee to generate Cenvat credit based on bogus invoices without any manufacture.

Assessee's Arguments

While the Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP, became fully exempt from duty w.e.f. 1-3-2008 under Notification No. 4/08-CE, the other final products remained dutiable. However, all the final products whether exempted or dutiable were being exported out of India. While Menthol/Menthol Crystals, BP/USP were being exported under bond without payment of duty under rule 19 of Central Excise Rules, 2002, the other final products flavouring agents were being cleared on payment of duty and were being exported under rebate claim.

When inputs are used in manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted final products and the exempted final products are exported out of India, the provisions of rule 6 (6) (V) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 would be applicable and the bar of rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules and the liability created under rule 6 (3) (b) would not be attracted.

The words "excisable goods" in rule 6 (6) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 are wide enough to include both dutiable as well as exempted goods.

Amendment to Notification No. 42/01- CE (NT) dated 26-6-2001 by Notification No. 24/10 - CE (NT) dated 26-5-2010 providing that the export of excisable goods which are chargeable to nil rate of duty or are fully exempted from payment of duty, other than the goods cleared by a 100% EOU, shall not be allowed under this notification cannot be given retrospective effect, as this amendment restricts the benefits.

Rule 11 (3) (ii) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 does not apply when a manufacturer manufacturers dutiable as well as exempted final products out of common Cenvat credit availed inputs.

Facts

The assessee was engaged in providing the services of Maintenance and Repairs, Erection, Commissioning & Installation services, Man Power Recruitment/Supply services.

On the ground that during the period from 2003-04 to 2005-06, the assessee had collected the Service Tax from the customers but not paid the same to the Department, proceedings were initiated.

Assessee did not contest the Service Tax liability but, after issue of Show Cause Notice, filed the ST 3 returns claiming CENVAT Credit on capital goods and debited same towards payment of Service Tax and sought to carry forward balance of credit.

The Department allowed credit of capital goods received on or after 10-9-2004, but, denied credit of capital goods received prior thereto.

Commissioner (Appeals) allowed credit of capital goods received prior to 10-9-2004 as well.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee was eligible for credit ?

During the period April 2008 to March 2011 the appellant/assessee received services from 'C' Ltd. The assessee made alterations in the invoices with respect to the quantity of service availed and the rate per unit of the service. This was done to reconcile the total amount of work done in their records. However, the amounts of service tax paid on those invoices were not altered.

The assessee's claim for Cenvat credit on such invoices containing alterations was rejected by revenue authorities.

On appeal:

The assessee was registered with the service tax department for providing services under the category of 'Port services', 'Goods Transport Services', 'Management Consultancy', 'Consulting Engineering Services', 'Sponsorship services' and 'Storage & warehousing services'. As the assessee was paying service tax on all the above services, it was availing the benefit of Cenvat credit of service tax paid on various inputs and input services utilized by it for providing output services. The Cenvat credit of duty paid on various input services are also being availed by it. The revenue held that since as per provisions of rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 in force up to 31-3-2008 assessee was entitled to avail credit up to 20 per cent, excess credit was not allowable. After reversing said credit, the revenue also imposed penalty on the assessee. The Commissioner however dropped penalty proceeding observing that since entire credit stands paid back by assessee much before issuance of show-cause notice and inasmuch as interest on the said amount was neither contemplated nor paid at stage, no penalty should be imposed upon assessee in view of the provisions of section 80.

On revenue's appeal:

Facts

•

Assessee was engaged in providing Construction of Complex Services, Commercial or Industrial Construction Service and Works Contract Services.

•

Under works contract services, assessee was paying service tax on full value and availing CENVAT credit benefit.

•

But, it was paying tax on abated value under Notification No. 1/2006-ST on two construction services on condition of non-availment of credit.

•

Assessee utilized CENVAT credit account for discharging service tax on two construction services on abated value.

•

Department argued that tax on two construction services could not be paid out of utilization of centralized CENVAT credit balance.

•

Department also alleged that assessee was not maintaining separate account of input/input service received by them in respect of services on which abatement had been claimed.

Issue Involved

•

Whether CENVAT credit balance could be utilized to pay service tax on abatement value of two construction services ?

held.text:
I. Trading an exempted service only from 1-4-2011

Provisions of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, which came into force with effect from 16-08-2002 govern the entitlement to availment and utilization of cenvat credit up to 9-09-2004, on which date the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 came into force. The 2004 Rules govern the field since 10-09-2004. [Para 5]

Under the Credit Rules, 2002 input service is defined in rule 2(c) as any taxable service received and consumed by a service provider in relation to rendering of output service. Rule 3(1) provided that an output service provider shall be allowed to take credit (service tax credit) of the service tax paid on input service, in the enumerated manner. Sub-clause (a) of this Rule provides that where an input service falls in the same category of taxable service as the output service, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 16-08-2002; sub-clause (b) stipulates that in any other case, service tax credit shall be allowed to be taken on such input service for which invoice, bill or challan is issued on or after 14-05-2003. Sub rule (2) of Rule 3 provides that for the purpose of these rules, two services shall be deemed to be falling in the same category of taxable service, if the input service or output service fall in the same sub-clause of clause (105) of Section 65 of the Act.

Sub-rule (4) of rule 3 states that where a service provider avails credit on any input service and renders output services which are chargeable to service tax as well as exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be, he shall maintain separate accounts for receipt and consumption of input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of taxable output services and input services meant for consumption in relation to rendering of exempted or non-taxable services, as the case may be. Sub-rule (5) of rule 3 enacts that where a service provider opts not to maintain separate accounts, as stipulated in sub-rule (4), he shall be allowed to utilize service tax credit for payment of service tax on any output service only to an extent of an amount not exceeding 35 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on such output services. [Para 6]

On a true and fair construction of the relevant provisions of the Credit Rules, 2002, it is apparent that credit could be taken on an input service falling in the same category of taxable service as the output service in respect of which the service tax liability arises and discharged from the available credit. It is axiomatic that trading in goods is neither a taxable service and could not, in the absence of a legislative/statutory fiction provided, capable of being construed as an exempted service. [Para 7]

Rule 6 of the Credit Rules, 2004 sets out the obligations of a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. Sub-rule (1) provides that no cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or exempted services except in circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). Sub-rule (2) enjoins maintenance of separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of input or input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products or in providing output service; and the quantity of input spent for use in the manufacture of exempted goods or services and authorizes taking of cenvat credit only on that quantity of input or input services which are intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods or in providing taxable output services. Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 carves out specified exclusions to the requirements set out in sub-rule (2). Sub-clause (c) of rule 6(3) stipulates that the provider of an output service shall utilise credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9]

The goods which the assessee had traded are imported goods. As per the definition of exempted goods under rule 2(d) of CCR exempted goods means excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-C.E., dated 1-3-2011 is availed.

Thus, exempted goods have to be excisable goods. By no stretch of imagination imported goods which are traded can be considered as exempted goods. If that be so, the question of invoking the provisions of rule 6(2) and 6(3) for payment of a sum at the rate of 10 per cent/5 per cent on the value of the exempted goods would not arise at all. On this ground alone the impugned notice and the order is not sustainable in law. [Para 5.2]

Secondly, as per rule 6(2) maintenance of separate accounts is envisaged only when a manufacturer or provider of output service avails CENVAT credit. In the present case, the assessee has not availed any CENVAT credit at all in respect of input services relating to the traded goods. Therefore, question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise at all. Consequently provision of sub-rule (3) of the said rule 6 mandating payment of an amount equal to 10 per cent/5 per cent of the value of the exempted goods and exempted service would also not apply.

Even assuming but not admitting that the assessee has availed input service credit on both dutiable/exempted goods and taxable/exempted service, rule 6(3A) which came into force w.e.f. 1-4-2008 provides for reversal of credit on the input service attributable to exempted goods/services on a proportionate basis based on the turnover. In the present case, the assessee has precisely done that ab initio and has not taken any credit in respect of input services attributable to the traded goods. Calculation done by the assessee has not been disputed by the revenue and the revenue has not shown that the credit taken by the assessee in respect of input services in relation to manufactured goods was in excess of what was eligible to be taken. Therefore, in the absence of any evidence led by Revenue proving that the assessee has taken ineligible credit, the question of assessee violating the provisions of Rule 6 of the CCR, 2004 would not arise at all. [Para 5.3]

If the assessee reversed input service tax credit attributable to trading activities according to standard accounting principles, the same would suffice for satisfying the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6. [Para 5.4]

As regards the wrong availment of credit during the period 2005-08, another show-cause notice has already been issued to the assessee which has been adjudicated and pending before Tribunal. Thus, the department was fully aware of the practices followed by the assessee and has also approved of the same. In view of the above, invocation of the extended period of time to demand service tax is also not sustainable in law. [Para 5.5]

20 per cent of the amount of service tax payable on a taxable output service. [Para 8]

The 2004 Credit Rules were amended with effect from 01-04-2011, by Notification No. 3/2011-CE (NT). To the extent relevant for this lis, by an Explanation added to Rule 2 of the 2004 Rules, it was clarified by this amendment that 'exempted services' include 'trading'. [Para 9] From the provisions of both, the Credit Rules, 2002 and the Credit Rules, 2004 it is clear that trading is neither a service nor an exempted service. Therefore no credit of the service tax paid on taxable input services used for trading could be taken and utilized for remittance of service tax on taxable services provided by the assessee, even for discharging a percentage (35 per cent or 20 per cent, as a case may be) of the service tax liability on the taxable service provided.

The Explanation added in 2011 though stated to be clarificatory in character can have only a prospective effect since the Finance Act does not authorize rules to be made with retrospective effect. Therefore, trading would be comprehended within the scope of an exempted service only with effect from 01.04.2011, the date of coming into force of the Explanation added to rule 2 of the 2004 Credit Rules. [Para 10]

The assessee not only availed cenvat credit of input services used/ consumed for its trading, by debiting in its cenvat credit account to that extent but had also utilized the credit for discharging its service tax liability for having provided taxable services, to the extent of 35 per cent up to 10-09-2004 and 20 per cent thereafter of the service tax payable on such taxable services, clearly contrary to the provisions of the 2002 Credit Rules and the 2004 Credit Rules, as the case may be. [Para 11]

II. Invocation of extended period valid :

Show-cause notices in both cases were issued invoking the extended period of limitation on the ground that the assessee had deliberately failed to disclose availment of cenvat credit utilized for trading which clearly does not amount to input service used for providing taxable or exempted services; and since trading would not in any event be considered an exempted service. The assessee's contention that 'this is a bona fide interpretational error on the part of the assessee and therefore invocation of the extended period is not justifiable' does not merit acceptance. Till the fiction was introduced that trading is an exempted service, by the Explanation introduced with effect from 01-04-2011 in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, trading which is a sale of goods could not have been considered as a service, a taxable service or an exempted service. The input services (on which cenvat credit was earned by the assessee) were consumed for its trading activities and could not have been availed or taken for discharging service tax on the services provided by the assessee, after the trading activity. There is no scope for any interpretational misconception on this aspect. Invocation of the extended period is therefore without error. Trading is purchase and sale of goods, covered by sales tax law and cannot be considered a service or an exempted service. [Para 13]

III. Option to pay penalty at 25 per cent of duty/tax granted, as said option was not granted by lower authorities

An Adjudication Authority should explicitly specify the option available to the assessee under section 11AC of the Act (which is similar to the option available under Section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994). In view of Board Circular dated 22-5-2008, all cases where penalty under section 11AC of the Central Excise Act is imposed, provisions contained in the first and second proviso of this Section should be mandatorily mentioned in the adjudication order. [Para 14]

Hence, the assessee was required to be provided an option to remit 25 per cent of the penalties imposed under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994, within thirty days from the date of the adjudication order, along with interest and the amount of cenvat credit disallowed, after taking credit for the service tax and interest if any already remitted. It requires to be noted that the total amount of disallowed cenvat credit was already remitted by the assessee in respect of both the adjudication orders impugned in these appeals, even prior to issue of the respective show-cause notices. If no such option was indicated in an adjudication order, the Tribunal must provide such option from the date of its order. [Para 15]

IV. Interest not leviable, if credit availed not utilized

Trading activity - Whether a service

As regards the issue as to whether trading activity can be called a service, it is quite clear that since trading activity is nothing but purchase and sales and is covered under Sales Tax Law, it may not be appropriate to call it a service. Trading activity cannot be called a service and, therefore, it cannot be considered as an exempted service also. [Para 5]

Applicability of Cenvat Credit Rules (and Service Tax Credit Rules) on trading activity

Sub-rule (3) of rule 6 provides that where output service provider does not maintain separate account, he is to follow the procedure or avail the options available under that rule. Rule 6 is applicable only when the output service provider is providing services which are chargeable to service tax and as well as exempted services. Similar is the situation in rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. Both these rules clearly speak of exempted services. Rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules also covers non-taxable services. Since trading activity was not at all a service, it is not correct to apply these provisions. [Para 7]

Eligibility for availing input service tax credit

In cases where an assessee is undertaking activities which cannot be called a service or which cannot be called manufacture, that activity goes out of the purview of both Central Excise Act as well as the Finance Act, 1994. Therefore, there arises a situation where an assessee would not be eligible to take input service tax credit on an output which is neither a service nor excisable goods. There is no provision to cover situations where an assessee is providing a taxable service and is undertaking another activity which is neither a service nor manufacture. In such a situation the only correct legal position appears to be that the appellant choose and segregate the quantum of input service attributable to trading activity and exclude the same from the records maintained for availment of credit. Naturally this cannot be done in advance since it may not be possible to forecast what will be the quantum of trading activity and other activity which is liable to service tax. The only obvious solution which would be legally correct appeared to be to ensure that once in a quarter or once in a six months, the quantum of input service tax credit attributed to trading activities according to standard accounting principles was deducted and the balance only will be availed for the purpose of payment of service tax of output service. This proposition was not against the law in view of the fact the there were several decisions of various High Courts and also of the Tribunal, wherein a view had been taken that subsequent reversal of credit amounts to non-availment of credit. [Para 8]

Uday Joshi for the Appellant. J.S. Negi for the Respondent.

Clearly, during the period in issue, i.e., 2006-07 and 2007-08, trading activity, which was one of the businesses, carried out by the appellant was not amenable to service tax. The amendment to rule 2(e), stated that there was no liability to pay service tax of trading activity, during the relevant period. [Para 9]

In this context, it may also be relevant to note, how exempted services was defined in rule 2(e) of the 2004 rules till 31-3-2011 and thereafter.

Both before and after amendment, 'exempted services' meant those taxable services, which were exempt from whole of service tax and, included those services on which service tax was not leviable, under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.2]

Therefore, given the rule position, what would govern the matter would be the determination of the issue as to whether or not, a particular service is amenable to service tax under section 66 of the Finance Act. [Para 10.3]

Since, the trading activity was not amenable service tax at the relevant period, surely, the apportionment as provided in rule 6(3)(c) would get triggered. [Para 10.4]

Having regard to the rule position and given the admitted fact that no separate accounts were maintained by the appellant, with regard to the taxable and non-taxable services, clause (c) of sub-rule 3 of rule 6 of 2004 rules would apply. [Para 11]

For the foregoing reasons, there was interference is called for with the order of the Tribunal. Accordingly, the questions of law framed are answered in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. [Para 12]

held, qua 'trading activity' vis-à-vis rule 6 mechanism, that it could not have been the intention of the Government to encourage trading by allowing full credit prior to 1-4-2011 and that the 'value' of exempt supply in nature of trading as provided after 1-4-2011 in law for complying with proportionate credit requirements should be made applicable to the period prior to 1-4-2011 as well. [Para 8] In the instant case, it is evident that the assessee had started taking only proportionate credit after receipt of Completion Certificate which was after due intimation to the revenue and also certified by independent CA. It is the case of the assessee that rule 6 in toto cannot apply prior to 1-4-2016 to the instant case, since sale of immovable property is not exempt service at all. In the light of the provisions of rule 3, the assessee cannot avail full cenvat credit on input services received after obtaining Completion Certificate. However, the assessee cannot be expected to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of sale price of immovable property after obtaining such Completion Certificate where no service tax is paid as if it is sale of immovable property, since rule 6 per se does not apply to the instant case until 1-4-2016 at all. Even after 1-4-2016, since the assessee had availed only proportionate credit, it is not legally required to pay 8%/10% amount under rule 6(3), since it can be said to have maintained separate accounts as required under rule 6(2). [Para 9]

Having taken only proportionate credit of service tax paid on input services after receipt of Completion Certificate, duly backed by CA certificate and certified work sheets for the proportionate credits availed after Completion Certificate and also demonstrated on sample basis during the course of hearing, the assessee has fulfilled its obligation under rule 3 read with rule 6 and as such it is not liable to pay an amount equal to 8%/10% of the 'sale price of immovable property' after receipt of completion certificate under rule 6. [Para 11]

The next question for consideration would arise as to whether the assessee was also required to reverse proportionate credit, out of the valid input service credits availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., availing during the time when whole of output service of construction of residential complex was taxable. [Para 12]

While the law does not intend to allow any undue benefit to a service provider in terms of cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services used in providing non-taxable output activity, cenvat credit is a vested right. Once it is legally and validly availed, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific provisions exist for the same. [Para 13]

It has been a consistent judicial view that credit entitlement is on the date of receipt of inputs when the output activity was wholly dutiable. Merely because the finished goods eventually became exempt later on, the credit availed on inputs which were contained in semi-finished/finished goods form was held as not deniable. [Para 14]

In fact, in order to overcome such legal position, transitional provisions were introduced in the Cenvat Credit Rules. Rule 11, as it existed during the material period, provides that where any inputs are contained in semi-finished or finished goods form, as on date when the finished goods become exempt or output services become exempt, such credit will have to be reversed. As clarified vide Clarification No.334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-2-2007 and also taken note of by the Madras High Court in the case of Tractor And Farm Equipment Ltd. v. CCE [2015] 54 taxmann.com 122/50 GST 68 and eventually upheld by the Apex Court, such embargo applies only to inputs and not to input services at all. Admittedly, in the instant case, the dispute is limited to credits availed on input services during a time when output service was wholly taxable. However, portion thereof became non-taxable on account of receipt of Completion Certificate later on. [Para 15]

This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

♦ Rule 3(4) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 permits utilization of CENVAT Credit for payment of service tax and excise duty. [Para 5]

♦ There is no provision for segregation of CENVAT credit for payment of excise duty and for payment of service tax. There is no requirement for one to one correlation of CENVAT credit availed on input services towards payment of output services. [Para 6]

♦ Hence, assessee was eligible for CENVAT Credit. [Para 7]

EDITOR'S NOTE

♦ A question of day-to-day importance stands raised in this judgment.

♦ The requirement to maintain separate accounts exists under Rule 6 only in case where a manufacturer is engaged in manufacture of dutiable and exempt goods or a provider of output services is engaged in provision of taxable and exempt services.

♦ Though CENVAT Credit Rules contain separate provision in respect of manufacturer of excisable goods and provider of services, it must be noted that once CENVAT Credit is validly availed, there is no restriction on its utilization except as stated in Rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

on tax audit under section 44AB has demonstrated with practical examples that under both the methods, i.e., 'inclusive method' also called as 'gross method' or 'exclusive method' also called as 'net method', the gross profits in trading account shall be the same. It is difficult to believe that the enterprise will make profits on taxes, duties, cess and fee payable to Government in the midst of prevailing law's concerning and with reference to doctrine of unjust enrichment. [Para 16] The Apex Court has already held in the case of Eicher Motors v. Union of India 1999 (106) ELT 3 that Cenvat credit once validly taken cannot be effaced and creates an accrued right in favour of enterprise. It becomes apparent that 'exclusive method' also called as 'net method' appears certainly to be better choice in the present scenario vis-à-vis 'inclusive method' also called 'gross method' of accounting for maintaining books of account for accounting for cost of purchases which is also stipulated by ICAI because these Cenvatable duties and taxes on procurement of goods and services paid by the enterprise are payments made by the enterprise with an attached and accrued right in favour of the enterprise that these Cenvatable taxes so paid on raw material; input services once validly taken cannot be effaced and shall be paid back to the enterprise by the Government by way of set off against the excise duty liability on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise and these 'Cenvat credit' is more akin to 'current assets' rather than part of the cost of purchases and inventory being taxes recoverable from Government by way of adjustment against the excise duty payable on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise. More-so the result by the both the methods of accounting viz. 'gross method' or 'net method' will be same as demonstrated by ICAI in its guidance note. The ICAI in view of divergence between AS-2 and mandatory requirements of section 145A has stipulated in the guidance note on tax audit that books of account are to be maintained by the enterprise following 'exclusive method' also called as 'net method', while due to mandatory requirement of section 145A while preparing return of income to be filed with Revenue, it is stipulated by ICAI to follow 'inclusive method' also called as 'gross method but the gross profits under both the methods will yield same profits which in any case will not cause any prejudice to the Revenue. The provisions of section 43B also protect the interest of Revenue that the taxes, duties, fee and cess payable as at the year end by the taxpayer shall only be allowed as deduction from the income under the Act if the same are actually paid to the credit of Government before the due date of filing of return of income as stipulated under section 139(1). The Excise laws, rules and regulation also requires the records to be maintained in prescribed manner whereby Cenvat credit availed and utilized can be clearly demarcated to establish that correct Cenvat credit is availed and utilized by the Enterprise. The Income Tax Act,1961 cannot work in vaccum in isolation but has to progress along-with the rapid development taking place in the economy as it is a living Act and harmonization of various laws is the need of the hour to reduce complexities and bring in the ease of doing business, of course, without compromising/sacrificing with the basic intent and mandate of the Act, to collect correct taxes as per provisions of the Act. During the last few decades, things have radically and drastically changed in the economy the way businesses are conducted as now e-commerce and international transactions have taken primacy in the economy which are now the key areas of challenge under the Income Tax Laws. It is for the Parliament to frame and amend laws to keep pace with the fast changing environment in the economy. Section 145A was brought into statute in 1998 when MODVAT scheme was prevalent which allowed credit/set off on specified inputs used in manufacture of excisable goods apart from capital goods but now with Cenvat Scheme in operation which allows both manufacturers and service providers to take input credits on goods and services apart from capital goods across cross sectors without any one to one correlation, there is a need to align section 145A with the present regime of indirect taxation which Parliament alone in its wisdom can do to keep pace with the developments taking place in economy. As far as the first category of taxes, fees, duties, cess having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods are concerned which are paid on raw materials and also during WIP stage on which no Cenvat credit is allowed by the law under Cenvat scheme and are absorbed in the Profit and Loss Account by the enterprise as one of the components and item of the cost, such taxes, duties, fees, cess (by whatever name called) having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods has to be included in the cost of purchase and valuation of the goods irrespective of whether the enterprise is following exclusive method' or 'inclusive method' of accounting to satisfy the mandatory requirement of section 145A

Capital goods was not available to service provider prior to 10-9-2004

During the relevant period i.e. prior to 10-9-2004, as per Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, credit could have been taken on the Service Tax paid on input services which fall under the same category of taxable service as that of output service and, therefore, the CENVAT Credit of duty paid on capital goods was not available prior to 10-9-2004. Hence, credit could not be allowed in view of transitional provisions in Rule 11 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. [Paras 4 and 6]

Separate proceedings were not required for denial of credit, as it was a part of assessment :

The submissions that separate proceedings should have been initiated for rejection of CENVAT Credit availment, especially because the original adjudicating authority has appropriated the amount debited from the CENVAT Credit account, were incorrect. Even in the cases of clandestine removal and in the cases where the assessee has not taken the registration from the Department and whole activity of the assessee was not known to the Department, it has been the practice to allow admissible CENVAT Credit to the assessee, if the assessee is able to show that capital goods are received, documents are available and used by the assessee for manufacture of finished goods even if procedure for availment of CENVAT Credit would not have been followed by the assessee. [Para 7]

Just because the returns were filed subsequent to issue of show-cause notice, the requirement under the law for the adjudicating authority to consider availability of CENVAT Credit and allow the benefit of admissible CENVAT Credit while confirming the duty demand does not undergo a change. Issue of another Show Cause Notice to deny the CENVAT Credit would only open a line for another round of litigation without any corresponding benefit to either side. [Para 8]

If a Show Cause Notice was to be issued and separate proceedings were to be initiated, the original adjudicating authority would not have allowed the appropriation and would not have allowed the benefit of credit itself since it would have been the subject matter of another litigation and thereby the assessee would have been required to make payment in cash and later on file refund claim resulting in further litigation regarding unjust enrichment and other aspects.
