The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order-in-original.

On second appeal:

HELD: The Adjudicating Authority discovered that the assessee has availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy service on traded goods rendered by 'C' and as per the reverse charge mechanism under section 66A, the assessee has wrongly taken the proportionate cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading activity. Further the cenvat credit has been reversed on being pointed out by the Adjudicating Authority. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) has discussed the whole issue with cogent reasoning and has rightly rejected the appeal of the assessee. Therefore, as far as confirmation of demand and interest is concerned, there is no infirmity in the impugned order.

As far as the levy of penalty is concerned, unless and until there is a finding that there was suppression of fact and irregular availement of credit, the question of levying penalty under rule 15(2) does not arise. Moreover, in the instant case, the assessee reversed the duty along with interest on being pointed out by the Adjudicating Authority and there was no intention to evade payment of duty as is required under rule 15 read with section 11AC. Therefore, the penalty levied upon the assessee was liable to be set aside. [Para 6]

CENVAT CREDIT – OPTION TO MAINTAIN SEPARATE ACCOUNTS

1. We are providing works contract services and job-work services where both services are liable for service tax one is at full rate and another is at abatement rate with reverse charge. We are taking Input of all input service and capital goods. Now we are doing some trading activity in same firm. Since we cannot separate common service like audit fees, accounting consultancy, bank charges etc. so we will be maintaining separate accounts. Whether this would be sufficient and if not, then, whether we have to give reverse 7% on trading turnover ?

Rule 6 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, as it stood before 1-4-2016, mandated maintenance of separate books of account for taxable and exempted activities, failing which credit was liable to be reversed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (viz. 6 or 7 per cent; or pro rata).

Now, the requirement to maintain separate accounts has been done away within. In case of exempted as well as taxable activities, the credit cannot be taken for exempted activities and said credit is to be computed as per rule 6(3) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The said rule provides for percentage-based payment or pro rata reversal, as opted for by the assessee.

Hence, you have options :

Do not take credit of common inputs and input services

If credit is taken of common inputs and input services, then, —

either opt for percentage-based reversal or

opt for pro rata reversal.

CENVAT CREDIT – REVERSAL ON DISCOUNT RECEIVED ON INPUT SERVICES

2. One of my client has availed CENVAT credit on input service on the entire amount of the bill. Subsequently service provider has given the discount on the bill. Whether proportionate CENVAT credit to be reversed on the portion of the amount of discount received ?

Assuming no reverse charge case, credit can be taken on receipt of invoice. Further, payment of value of service and service tax should be made to the service provider within 3 months of date of invoice, failing which credit has to be reversed and can be re-taken only after full such payment.

As regards Part/Discounted Payment, it is provided in Circular No. 122/3/2010-S.T., dated 30-4-2010 that, in cases where receiver of service makes part/discounted payment only after 3 months, then, he is entitled to take full or pro rata credit provided he has also paid the amount of service tax, (whether proportionately reduced or the original amount) to the service provider.

Going by the Circular, if original amount of service tax is paid to the service provider, then, credit would not be touched. Accordingly, we opine as under :

[a]

If service tax amount is not changed and only value is reduced/negotiated, then, full credit may be taken [full and final settlement towards value would amount to 'payment of value' and would suffice requirements of rule 4(7)].

[b]

Alternatively, if service tax amount is also changed [say, original service tax is Rs. 14 and service tax as per revised value is Rs. 9.8], then, service provider may take benefit of rule 6(3) [credit of Rs. 4.2 may be taken by service provider] and service receiver may take credit of Rs. 9.8.

SERVICE TAX – GOVERNMENT/LOCAL AUTHORITY CAN BE BUSINESS ENTITY

3. Can Government/Local Authority be Business Entity for the purpose of section 65B of the Finance Act, 1994 ?

All services by government or local authority to any business entity are liable to service tax. Business Entity [Section 65B(17)]means any person ordinarily carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession. Since even government or local authority can be carrying out any activity relating to industry, commerce or any other business or profession, hence, they can also be business entity. Accordingly, the services might be liable to service tax.

However, by virtue of Entry 54 of Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012, services provided —

by Government or a local authority

to another Government or local authority

falling under section 66D(a)(iv),

are exempt from service tax.

Hence, even if government or local authority is business entity, services availed by it from another government or local authority falling under section 66D(a)(iv) are exempt.

3.2 Calculation of value of common inputs in case of exempted final products - The formulae as given in rule 6(3A) are only in respect of Cenvat credit attributable to (a ) inputs used for provision of exempted services and (b) input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services.

There is no formula to calculate Cenvat credit attributable to value of inputs used in manufacture of exempted final product, when inputs are common. In any case, consumables, fuel, dies, toolings, etc., will be ‘common inputs’ in most of the cases.

In absence of any formula, the only option with the assessee is to calculate the same either on basis of input-output ratio, or on the basis of formula similar to the one applicable for calculation of inputs used for provision of exempted services.

3.3 Treatment of traded goods - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods. The sale may be within India or outside. Obviously, there will be many common input services. Now, traded goods are not ‘exempt goods’. It is also not ‘service’, since one is not providing services to anyone else. Further, one cannot provide service to oneself.

Including the entire value of turnover of traded goods into dividend (above line) will be highly unfair to the assessee since the services attributable to such traded goods will certainly not be proportional to value of the traded goods, in cases where the assessee is both manufacturer as well as trader.

As the formulae stand today, turnover of traded goods can neither be included in divisor (below the line) nor the dividend (above the line). This would give higher Cenvat credit to the assessee. It would be fair to provide some percentage of turnover of traded goods (by way of rules), which should be added to dividend (above the line) to give fair results.

If no such provision is made in rules, there is a strong case to argue that it is not includible in divisor as well as dividend at all, since it is neither exempted goods nor exempted service (rather it is not ‘service’ at all).

3.4 Supplies to EOU, SEZ, etc. - Rule 6(6) states that provisions of rules 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

According to strict interpretation, this turnover shall not come either in denominator or in dividend. This would be unfair. It will give absurd results, particularly when sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., are large, as amount to be reversed will be very heavy. Sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., should appear in denominator, as per correct VAT principles.

3.5 Services specified in rule 6(5) - As per rule 6(5) in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. This rule has not been amended even if rule 6(3) has been recast with effect from April 1, 2008. Cenvat credit in relation to these services should be outside the calculations made as per rule 6(3A) and entire credit will be available, without any reversal.

3.6 Treatment of opening balance - An assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible, particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services.

Principally, the formula should apply to opening balances also.

3.7 Service tax paid under reverse charge method - In cases where service tax is paid under reverse charge method (particularly GTA services and sponsorship services), what would be the treatment ? As per amended rules, in case of GTA service, this amount should be paid by GAR-7 challan and not by cash with effect from March 1, 2008. However, this is not ‘output service’ as per amended rule 2(p). Hence, it appears that this amount is ‘input service’ and will be ‘service tax paid’. It will neither appear in divisor nor in dividend, but proportional reversal will have to be made.

Credit Rules are amended to provide options for availing credit of common inputs and services in case of manufacture of exempted and dutiable goods and provision of taxable and exempted services. This article intends to interpret the amended law in general with an example for a service provider in particular.

1. Basic Principles underlying the Amended Rules

1.1 Inputs/Input services [Rule 6(1)]

u No credit of inputs and input services is allowed if final product or output service is exempt from excise duty or service tax.

1.2 Capital goods [Rule 6(4)]

u Exclusive usage for manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services: No credit is allowed.

u Partly usage in dutiable goods or taxable services : Full credit allowed.

1.3 Specified services [Rule 6(5)]

u Exclusive usage of services for manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services: No credit is allowed.

u In case of part usage in dutiable goods or for providing taxable service: Full credit allowed.

2. In order to adjudicate upon the issues arising in the appeal, the following facts are required to be noticed:

2.1 The appellant herein is engaged in trading activities as well as in commission business. 2.4 It appears that the appellant had obtained Centralized registration with the Service Tax Department for services provided by them under the category "Business Auxiliary Services".

2.5 Evidently, the appellant's records were examined by the internal audit party of the Department on two consecutive days, i.e., 23.06.2008 and 24.06.2008. 2.6 Admittedly, in so far as the Commission Agency business was concerned, service tax was paid by the appellant, while no service tax was paid for trading activity. 21. The Parliamentary intent has to be gathered from the language used. If the words are plain, simple and clear, there is no scope for interpretation or applying any principle thereof. Once the Tribunal is bound to decide the controversy in the backdrop of the object and purpose sought to be achieved but has not arrived at any conclusion bearing in mind the same, then, we are required to step in. Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

Proportional Cenvat in case of general insurance companies providing taxable as well as exempt services - Rule 6(3)(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2007 provided an option to general insurance service providers providing taxable as well as exempted insurance schemes and who do not maintain separate input/input services credit accounts, to utilise Cenvat credit proportionate to the inputs and input services used in providing output services. HIRAL RAJA*

CENVAT CREDIT OF INPUT SERVICES IN RESPECT OF TRADED GOODS - A VEXED ISSUE

In this article, a vexed issue, namely, whether the assessee is entitled to take credit in respect of input services that are specifically pertaining to traded goods as well as common input services that are used both for dutiable goods/taxable services and for traded goods has been taken up for discussion. The author here explains the concerned provisions and relevant case-laws on the subject. ‘Specifically’ he makes a pointer to the decision of CESTAT in Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd. - CESTAT) and opines that the said decision deserves kudos because the CESTAT has preferred a very well-reasoned and fair judgment on an issue, which has wide ramifications to majority of the assessees across the country as well as for the department.

And he suggests that as this issue has been discussed and litigated over a period of time since the introduction of Cenvat credit in respect of service tax, it is high time that CBEC realizes the need for providing a clarification on the same so as to ensure that the litigation on the same is put to rest.

Introduction

1. There are a number of assessees who are engaged in provision of taxable services as well as sale of traded goods or are engaged in the manufacture of dutiable goods as well as sale of traded goods. In case of such assessees, there would be input services specifically pertaining to traded goods as well common input services that are used both for duitable goods/taxable services and for traded goods.

The question that arises in such cases is whether the assessee is entitled to take credit in respect of input services that are specifically pertaining to traded goods as well as common input services that are used both for dutiable goods/taxable services and for traded goods?

Some relevant provisions

2. Section 37 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 94 of the Finance Act, 1994 provide powers to the Central Government to make rules to provide for credit of duty or service tax paid/deemed to have been paid on the goods used in, or in relation to manufacture of excisable goods or provision of taxable services. In exercise of these powers, the Central Government has made Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules provides that a manufacturer of final product or provider of taxable service shall be allowed to take credit (Cenvat credit) in respect of any input service received by the manufacturer of final product or by provider of output service.

Rule 2(l) defines ‘input service’ to mean any service;—

"(i )used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service; or

(ii )used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products, up to the place of removal,

and includes services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal;"

Above definition makes it clear that input services would mean only those services which are used by a provider of taxable service for providing output service or used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture. Hence, any services exclusively used for traded goods would not get covered under the definition of ‘input service’ and Cenvat credit would not be available for the same.

Rule 6 provides for the mechanism for availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and providers of taxable and exempted services. Let us try to analyse and see whether traded goods can be considered as exempted goods or exempted services.

Rule 2(d) defines ‘exempted goods’, as excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘nil’ rate of duty.

Credit Rules, 2004 provides for the manner of distribution of credit of Input service. The evolving changes in the same has been elucidated infra:

3.1.1. Prior to 2012

Rule 7 (Manner of distribution of credit by input service distributor) provides that "The input service distributor may distribute the CENVAT credit in respect of the service tax paid on the input service to its manufacturing units or units providing output service, subject to the following condition, namely:- (a)

the credit distributed against a document referred to in rule 9 does not exceed the amount of service tax paid thereon; or

(b)

credit of service tax attributable to service use in a unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed."

Till this period, ISD could distribute credit amongst units in any ratio in absence of specific method prescribed in law. The same was held in the case of CCEx., Bangalore-I v. Ec of Industries Pvt. Ltd. [2011 (271) E.L.T. 58 (Kar.)] that "Given the absence of any other condition in rule 7 of the Credit Rules, an Input Service Distributor was permitted to allocate / distribute the credit entirely to a single recipient unit."

3.1.2. From April 2012 to March 2014

Due to amendment made in 2012, an additional restrictions have been introduced as regards the manner of allocation / distribution of credit to the credit recipient units viz.

(i)

credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly in a unit shall be distributed only to that unit; and

(ii)

credit of service tax attributable to service used in more than one unit shall be distributed pro rata on the basis of the turnover during the relevant period of the concerned unit to the sum total of the turnover of all the units to which the service relates during the same period.

The amended rule also incorporates provisions as regards the calculation of turnover values and relevant period to be considered for determination of credit distribution ratios.

3.1.3. From April 2014 to March 2016

From 1 April 2014, Rule 7 was further amended to provide that Turnover of previous month/quarter was replaced by the turnover of units in the preceding year and Turnover of only such units is to be considered which are operational in current year.

3.2. Predicaments in the vivid provisions prevailing till March 2016

3.2.1. The language of Rule 7 was producing doubt in the mind of manufacturers /Service provider as to whether the credit of common Input Service need to be distributed among all the units or to the units to which that service relates. It is clarified vide circular no 178/4/2014­ST that in case of services attributable to more than one unit, credit shall be distributed to all the units (without nexus of input services with the units) in the prescribed ratio irrespective of actual use of services by the units. This creates an absurd situation and also results in loss of credit in some cases when any unit was engaged in providing only exempted service.

3.2.2. Applicability of Rule 6 to the ISD has been the debatable issue since long past. The dissenting views of the departments can be substantiated below:

CBEC circular of 2008 provides that "ISD does not provide any service and is like a trader. Hence question of either option as per Rule 6 of CCR does not arise."

In a Tribunal judgment of 2011 in case of Colgate Palmolive it was held that "assessee is required to reverse cenvat credit on proportionate basis while distributing credit if it is manufacturing both exempted as well as taxable goods."

A guidance note issued by CBEC in 2012 states that "credit is distributed on the strength of a challan issued by ISD and it shall be subject to Rule 6 of CCR"

Accordingly, it can be recapitulated that assessees were pinned between the ambiguity of loosely drafted provisions and its contradicting interpretation by adjudicating and appellate authorities.

3.3. Budget 2016- Problem Solver or Mystery in abundance?

3.3.1 Conquering the infirmity in the prevailing position, Budget 2016 came up with some extoling amendments provided below:

It was provided that Credit attributable to more than one unit but not all units should be distributed to only such units whereas earlier such credit could be distributed to all operational units.

Clause (b) of Rule 7 was deleted which did not permit distribution of credit of service used in a unit exclusively engaged in exempted activity.

Earlier, there prevailed doubts whether credit is to be distributed firstly as per Rule 7 and then, the Cenvat credit entitlement under Rule 6 is to be determined by the unit receiving credit. A Ltd. has procured convention services for its business activities. As a part of the package deal, the hotel provides to airport pick and drop facility, promotion material alongwith the conference hall. Hotel raises a single invoice for all the three activities and recovers service tax on the gross consideration. Whether A Ltd. is eligible to claim Cenvat credit of the entire service tax so paid or A Ltd. would need to proportionately reduce the Cenvat credit relating to airport transfer facility? The provision of convention services by the hotel will be considered as bundled service comprising of conference hall, promotion material and cab facility. As per section 66F of the Act, "bundled service" means a bundle of provision of various services wherein an element of provision of one service is combined with an element or elements of provision of any other service or services. If such services are bundled in the ordinary course of business, then the bundle of services is treated as consisting entirely of such service which determines the dominant nature of such a bundle. In the present case, the intention of A Ltd. is to obtain convention services and provision of cab facilities for travel to and from airport is naturally bundled with the same. Hence, A Ltd., should be eligible to claim entire Cenvat credit and there is no need to reduce the Cenvat credit in proportion to the service tax pertaining to cab services.

A Ltd. has purchased Software for provision of output services. The cost of the software is expensed off in the profit and loss account. Whether A Ltd. is eligible to claim Cenvat credit on software as 'inputs' or as 'capital goods'?

As per rule 2(a) of the Credit Rules, the term capital goods has been defined in an exhaustive manner. It includes all goods falling in specified Chapter headings which, inter alia, include Chapter 82, Chapter 84, Chapter 85, etc. Thus, the software that falls under Chapter 85 (i.e., information technology software on a media), shalls be treated as capital goods when used for providing output service. Even if the value of software has been expensed off in the profit and loss account, the same will be treated as capital goods for the Cenvat credit purposes. Treatment in the books of account will not decide the Cenvat credit eligibility. Hence, A Ltd. will be eligible to the Cenvat credit on software as 'capital goods'. Given this, the Cenvat credit will be available in two equal annual instalments. However, softwares other than those covered under Chapter 85 (i.e., softwares procured electronically) will qualify as input service if used for providing output service and CENVAT credit thereon can be claimed in one go.

Whether Cenvat credit on telephone bills addressed in the name of the company can be claimed on the basis of the electronic invoices received via e-mails or the company would require original hard copy of invoices for claiming the Cenvat credit?

In terms of rule 9(1) of the Credit Rules, the provider of output services can claim Cenvat credit on the telephone bills addressed in the name of the company on the basis of the 'invoice issued' by the provider of an output service. The eligibility of Cenvat credit is not dependent upon the mode of receipt of the invoice. Thus, so long as the invoice issued by the telecom company is addressed in the name of the recipient-company and all other conditions for claiming credit, such as nexus with the output service, are fulfilled the service recipient will be eligible to claim Cenvat credit. Receipt of invoice via e-mail will not disentitle the company from claiming the Cenvat credit.

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - when credit attributable to inputs in exempted product is reversed by the assessee

6.15 The most significant amendment effected by the Finance Act, 2008 is with respect to the availment of credit on common input goods and services used in taxable and exempt output goods and services. As per the amended provisions where a manufacturer of final product or a provider of output service uses common inputs for manufacture of exempted and taxable goods or for providing exempt and taxable services, and opts not to maintain separate books of account, there are two options for the utilisation of the common CENVAT credits.

u First; the manufacturer can avail of common Cenvat credit and pay excise duty equivalent to 10% of the value of exempted goods. Similarly, the provider of output service can avail of common Cenvat credit and pay service tax equivalent to 8% of the value of exempted services.

u Second; the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service can avail common Cenvat credit and pay an amount equivalent to Cenvat credit attributable to input goods and services consumed in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or the provision of exempted services, as per conditions specified in sub-rule 3A of Rule 6.

The option to choose either of the above options has to be exercised and intimated to the department at the beginning of the year and once the option is exercised, it would be in force throughout the relevant financial year. But the question is-whether when credit attributable to inputs in exempted product is taken wrongly by the assessee but the same is reversed, whether demand can still be made against the assessee?

In one case the assessee was manufacturer of cartons and printed paper labels. The cartons were dutiable whereas the paper labels were exempted. The manufacturer maintained separate accounts of receipt, consumption and inventory in respect of common inputs utilized for the manufacture of the above products. However, such accounts were not maintained in respect of input services. After due process of law, the Commissioner demanded an amount of Rs. 1,29,09,031 being 10 per cent of the value of exempted goods cleared during the period from September 2004 to February 2006; appropriate interest and equivalent amount of penalty, even though the assessee had reversed the entire input service credit availed by it. The Commissioner confirmed the demand by invoking rule 6(3) for having contravened the provisions of rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

The Tribunal held that in a catena of decisions, it has been held that once the credit availed on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods is reversed, no demand can be made under Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules, 1944/Rule 26 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. So the Tribunal held that when credit attributable to inputs of exempted product is reversed by assessee, demand cannot be made against the assessee.

Tax credit illusory

6. It appears that cross settlement of input tax credit between the services and the goods is more on paper than real. Often the input tax credit for goods consumed in the service sector is obtained from dealers who cannot provide cenvatable invoices. The supply of goods is widespread among various dealers not all of whom provide cenvatable bills or cater to the requirements of the end-user who is a taxable service provider.

Similarly goods used in service contracts are not necessarily purchased from the first stage or second stage dealer or from the manufacturer directly. The input credit for goods consumed in service contracts is largely illusory as the output service provider purchases inputs from available sources of supply and on such terms as to credit and quantity which suit his business needs. Certain identified issues in Rule 6(3) and 6(3A):

6. Though the issues are numerous which still need clarity since the statute is still in its nascent stage, some of the identified issues are as under :

(i) Rule 6(3), Opt in - your choice, Opt out - no choice during the financial year

The sub-rule clarifies that an option would be exercisable both in the case of goods and services as manufactured or provided by the assessee. He cannot opt for Option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Also, exercise of such option cannot be withdrawn at any point of time during the financial year. He may change his option from the next year onwards. Thus, though the choice of opting in for the non-maintenance of separate books of account is open during the financial year, yet the option to opt out of it is unavailable to the manufacturer of service provider for that financial year.

(ii) Meaning of the term - ‘exempt’

The sub-rule does not define the term ‘exempt’ for the purpose of this sub-rule. Technically speaking, exempted goods/services are a sub-set of taxable goods/services. Exempted goods/services are specified by a notification by the Central Government and, accordingly, no duty/tax is leviable on them. However, there are other goods or services which are non-taxable and cannot be called ‘exempt’ technically. For example services of an advocate.

Having said this, the interpretation of the term ‘exempt’ is important for the calculation of duty/tax in respect of the Cenvat credit attributable towards exempted goods/services. Thus, extension of the term ‘exempt’ on non-taxable goods/services or otherwise would change the entire computation. For example when a provider of taxable services is providing exempt services and also is engaged in trading of goods (non-taxable), whether he needs to pay an amount equal to Cenvat credit attributable towards trading activity also, as he has to do in the case of exempt services. The answer is in affirmative when we equate trading to an exempt service and not otherwise.

Further, a larger question would be whether in case of an assessee engaged in the provision of taxable service and non-taxable service, would the computation under rule 6(3A) be applicable on him ? The question would be answered as ‘YES’ when non-taxable is equated as ‘exempt’ otherwise the answer is ‘NO’.

The more logical calculation would be to take out the Cenvat credit attributable towards non-taxable activities and then apply rule 6(3) on the balance Cenvat credit. Thus, the assessee should avail only the credit excluding that which is attributable towards non-taxable activities.

(iii) Choice of option - whether premises-wise or assessee-wise

Further, another point worth mentioning here is that the term used by the statute for availment of choice is manufacturer/service provider and not premises of manufacturer (factory) or service provider. Even the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under central excise uses the word ‘person’ and not ‘factory’. Accordingly, one school of thought might interpret that the availment of the options above should be same throughout all locations across India and the option cannot be availed of differently for different premises.

Expressing it with an example, Mr. X is a service provider having offices in Delhi, Mumbai and Pune, all three offices being separately registered with service tax department. Mr. X is providing taxable services under the category of ‘chartered accountant services’ and also availing the exemption provided thereunder. Thus, he is the provider of both taxable as well as exempt services. Now, the question is whether he can opt for option I for his Delhi and Mumbai offices and option II for Pune or will he have to opt for a single option for all his offices since the sub-rule uses the words ‘service provider’ when offering the choice.

Despite having various positive aspects, levying tax on the basis of value addition has its own set of problems. In cases where tax cannot be charged for various reasons, generally an issue arises, that is, how to deal with Input Credit (IC). Determination of IC attributable to taxable services is much simpler than in case of exempt services. Budget 2008 made drastic changes in this area by making amendment in rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In the opinion of the author, this contains lot of confusion and contradictions as the terminology used is confusing and some of the provisions are contradictory to other provisions. An attempt has been made in this comprehensive article to explain the provisions of rule 6 and the terminology associated with it in detailed manner.

Introduction

1. Despite having various positive aspects, levying tax on the basis of value addition has its own set of problems. The tax structure has to take cognizance of certain special cases wherein tax cannot be charged for various reasons. An issue that arises in such cases is, how to deal with Input Credit (IC) availed in respect of such services. Since the Government is not deriving any revenue, it will be reluctant to permit IC on it. If the services dealt with are the only taxable item for the assessee, the things would have been much simpler. However, the issue arises in the case where both, i.e., taxable and exempt, services are dealt with. Determination of IC attributable to exempt services raises various issues. Ideally the assessee can be asked to maintain separate records in respect of IC as applicable to taxable and exempt services and claim IC as applicable to taxable services only. To some extent it may be possible in the case of tangible goods. However, it may not be so in the case of services which are intangible. Apart from that, in real life, it may not be possible to maintain so much of detailed records. Even if one tries to do so the cost may outweigh the benefits derived.

Scenario before Budget 2008

2. Prior to 2008 the assessees were given two options, viz., to maintain separate records with respect to inputs and Input Services (IS) for receipt and consumption, etc., and for Exempt Services (ExS). Rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 (‘the Rules’) made detailed provisions in this respect. Another option as provided under rule 6(3)(i ) was to keep the IC restricted to 20 per cent of the ST payable. Under this arrangement, the assessee, despite having substantial IC entitlement, was required to pay ST. In the case of Service Providers (SP), having substantial volume of taxable services and low volume of ExS, this was turning out to be a losing proposition as it involved cash-outflow. To some extent it was not logical in the sense that the assessee was required to pay tax while large amount of IC was forced to remain unutilised.

Post-Budget Scenario

3. Budget 2008 made drastic changes in this area. The assessee has been provided with more options. Without disturbing the provisions of rule 6(2), i.e., permitting the assessee to maintain detailed records for IC for ExS and ExG, erstwhile rule 6(3) has been replaced with new rule giving two more options to the assessee. Initially, while reading the Finance Minister’s Budget Speech one was led to believe about pragmatic approach of the revenue to the problems of the assessee. However, as it happens in the life wherein things can never be so simple, there is no reason for taxation to be the exception to the said rule. Even a cursory glance at the provisions of rule 6(3) will make the reader uncomfortable as it involves the terminology which looks the same every where. Secondly, the formula for computation which should have been put in mathematical format has been described in text format.

Understanding the basic terms

4. Before trying to understand the provisions of rule 6, it will be appropriate to have basic understanding of certain terms used most frequently. They are ‘exempt goods’, ‘exempt services’, ‘export of goods’ services’, ‘services not liable to tax’, ‘availment of Cenvat credit’ and ‘utilisation of Cenvat credit’.

INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

The definition of 'exempted service' specifically excludes export services from within its ambit however question is whether same shall be included in taxable turnover and total turnover as well. A manufacturing company manufactures twisted and texturising yarn. It pays excise duty on such yarn. It is also appointed dealer of POY/PFY of a Ltd. Co. Some quantity of above yarn (raw-material yarn) is consumed in manufacture of excisable yarn and he does trading for rest of the quantity. He receives commission on whole quantity of yarn purchased as a dealer. Service tax is paid on commission received on whole lot of yarn received as a dealer. The same company also manufactures machines for own use and for public sale. Excise duty is paid on manufacturing of final machines. It pays service tax on job charges paid in manufacture of making machines and also on repairs and maintenance on machines. The company is registered under excise and service tax provisions. Query - (a) Whether service tax paid on (input services) relating to job work and R and M can be set-off against service tax payable by company on output service tax on yarn commission? (b) It is said that with Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, across the board sectorial credit can be enjoyed by manufacturer-cum-service provider? (c) What are restrictions for a manufacturer-cum-service tax provider in Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004?

Basically, Cenvat provisions do not require one to one relationship. Cenvat is a common pool of credit of all duties as specified in rule 3(1). This credit can be utilised for payment of any duty or tax, as specified in rule 3(4), subject to restrictions as specified in rule 3(7). Thus, except restrictions under rule 3(7), the credit is completely inter-changeable.

Moreover, definition of input service is very wide. Any service in relation to business is ‘input service’. Any relation with manufacture or provision of service is not required. Hence, in my view, Cenvat credit of any input service is available for payment of service tax on any output service.

Of course, department may not easily agree to this but I think legal position is quite clear.

Is he entitled to utilise Credit of the duties paid on ‘inputs’ or ‘capital goods’ for paying the service tax?

It provides that if a manufacturer of the final product shifts his factory to another site or the factory is transferred on account of change in ownership or on account of sale, merger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the factory to a joint venture with the specific provision for transfer of liabilities of such factory, then the manufacturer shall be allowed to transfer the CENVAT credit lying unutilized in his accounts to such transferred, sold, merged, leased or amalgamated factory.

If a provider of output service shifts or transfers his business on account of change in ownership or on account of sale, merger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the business to a joint venture with the specific provision for transfer of liabilities of such business, then the provider of output service shall be allowed to transfer the CENVAT credit lying unutilized in his account to such transferred, sold, merged, leased or amalgamated business.

Further, sub-rule (3)(c) of the above said rules reads as under : "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) and sub-rule (2), the manufacturer or the provider of output service opting not to maintain separate accounts shall follow either of the following conditions as applicable to him, namely :

The provider of output service shall utilize the credit only to the extent of an amount not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on taxable output services."

From the above-said provision, it is clear that where an output service provider is availing credit on inputs and input services and providing taxable as well as exempted services without opting to maintain separate account of inputs and input services received and used for the exempted services and refrains to avail Cenvat Credit on such inputs/input services, he has no other option but to use Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the amount of service tax payable on the output services. Therefore, the intention of the law is, the assessee shall either maintain separate account of input and input services for exempted output services and not to avail Cenvat Credit thereon or to utilize Cenvat Credit not exceeding 20% of the service tax payable on output services. Therefore, if the assessee decides to avail Cenvat Credit directly related to the taxable output services and utilizes the same fully for payment of service tax on output services and simultaneously avails Cenvat Credit on common inputs and input services without maintaining separate account and utilizing such credit only to the extent of 20% of service tax payable, it will defeat the intention of the legal provision which is explained in the example given below :

Let the input service credit availed on input services used exclusively for taxable output service is Rs. 10,000.

Common input services which are used partly for taxable and partly for exempted services, credit availed fully of Rs. 20,000.

Let service tax payable on the taxable output service be Rs. 50,000.

The correct way to utilize the Cenvat Credit for the above said situation would be 20% of Rs. 50,000, i.e., Rs. 10,000 which can be utilized out of the total credit of Rs. 30,000 (Rs. 10,000 related to the taxable output services and Rs. 20,000 credit on common input services used for taxable as well as exempted output service). Therefore, the balance amount, i.e., Rs. 50,000 minus Rs. 10,000 Cenvat Credit utilized = Rs. 40,000 has to be used as to be paid through TR-6 challan.

Had Cenvat Credit been utilized as explained in the query, the assessee can utilize the credit of Rs. 10,000 which is directly related to taxable output service plus another Rs. 10,000 i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 service tax payable on output service = Rs. 20,000 and the balance amount of Rs. 30,000 would have been paid through TR-6 challan.

However, it may be noted that the provisions of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, do not provide for more than one set of Cenvat Credit record for input service credit i.e. one for the input service credit related to taxable output service and second common input services credit account which are partly used for taxable output service and party for exempted services nor this sort of arrangement is prohibited, but considering the practice followed under Central Excise, I am of the opinion, that under above stated example, the assessee can avail total credit on Rs. 30,000 (10,000 + 20,000), but utilization will be restricted to 10% of service tax payable i.e. 20% of Rs. 50,000 = Rs. 10,000 and balance amount of Cenvat Credit unutilized (Rs. 30,000 total Cenvat Credit minus Rs. 10,000 credit utilized = Rs. 20,000) will be carried forward to the next month. It is further clarified that the law does not restrict the assessee to take Cenvat Credit on common input service only to the extent of 20% of service tax paid.

In the above said example the common input service credit of entire Rs. 20,000 can be availed and it is not restricted for availment of credit upto 20% of Rs. 20,000 i.e. Rs. 4,000.

Opinion : In short, if the assessee does not opt for separate account as envisaged under Rule 6(3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, he can avail the credit on the common inputs services fully but he can utilize the total credit available at the end of the month not exceeding 20% of service tax payable.

NEW CENVAT CREDIT RULE 6(3) AND 6(3A) - A PANDORA’S BOX

New Cenvat credit rule 6(3) (to be effective from April 1, 2008) is correct so far as Cenvat principles are concerned. However, in practice the calculations as provided in rule 6(3) and 6(3A) are so complicated that even with help of professional chartered/cost accountant, the calculation of amount of Cenvat credit is going to be a big problem. Many issues remain unanswered in the rule and it is bound to open Pandora’s Box. In this article, the provisions of new rule are discussed and difficulties analyzed. As drafted, the new rule is incomplete and does not provide for many situations. There are some drafting mistakes also.

No Cenvat credit if final product/service exempt

1. As per the basic principle of VAT, credit of duty or tax can be availed of only for payment of duty on final product or output services. As a natural corollary, if no duty is payable on final product or output services, credit of duty/tax paid on inputs or input services cannot be availed. This principle has been embodied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

As per rule 6(1) of the Rules, Cenvat credit is not admissible on such quantity of inputs or input service which is used in manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services [The words ‘provision of’ are inserted with effect from April 1, 2008, but this is only clarificatory amendment]. Thus, if inputs and input services are partly used in exempted final product/output service, Cenvat credit of that portion of inputs/input service will not be available.

(a) Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services - Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/taxable services and partly for exempted goods/services.

In such cases, the earlier rule 6 provided two options - (a) Forget about Cenvat credit of common inputs and input services (b) Pay 10 per cent ‘amount’ on exempted goods and/or restrict Cenvat credit to 20 per cent of service tax on output services.

Now, under new rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider has following three options with effect from April 1, 2008 -

(i) Maintain separate accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services and take Cenvat credit only of inputs and input services used in dutiable goods and taxable output services - Rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules - same as earlier rule.

(ii) Pay amount equal to 10 per cent of value of exempted goods (if he is ‘manufacturer’) and/or 8 per cent of value of exempted services (if he is service provider), if he does not maintain separate accounts of inputs and input services - Rule 6(3)(i) with effect from April 1, 2008.

(iii) Pay an ‘amount’ equal to proportionate Cenvat credit attributable to exempted final product/exempted output services, if he does not maintain separate accounts of inputs and input services - Rule 6(3)(ii) with effect from April 1, 2008.

(b) Cenvat credit on capital goods - If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and partly for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products - rule 6(4).

(c) Some services eligible even if partly used for manufacture of exempted goods/output services - Rule 6(5) provides that in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. Rule 6(5) has been given overriding effect over rules 6(1), 6(2) and 6(3).

In case of these services, reversal of Cenvat or payment of ‘amount’ is not required, if these services are even partly used for providing output service or manufacture of dutiable final product. Cenvat credit will be disallowed only when these services are used exclusively in manufacture of exempted final product or exempted output service.

4.1-2 Condition of use of input in factory for manufacturer but not applicable to service providers

The service provider is entitled to the credit of goods which is used in providing output service. The condition of use of goods in the factory is not applicable to service provider. Thus if the service provider avail the input which are consumed in any place not considered as factory, the credit will be available to the service provider.

So far as manufacturer is concerned, the Cenvat credit of inputs is available only if these are used in the factory - CBEC Circular No. 637/28/2002-CX dated 8-5-2002 - See Appendix.

However, this view has not been accepted by Supreme Court and Tribunal. See para 4.3-4 for case law on this issue.

4.1-3 Capital goods are not 'inputs' but parts and components can be 'inputs'

The capital goods [as defined in rule 2(a)] will not be normally considered as 'input'. The definition of 'capital goods' covers parts, components and accessories of capital goods. If such parts or components are used in manufacture of final product, these will be eligible as 'inputs'. For example, if a manufacturer of automobile uses parts and components to manufacture an automobile, these parts and components will be eligible for Cenvat Credit as 'input', even if these are covered in definition of 'Capital Goods' as per rule 2(a).

As per Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 31-3-2012, the Cenvat Credit could be distributed by Input Service Distributor in any ratio. Only restriction was that Cenvat credit distributed should not be more than available credit.

However, after 1-4-2012, the distribution is required to be on basis of turnover.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Credit of whole service tax paid on taxable services specified in rule 6(5)

4.17 The assessee was a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. The assessee utilized service tax credit for exempted as well as non-exempted category of services provided to it. The revenue denied credit on ground that the assessee had not maintained separate records for services received by it for exempted and for non-exempted categories and, therefore, in terms of rule 6(3)(c ), the assessee was entitled to utilize only 20 per cent of amount of credit. The revenue filed an appeal aggrieved by the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the ground that the Commissioner (Appeals) has not considered the provisions of the Cenvat Credit Rules 6(3) and 6(5). The adjudicating authority after examining in depth rule 6(5) has said that it is clear that a service provider, who provides taxable and exempted services, shall be allowed, credit of the whole of service tax paid on taxable services specified in the said rule 6(5) unless the said service is exclusively used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services although no separate amounts for receipt/consumption of the input services are maintained. In rule 6(5) the important word is ‘notwithstanding’. The very use of this word means that rule 6(3) is not applicable to the input services mentioned under rule 6(5). The credit which has been taken by the party is on some of the 17 services, which are covered under rule 6(5) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. This rule does not talk about taking or utilization, so the credit is allowed to both taken and utilized services.

The Tribunal held that impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is correct and does not suffer from any infirmity.

[CCE v. V.M. Salgaonkar & Bros. (P.) Ltd. [2008] 15 STT 76 (Mum. - CESTAT)]

10.1-3 Manner of distribution of Cenvat Credit w.e.f. 1-4-2016

Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules has been revamped w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

As per revised rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2016, the distribution should be as follows —

(a)

Credit distributed should not be more than credit of input service tax available.

(b)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly by a unit shall be distributed only to that unit.

(c)

Credit of service tax attributable to services used by more than one unit (but not to all units) shall be distributed pro-rata on the basis of turnover of such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of such units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(d)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used by all the units shall be distributed pro-rata on the basis of turnover of all such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of all the units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(e)

"2. The issue has been examined. Since, the discount in such cases are given in respect of the value of inputs and not in respect of the duty paid by the supplier, the effect of reduction of value of inputs may be that the duty required to be paid on the inputs was less than what has been actually paid by the inputs manufacturer. However, the fact remains that the inputs manufacturer had paid the higher duty. Rule 3 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 allows credit of duty ‘paid’ by the inputs manufacturer and not duty ‘payable’ by the said manufacturer. There are many judgments of Hon’ble Tribunal in this regard which have confirmed this view.

3. In view of above, it is clarified that in such cases, the entire amount of duty paid by the manufacturer, as shown in the invoice would be available as credit irrespective of the fact that subsequent to clearance of the goods, the price is reduced by way of discount or otherwise. However, if the duty paid is also reduced, along with the reduction in price, the reduced excise duty would only be available as credit. Note 2 — Amendment in rule 6(3A) — Procedure for reversal payment of duty (CENVAT Reversal) under sub-clause (ii) of Rule 6(3):

No CENVAT is allowed for Inputs & Inputs Services used exclusively or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods removed or for provision of exempted services. This credit is called 'Ineligible Credit'. The whole amount of CENVAT paid on Input has to be paid/reversed. This is denoted by "A".

100% of CENVAT Credit shall be allowed for Inputs & Inputs Services used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of non-exempted goods removed or for the provision of non-exempted services. This credit is called 'Eligible Credit'. This is denoted by "B". No payment or reversal in this case.

Credit left after reducing 'A' & 'B' from the Total Credit (denoted by "T") shall be the "Common Credit" denoted by "C". C = T – (A + B)

Common Credit (C) shall be attributed towards exempted goods and exempted services by multiplying the common credit with the ratio of value of exempted goods manufactured or exempted services provided to the total value of exempted and non-exempted goods and exempted and non-exempted services in the preceding financial year.

D = (E/F) × C

Where,—

D = Ineligible Common Credit

E = Sum total of value of exempted goods manufactured or exempted services provided

F = Sum total of value of exempted and non-exempted goods and exempted and non-exempted services

A deemed rate of 50% shall be taken as "D" if there were no final products manufactured or no output service was provided during the previous Financial Year.

The remaining Common Credit (Eligible Common Credit, denoted by "G") shall be computed in following manner : G = C – D

The above-mentioned calculation shall be done on monthly provisional basis on turnover of previous year and subsequently shall be calculated on actual basis on or before 30th June of subsequent year. The differential amount, if any is to be paid along with interest.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

It was found that these provisions are in pari materia with the provisions of rule 57CC and rule 57AD of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. Combined reading of rule 57CC (1) and 57CC (9) would indicate that rule 6(3)(b) has been carved out of a combination of the said sub-rule of rule 57CC. It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts has to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods by way of formula as provided in the rule itself; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It is the settled law that reversal of the credit taken on the inputs is as good as non-availment of the credit on the inputs.

Under the Central Excise Act, 1944, levy is on manufacture but payment is at the time of clearance. It has been decided by the Board that credit of the duty paid on common inputs is admissible when used in the manufacturer of the final product (exempted and dutiable) provided the said credit of duty paid on inputs going into the exempted category of the final product is debited in the RG 23A-Part II account before the removal of exempted final product on actual or pro rata (estimated) basis. The facility of reversing the credit taken is neither explicitly given nor necessarily implied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002. It was held in that context that the credit taken but before utilization reversed, will amount to not taking the credit and the benefit of exemption cannot be denied.

In view of the above reasoning, the Tribunal held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are not applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. In other words, it is equivalent to reversal of credit on inputs. Therefore, according to Tribunal, the appellant had satisfied the requirement of not taking Modvat Credit on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Their case is specifically covered by rule 57CC as well as the decision of Supreme Court with regard to not availing of Modvat Credit on inputs in the case of Chandrapur Magnet Wires (P.) Ltd. v. EXPERTS’ OPINION : CENVAT CREDIT

Thus Spake Experts

An assessee is pro-viding both taxable and exempt services. He utilises various input services for providing his output services. In respect of some of the input services, he is in a position to establish direct correlation between his input service and taxable output service. In respect of general (common input services like telephone, courier, manpower supply, bank services etc., he is not able to establish direct relation with either exempt output service or taxable output service. He is utilising full Cenvat credit in respect of input services where he is able to establish direct relation between input service and output taxable service, as per rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules. In addition, in respect of common input services where he is not able to establish any direct relation with output service, he is availing Cenvat credit to the extent of 20% of amount of service tax payable on taxable output service, as provided in rule 6(3)(c) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

For example, service tax payable by him is Rs. 100. Service tax paid on his common input services is Rs. 25. Service tax paid on services where he can directly establish relation with his taxable output service is Rs. 10. He is availing Cenvat credit of Rs.10 [rule 6(2)] plus Rs. 20 [rule 6(3)(c)]. Is it legally correct? In short, whether rules 6(2) and 6(3)(c) are mutually exclusive or they can be used simultaneously.

V.S. DATEY

The issue will arise in due course and it appears to be a borderline case. There is no specific prohibition in simultaneous availment of credit under rules 6(2) and 6(3). Hence, it can be argued that what is not prohibited is deemed to have been permitted and hence simultaneous availment of rules 6(2) and 6(3) is permissible. This is also justifiable on the principle that ambiguity in taxation provision should be resolved in favour of tax payer.

Counter View - Rule 6(3) starts with the words ‘notwithstanding anything contained in rules 6(1) and 6(2)’. Thus, rule 6(3) overrides provisions of rules 6(1) and 6(2). From this, it appears that assessee has to follow either rule 6(2) [which allows full credit if he can maintain separate accounts of input service] or rule 6(3)(c) [which allows use of common input services for providing dutiable as well as exempted/excluded taxable services].

In other words, if he is not able to maintain separate accounts even in respect of some of the input services, he has to either completely forego input credit on those services and go under rule 6(2) for services where he can identify separately, or avail rule 6(3)(c ) in respect of all input services and take credit to the extent of 20% of service tax payable on output services.

However, there is no clear provision that these are mutually exclusive and assessee cannot avail partially rule 6(2) and partially rule 6(3)(c).

Hence, if assessee is slightly risk taking type, he may avail simultaneously rules 6(2) and 6(3), as one never knows which view will ultimately prevail in such borderline cases.

It is difficult to believe that the enterprise will make profits on taxes, duties, cess and fee payable to Government in the midst of prevailing law's concerning and with reference to doctrine of unjust enrichment. [Para 16] The Apex Court has already held in the case of Eicher Motors v. Union of India 1999 (106) ELT 3 that Cenvat credit once validly taken cannot be effaced and creates an accrued right in favour of enterprise. It becomes apparent that 'exclusive method' also called as 'net method' appears certainly to be better choice in the present scenario vis-à-vis 'inclusive method' also called 'gross method' of accounting for maintaining books of account for accounting for cost of purchases which is also stipulated by ICAI because these Cenvatable duties and taxes on procurement of goods and services paid by the enterprise are payments made by the enterprise with an attached and accrued right in favour of the enterprise that these Cenvatable taxes so paid on raw material; input services once validly taken cannot be effaced and shall be paid back to the enterprise by the Government by way of set off against the excise duty liability on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise and these 'Cenvat credit' is more akin to 'current assets' rather than part of the cost of purchases and inventory being taxes recoverable from Government by way of adjustment against the excise duty payable on finished goods manufactured by the enterprise. More-so the result by the both the methods of accounting viz. 'gross method' or 'net method' will be same as demonstrated by ICAI in its guidance note. The ICAI in view of divergence between AS-2 and mandatory requirements of section 145A has stipulated in the guidance note on tax audit that books of account are to be maintained by the enterprise following 'exclusive method' also called as 'net method', while due to mandatory requirement of section 145A while preparing return of income to be filed with Revenue, it is stipulated by ICAI to follow 'inclusive method' also called as 'gross method but the gross profits under both the methods will yield same profits which in any case will not cause any prejudice to the Revenue. The provisions of section 43B also protect the interest of Revenue that the taxes, duties, fee and cess payable as at the year end by the taxpayer shall only be allowed as deduction from the income under the Act if the same are actually paid to the credit of Government before the due date of filing of return of income as stipulated under section 139(1). The Excise laws, rules and regulation also requires the records to be maintained in prescribed manner whereby Cenvat credit availed and utilized can be clearly demarcated to establish that correct Cenvat credit is availed and utilized by the Enterprise. The Income Tax Act,1961 cannot work in vaccum in isolation but has to progress along-with the rapid development taking place in the economy as it is a living Act and harmonization of various laws is the need of the hour to reduce complexities and bring in the ease of doing business, of course, without compromising/sacrificing with the basic intent and mandate of the Act, to collect correct taxes as per provisions of the Act. During the last few decades, things have radically and drastically changed in the economy the way businesses are conducted as now e-commerce and international transactions have taken primacy in the economy which are now the key areas of challenge under the Income Tax Laws. It is for the Parliament to frame and amend laws to keep pace with the fast changing environment in the economy. Section 145A was brought into statute in 1998 when MODVAT scheme was prevalent which allowed credit/set off on specified inputs used in manufacture of excisable goods apart from capital goods but now with Cenvat Scheme in operation which allows both manufacturers and service providers to take input credits on goods and services apart from capital goods across cross sectors without any one to one correlation, there is a need to align section 145A with the present regime of indirect taxation which Parliament alone in its wisdom can do to keep pace with the developments taking place in economy. As far as the first category of taxes, fees, duties, cess having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods are concerned which are paid on raw materials and also during WIP stage on which no Cenvat credit is allowed by the law under Cenvat scheme and are absorbed in the Profit and Loss Account by the enterprise as one of the components and item of the cost, such taxes, duties, fees, cess (by whatever name called) having bearing on bringing the goods to the place of its location and conditions as on the date of valuation of the goods has to be included in the cost of purchase and valuation of the goods irrespective of whether the enterprise is following exclusive method' or 'inclusive method' of accounting to satisfy the mandatory requirement of section 145A

40.6-2 Motor vehicle is not 'input' but 'capital goods' in case of some services

There is parallel provision in respect of input services.

40.6-3 Small value capital goods are 'inputs' - not capital goods

Small value capital goods which have a value upto ten thousand rupees per piece will be eligible as 'inputs' and not 'capital goods' w.e.f. 1-4-2016 [clause (v) inserted to rule 2(k) w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

Goods used for pumping of water are eligible for Cenvat credit even if these are used outside the factory [clause (iii) to rule 2(k) of Cenvat Credit Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2016]

40.6-5 Distribution of credit by warehouse of manufacturer

A manufacturer may have central warehouse from which he may be distributing inputs to his various factories.

In such case, the warehouse can get registered under Central Excise and issue invoices like those issued by first stage dealer or second stage dealer. The manufacturing unit can take Cenvat credit on basis of such invoice - rule 7B of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016].

40.6-6 Goods for personal consumption of employees not eligible

Goods such as food items, goods used in guest house, residential colony, club or recreational facility and clinical establishment when such goods/services are used primarily for personal use or consumption of employees are not eligible as inputs.

There is parallel provision in respect of input services.

40.6-7 Partial or full write off of inputs

As per rule 3(5B) of Cenvat Credit Rules (inserted w.e.f. 11-5-2007 and as amended w.e.f. 1-3-2011), if (i) inputs or (ii) capital goods before being put to use, are written of fully or partly or any provision is made in books of account to write off fully or partially, the manufacturer or service provider is required to pay an 'amount' equal to Cenvat credit taken in respect of such inputs or capital goods. If these are subsequently used in manufacture of final products or provision of output service, manufacturer/service provider can take Cenvat credit of amount which was paid earlier. 40.6-8 Input goods in respect of service providers

Duty paid on input goods used by service providers is also eligible for Cenvat credit, but in a restricted way.
