However, in case of export of services, these are ‘exempt services’ since, as per rule 2(e) service on which no tax is payable is also ‘exempt service’. It can be said that both export of goods and export of services should be taken in denominator (divisor), i.e., below the line to give correct and fair results. If these are taken in dividend (above the line), it will amount to reversal of Cenvat credit attributable to these services, which certainly is illogical.

3.2 Calculation of value of common inputs in case of exempted final products - The formulae as given in rule 6(3A) are only in respect of Cenvat credit attributable to (a ) inputs used for provision of exempted services and (b) input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services.

There is no formula to calculate Cenvat credit attributable to value of inputs used in manufacture of exempted final product, when inputs are common. In any case, consumables, fuel, dies, toolings, etc., will be ‘common inputs’ in most of the cases.

In absence of any formula, the only option with the assessee is to calculate the same either on basis of input-output ratio, or on the basis of formula similar to the one applicable for calculation of inputs used for provision of exempted services.

3.3 Treatment of traded goods - A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods. The sale may be within India or outside. Obviously, there will be many common input services. Now, traded goods are not ‘exempt goods’. It is also not ‘service’, since one is not providing services to anyone else. Further, one cannot provide service to oneself.

Including the entire value of turnover of traded goods into dividend (above line) will be highly unfair to the assessee since the services attributable to such traded goods will certainly not be proportional to value of the traded goods, in cases where the assessee is both manufacturer as well as trader.

As the formulae stand today, turnover of traded goods can neither be included in divisor (below the line) nor the dividend (above the line). This would give higher Cenvat credit to the assessee. It would be fair to provide some percentage of turnover of traded goods (by way of rules), which should be added to dividend (above the line) to give fair results.

If no such provision is made in rules, there is a strong case to argue that it is not includible in divisor as well as dividend at all, since it is neither exempted goods nor exempted service (rather it is not ‘service’ at all).

3.4 Supplies to EOU, SEZ, etc. - Rule 6(6) states that provisions of rules 6(1) to 6(4) shall not apply in case of excisable goods removed to SEZ, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting.

According to strict interpretation, this turnover shall not come either in denominator or in dividend. This would be unfair. It will give absurd results, particularly when sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., are large, as amount to be reversed will be very heavy. Sales to SEZ, EOU, etc., should appear in denominator, as per correct VAT principles.

3.5 Services specified in rule 6(5) - As per rule 6(5) in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. This rule has not been amended even if rule 6(3) has been recast with effect from April 1, 2008. Cenvat credit in relation to these services should be outside the calculations made as per rule 6(3A) and entire credit will be available, without any reversal.

3.6 Treatment of opening balance - An assessee always tries to utilise Cenvat credit first and then pay through PLA/GAR-7. However, despite his efforts, some opening balance is possible, particularly in initial stages of production/provision of services.

Principally, the formula should apply to opening balances also.

3.7 Service tax paid under reverse charge method - In cases where service tax is paid under reverse charge method (particularly GTA services and sponsorship services), what would be the treatment ? As per amended rules, in case of GTA service, this amount should be paid by GAR-7 challan and not by cash with effect from March 1, 2008. However, this is not ‘output service’ as per amended rule 2(p). Hence, it appears that this amount is ‘input service’ and will be ‘service tax paid’. It will neither appear in divisor nor in dividend, but proportional reversal will have to be made.

It was held that this is simple trading. Rule 3(4) of Cenvat Credit Rules applies and tubes and flaps were removed 'as such'.

CBE&C, vide circular No. 911/1/2010-CX dated 14-1-2010 has clarified that assessee should not avail Cenvat credit on inputs and pay excise duty on output if the activity is not 'manufacture'.

In fact, in such case, there is no duty liability at all and hence question of Cenvat really should not arise.

However, in various cases, it has been held that if assessee still pays duty, Cenvat credit is not required to be reversed and receiver of goods can avail Cenvat credit (case law discussed in another chapter).

In case of service provider, question of 'manufacture' does not arise.

Service Provider eligible for Cenvat credit

20.3-5 As per rule 3(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules, provider of output service shall be allowed to take Cenvat credit of specified duties and taxes. Thus, only a person who is providing taxable output service will be eligible to take Cenvat credit.

Output Service - "Output service" means any service provided by a provider of service located in the taxable territory but shall not include a service - (1) specified in section 66D of the Finance Act, 1994; or (2) where the whole of service tax is liable to be paid by the recipient of service [Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules, as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012] [Section 66D of Finance Act, 1994 covers list of services in negative list].

Rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules (as existing upto 1-7-2012 and from 29-2-2008) was reading as follows - "output service" means any taxable service, excluding the taxable service referred in section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 (This is GTA service) provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

Till 29-2-2008, rule 2(p) of Cenvat Credit Rules stated that "output service" means any taxable service provided by the provider of taxable service, to a customer, client, subscriber, policy holder or any other person, as the case may be, and the expressions 'provider' and 'provided' shall be construed accordingly.

The reference to Goods Transport Agency Service (falling under section 65(105)(zzp) of Finance Act, 1994 of Finance Act, 1994) has been inserted to clarify that GTA service will not be treated as 'output service' where consignor/consignee is liable to make payment of service tax. Thus, service tax on GTA service will have to be paid by consignor/consignee only by cash and not through Cenvat credit.

We also note that Revenue has denied credit of service tax in proportion of trading goods. 7. Learned counsel's contention is that in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. (supra) the Tribunal has held that in computing the ratio of exempted turnover, the value of trading i.e. without deduction of cost of goods sold shall be considered as value of exempted turnover and quoted para 17 of the said judgment. It was further submitted that Tribunal has not laid down general proposition. We have gone through the said judgment and one of us was in the Division bench that decided the said case. The issue in para 17 was that a particular assessee is manufacturing and also undertaking trading and trading is not considered as service (being neither taxable under service tax or excise), then how to apportion the credit on input services used in both the activities. This question has arisen as it was not possible to quantify how much of a particular service is used for trading and how much of that service is used for manufacturing. (It is added that where it was possible to identify a particular invoice, payment or service with manufacturing unit is that already allowed and there is no dispute). Since it is not possible to bifurcate the portion of service used for trading and manufacturing, the only way is to have some broad criteria which would be just and reasonable. However, no such criteria will be perfect. It was in that context that during the argument of that case the learned senior counsel submitted that in the case of trading, the value addition is 10% or near about that and because of that reason, in respect of the trading 10% of the value of the trading is taken while for manufacturing the whole value is taken. It is in that context the bench asked the learned senior counsel that how can one say that the whole of the value of the manufactured goods is value addition because even in case of manufactured goods there would be cost of inputs. It was reiterated that in case of manufactured goods it is very difficult to estimate value addition because in the manufacturing process not only the inputs, but labour, electricity and many other services are used. Moreover, value addition will vary from product to product. Hence, value addition criterion is not practically feasible to be used. Instead of value addition, simple and more appropriate criteria will be the ratio of total turnover of the trading goods, and that the manufactured goods and apportion of the input credit on services in the same proportion. Incidentally in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. (supra) on analysis it was also found that the main common input service were advertising event management, business auxiliary service and business support service and certain other services and utility of such service will result in higher turnover of traded and manufactured goods. Thus, turnover was considered as appropriate criteria. In fact this would be true not only in that case but practically in all cases. Thus, even though there was a discussion relating to specific various services used but the conclusion was that the credit on input services should be apportioned in the same ratio as that of turnover of traded and manufactured goods. In view of the above analysis we are unable to agree with the contention of the learned counsel for the appellant and in our view the ratio of the judgment in the case of Mercedes Benz equally apply in the present case, and all other cases of similar nature.

8. We also note that the learned counsel of appellant has given a table indicating categorywise break up of credit and submitted that the credit mainly relates to management, maintenance or repair service and business auxiliary services. Learned counsel has also explained the nature of the services. We have given considerable thought. Even in this case one cannot say that the SAP system was used for the purpose of manufactured goods and not for the trading and changes in any computer software or SAP system are not determined based upon each click or transaction. Even if that is so, no conclusion can be drawn that it is used more for manufactured goods and less for traded. Revenue has proposed demand in proportion to the turnover of traded goods and the manufactured goods. Learned counsel has not been able to provide any alternative solution. Just saying value addition will not help. We do not consider value addition in the present case will lead to more just and reasonable criteria. In our considered view, the submission made by the appellant requires to be out rightly rejected.

CENVAT CREDIT

HIRAL RAJA*

CENVAT CREDIT OF INPUT SERVICES IN RESPECT OF TRADED GOODS - A VEXED ISSUE

In this article, a vexed issue, namely, whether the assessee is entitled to take credit in respect of input services that are specifically pertaining to traded goods as well as common input services that are used both for dutiable goods/taxable services and for traded goods has been taken up for discussion. The author here explains the concerned provisions and relevant case-laws on the subject. ‘Specifically’ he makes a pointer to the decision of CESTAT in Orion Appliances Ltd. v. CST [2010] 27 STT 319 (Ahd. - CESTAT) and opines that the said decision deserves kudos because the CESTAT has preferred a very well-reasoned and fair judgment on an issue, which has wide ramifications to majority of the assessees across the country as well as for the department.

And he suggests that as this issue has been discussed and litigated over a period of time since the introduction of Cenvat credit in respect of service tax, it is high time that CBEC realizes the need for providing a clarification on the same so as to ensure that the litigation on the same is put to rest.

Introduction

1. There are a number of assessees who are engaged in provision of taxable services as well as sale of traded goods or are engaged in the manufacture of dutiable goods as well as sale of traded goods. In case of such assessees, there would be input services specifically pertaining to traded goods as well common input services that are used both for duitable goods/taxable services and for traded goods.

The question that arises in such cases is whether the assessee is entitled to take credit in respect of input services that are specifically pertaining to traded goods as well as common input services that are used both for dutiable goods/taxable services and for traded goods?

Some relevant provisions

2. Section 37 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and section 94 of the Finance Act, 1994 provide powers to the Central Government to make rules to provide for credit of duty or service tax paid/deemed to have been paid on the goods used in, or in relation to manufacture of excisable goods or provision of taxable services. In exercise of these powers, the Central Government has made Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Rule 3 of the Cenvat Credit Rules provides that a manufacturer of final product or provider of taxable service shall be allowed to take credit (Cenvat credit) in respect of any input service received by the manufacturer of final product or by provider of output service.

Rule 2(l) defines ‘input service’ to mean any service;—

"(i )used by a provider of taxable service for providing an output service; or

(ii )used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products, up to the place of removal,

and includes services used in relation to setting up, modernization, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises, advertisement or sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs, activities relating to business, such as accounting, auditing, financing, recruitment and quality control, coaching and training, computer networking, credit rating, share registry, and security, inward transportation of inputs or capital goods and outward transportation up to the place of removal;"

Above definition makes it clear that input services would mean only those services which are used by a provider of taxable service for providing output service or used by a manufacturer in or in relation to manufacture. Hence, any services exclusively used for traded goods would not get covered under the definition of ‘input service’ and Cenvat credit would not be available for the same.

Rule 6 provides for the mechanism for availment of Cenvat credit by a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and providers of taxable and exempted services. Let us try to analyse and see whether traded goods can be considered as exempted goods or exempted services.

Rule 2(d) defines ‘exempted goods’, as excisable goods which are exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon, and includes goods which are chargeable to ‘nil’ rate of duty.

The assessee-firm had availed of the Cenvat credit in terms of rule 3. The credit was disallowed by the Commissioner on the ground that the payment of service tax made by assessee under TR-6 challan could not be treated as evidence and same could not be considered as a prescribed document for the purpose of taking the Cenvat credit.

CCE (2014) 310 ELT 770 (CESTAT). There is no one to one co-relation in Cenvat scheme - PSL Corrosion Control v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 495 (CESTAT).

One to one correlation between credit availed on inputs and its utilisation of final products is not required under Cenvat. The rules do not provide for segregated credits, depending upon inputs and final products made from the inputs - Indian Aluminium v. CCE (2001) 137 ELT 1092 (CEGAT).

No one to one correlation is required for taking Cenvat credit - CCE v. National Trading Co. - (1996) 83 ELT 636 (CEGAT) - both members agreed on this point, though they differed on other points.

CBE&C, vide para 2(viii) of circular No. 33/33/94-CX dated 4-5-1994 has confirmed that there is no 1:1 correlation between input and final product under the Cenvat scheme for utilisation of credit.

Credit by assessee who is manufacturer as well as service provider - Cenvat credit of manufacturing activity can be utilised for payment of service tax since there is no such restriction in Cenvat Credit Rules or CBEC manual - CCE v. Nahar Industrial Enterprises Ltd. (2007) 10 STT 117 (CESTAT SMB) - followed in CCE v. Vardhman Spinning (2008) 14 STT 503 (CESTAT SMB).

Cenvat credit of input service tax can be utilized for payment of excise duty - S S Engineers v. CCE (2015) 317 ELT 597 (CESTAT).

There is no provision in Cenvat credit rules for segregation of input services, which are utilised in manufacture or to provide output service - Forbes Marshall v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT (CESTAT SMB).

There is no provision in Cenvat Credit Rules for segregation of Cenvat credit for payment of excise duty and for payment of service tax. There is no requirement for one to one correlation of Cenvat credit availed on input services towards payment of output service - Jyoti Structures Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 36 STT 645 = 24 taxmann.com 263 = 285 ELT 356 (CESTAT)

Fragmentation of credit not required - Cenvat credit is indefeasible. Its fragmentation to restrict earned credit to particular lines of production is not permissible. Such an allocation of credit raw-material wise or final product-wise is not permitted by the Rule nor it is practicable - Vardhman Spinning v. CCE 2006 (199) ELT 827 (CESTAT).

Thus, Cenvat on inputs for one product may be used for payment of duty on other product of different Chapter. Such credit can be denied only if one product is fully exempt from duty.

Same principle applies to State Vat - In Hindustan Unilever Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2015) 80 VST 370 (T & A HC DB), assessee had manufacturing and trading division. TIN number of same. It was held that input tax credit of one division can be used for payment of sales tax (vat) of other division - same view in Maxwroth Plywoods v. AC(CT) (2013) 62 VST 573 (AP HC DB).

FACT: • During the course of the audit of the records, it was found that the assessee had availed credit of service tax paid on manpower supply service and security service during the period 2005-06 and 2006-07 up to January 2007.

• It was found that even though the invoices issued by the service providers charged service tax but no service tax was paid to the Government.

• Subsequent investigations revealed that the premises given in the invoice and the registration number were found to be wrong and no service tax had been paid by the service providers.

• The assessee pleaded that it was not aware that the firms were non-existent and they were not paying the service tax.

• The assessee objected to invocation of extended period of limitation and imposition of personal penalty on its employee.

• The assessee had also availed credit of telephone services and not made reversal required under rule 6 though it was engaged in trading activity and manufacture of exempted goods.

Assessee's contentions

• They had received the service during the relevant period.

• Since the registration number and the address were available and service was being received, they had a bona fide belief that service tax paid by them to the service providers was in turn paid to the Government of India.

• They had taken all reasonable steps that an ordinary person could have taken.

Revenue's contentions

• The employee of the assessee had clearly stated that they were receiving the services from the two service providers and the service provider suddenly disappeared in January 2007.

• He also admitted that the company had not verified the existence of the service providers and service providers had come to the factory and collected the cheques.

• Thus, it cannot be said that the assessee were not aware of the fraud played by the two service providers.

• Thus, credit was deniable invoking extended period of limitation.

Issue involved

• Whether credit was available ?

• Whether personal penalty could be imposed upon assessee ?

HELD: Assessee failed to take proper steps before availing credit

• The assessee aware of the disappearance of the service provider after January 2007. They did not put any effort to find out even at that stage as to whether the service providers were in existence and whether they had paid service tax collected from them to the Government.

• It was strange that appellants received, services from a service provider whose existence they knew only because he used to come to collect the cheque and they did not even bother to verify whether the office premises in the invoice was in existence or not.

• Since the service provider was located in Vapi itself (place of assessee) would also go against the assessee since it cannot even be their case that ascertaining the existence or otherwise of the service provider was a difficult task.

• The fact that appellant did not make any efforts to locate the service provider nor did they make any effort to intimate the department nor did they debit the amount of credit taken goes against the appellants and therefore it has to be held that the invocation of extended time-limit for demand in this case is sustainable.

• Further, for the same reasons, the assessee is liable to penalty also. [Para 9]

Coming first to the disputed cenvat credits held as ineligible, it is seen that, all of them have been availed after the amendment to rule 2(l) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from 1-4-2011. However, cenvat credits claimed for housekeeping services was very much required for the proper upkeeping of the assessee's premises and in any case the same was not barred from the exclusion clauses of rule 2(l) of CCR 2004. For this reason, the assessee is very much eligible to avail cenvat credit in respect of said housekeeping services, hence appeal on this score is allowed. [Para 8.3]

Coming to the issue of rejected export turnover, it is seen that a part of turnover has been rejected by original authority which decision has been upheld by the lower appellate authority in the impugned order. [Para 9.2]

Discernably, original authority has reduced the export turnover for the reason that said amount relates to FIRCs though received in the relevant quarter, however, export invoices thereof have been raised before 21-6-2012 and hence are beyond the period of one year stipulated under section 11B of the Central Excise Act, since claim has been filed by appellant only on 21-6-2013. [Para 9.4]

There is merit in the contention of assessee that there is a distinction between the definition of Export Turnover of Goods and that of Export Turnover of Services, in rule 5 of the CCR 2004. [Para 9.6]

From the perusal of rule 5, what emerges is that for considering the export turnover of goods, value of final products and intermediate products cleared and exported during the relevant period alone can be taken. However, for calculating export turnover of services, while advances received for export services where provision of service has not been completed during the relevant quarter, will not be taken into account, nonetheless, two other types of turnover will be definitely taken into account as follows :

(i)

Exported services for which advance payment had been received in earlier quarters, but actual export thereof has been effected only during the relevant quarter.

(ii)

Payment received during the relevant quarter for export of services. There is no condition indicated that such payment will be related only for services exported during the relevant quarter. By implication, there is no bar to inclusion of payment received during the relevant period for export of services which have been effected in an earlier quarter. [Para 9.7]

Thus, relevant quarter/period for which refund has been claimed under rule 5 ibid can very well also relate to export of services effected earlier. From a combined reading of the various portions of the definition of 'export services' in rule 5(D), the only requirement is that both receipt of payment and provision of export services should have been completed by, or within the quarter for which the refund claims under rule 5 are being made. That is, if payments had been received earlier and actual export effected only in the relevant period, claim of corresponding credit refund can only be made during the relevant period. So also, if any export of services has been effected earlier but inward remittances/FIRCs have been received only during the relevant quarter for which claim is made, refund of credit amount corresponding to the payments received can only be made during the relevant quarter. In this way, the Government is ensuring that not only services are exported but also payments thereof are received at the point when the refund claim under rule 5 is made. [Para 9.8]

No doubt, the provisions of section 11B have been made applicable to service tax vide section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994. Nonetheless, by the rule of implied exception, the specific provisions of rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, will definitely take precedence following the maxim Generalia Specialibus non derogant according to which when a matter falls under a specific provision, then it must be governed by that provision and not by the general provision. [Para 9.9]

Even in the cases of clandestine removal and in the cases where the assessee has not taken the registration from the Department and whole activity of the assessee was not known to the Department, it has been the practice to allow admissible CENVAT Credit to the assessee, if the assessee is able to show that capital goods are received, documents are available and used by the assessee for manufacture of finished goods even if procedure for availment of CENVAT Credit would not have been followed by the assessee. Just because the returns were filed subsequent to issue of show-cause notice, the requirement under the law for the adjudicating authority to consider availability of CENVAT Credit and allow the benefit of admissible CENVAT Credit while confirming the duty demand does not undergo a change. As per the Cenvat credit return filed along with the ST-3 returns, it was observed that the appellants were availing the credit on advertising, security, courier, telephone and banking services. These services were not entirely used in providing maintenance and repair services but also used in trading activity. Credit of input services, which were entirely used in trading activity, was not available to the appellants for payment of service tax. The total service tax payable for the half-year ending March, 2005 was Rs. 34,143. As per rule 6(3) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, the total Cenvat credit available to the appellants was Rs. 6,828 (20 per cent of Rs. 34,143) only and rest of the amount, i.e., Rs. 27,315 was to be paid by the appellants in cash only. The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and had availed the excess Cenvat credit of Rs. 27,315 which was not admissible to the appellants. Further, it was observed that the total service tax payable for the half-year ending September, 2004 was Rs. 25,363. As per rule 3(5) of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 the total service tax credit available to the appellants was Rs. 8,877 (35 per cent of Rs. 25,363) only and rest of the amount, i.e., Rs. 16,486 was to be paid in cash only. The appellants had adjusted the service tax amount fully from Cenvat credit and had availed the excess Cenvat credit of Rs. 16,486 which was not admissible to the appellants. Accordingly, the appellants had wrongly availed/utilized the Cenvat credit amounting to Rs. 43,801.

2. The lower authorities have taken a view that in view of the provisions of rule 3 and rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, the appellants should have maintained separate accounts in respect of input services used for trading activity and other services which are liable to service tax. Accordingly, the Cenvat credit of Rs. 43,801 availed by the appellants was demanded.

3. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that trading activity is not at all a service. According to rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules, the appellant is required to maintain separate account only in respect of exempted service and dutiable service. Since trading activity cannot be considered a service at all, the question of maintenance of separate accounts does not arise. Further, he also submits that services such as advertisement, security, courier, telephone, banking and professional charges are used commonly for trading activity as well as maintenance and repair, commissioning and installation services. It is not correct to say that these services are not required or have not been utilized for trading activity also. He submits that entire credit has been disallowed without taking this aspect into account even though it had been submitted by the appellants that these services had been used for both the activities. On the other hand, learned DR would submit that the lower authorities after verifying the records have come to the conclusion that these services have not been utilized for trading activity. Further, he also submits that duty demand has been made as per rule 3 of Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. It is his contention that since trading activity is not at all a service, the provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules and provisions of Service Tax Credit Rules cannot be applied.

4. The issues to be decided in this case are :

(i)Whether trading activity can be called a service?

(ii)Whether rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002 and Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002 would be applicable when input services are used in respect of trading activity as well as taxable services?

(iii)If Cenvat Credit Rules and Service Tax Credit Rules are not applicable, what is the procedure to be followed by the assessee for availing input service tax credit?

Credit Rules, 2004 provides for the manner of distribution of credit of Input service. The evolving changes in the same has been elucidated infra:

3.1.1. Prior to 2012

Rule 7 (Manner of distribution of credit by input service distributor) provides that "The input service distributor may distribute the CENVAT credit in respect of the service tax paid on the input service to its manufacturing units or units providing output service, subject to the following condition, namely:- (a)

the credit distributed against a document referred to in rule 9 does not exceed the amount of service tax paid thereon; or

(b)

credit of service tax attributable to service use in a unit exclusively engaged in manufacture of exempted goods or providing of exempted services shall not be distributed."

Till this period, ISD could distribute credit amongst units in any ratio in absence of specific method prescribed in law. The same was held in the case of CCEx., Bangalore-I v. Ec of Industries Pvt. Ltd. [2011 (271) E.L.T. 58 (Kar.)] that "Given the absence of any other condition in rule 7 of the Credit Rules, an Input Service Distributor was permitted to allocate / distribute the credit entirely to a single recipient unit."

3.1.2. From April 2012 to March 2014

Due to amendment made in 2012, an additional restrictions have been introduced as regards the manner of allocation / distribution of credit to the credit recipient units viz.

(i)

credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly in a unit shall be distributed only to that unit; and

(ii)

credit of service tax attributable to service used in more than one unit shall be distributed pro rata on the basis of the turnover during the relevant period of the concerned unit to the sum total of the turnover of all the units to which the service relates during the same period.

The amended rule also incorporates provisions as regards the calculation of turnover values and relevant period to be considered for determination of credit distribution ratios.

3.1.3. From April 2014 to March 2016

From 1 April 2014, Rule 7 was further amended to provide that Turnover of previous month/quarter was replaced by the turnover of units in the preceding year and Turnover of only such units is to be considered which are operational in current year.

3.2. Predicaments in the vivid provisions prevailing till March 2016

3.2.1. The language of Rule 7 was producing doubt in the mind of manufacturers /Service provider as to whether the credit of common Input Service need to be distributed among all the units or to the units to which that service relates. It is clarified vide circular no 178/4/2014­ST that in case of services attributable to more than one unit, credit shall be distributed to all the units (without nexus of input services with the units) in the prescribed ratio irrespective of actual use of services by the units. This creates an absurd situation and also results in loss of credit in some cases when any unit was engaged in providing only exempted service.

3.2.2. Applicability of Rule 6 to the ISD has been the debatable issue since long past. The dissenting views of the departments can be substantiated below:

CBEC circular of 2008 provides that "ISD does not provide any service and is like a trader. Hence question of either option as per Rule 6 of CCR does not arise."

In a Tribunal judgment of 2011 in case of Colgate Palmolive it was held that "assessee is required to reverse cenvat credit on proportionate basis while distributing credit if it is manufacturing both exempted as well as taxable goods."

A guidance note issued by CBEC in 2012 states that "credit is distributed on the strength of a challan issued by ISD and it shall be subject to Rule 6 of CCR"

Accordingly, it can be recapitulated that assessees were pinned between the ambiguity of loosely drafted provisions and its contradicting interpretation by adjudicating and appellate authorities.

3.3. Budget 2016- Problem Solver or Mystery in abundance?

3.3.1 Conquering the infirmity in the prevailing position, Budget 2016 came up with some extoling amendments provided below:

It was provided that Credit attributable to more than one unit but not all units should be distributed to only such units whereas earlier such credit could be distributed to all operational units.

Clause (b) of Rule 7 was deleted which did not permit distribution of credit of service used in a unit exclusively engaged in exempted activity.

Earlier, there prevailed doubts whether credit is to be distributed firstly as per Rule 7 and then, the Cenvat credit entitlement under Rule 6 is to be determined by the unit receiving credit. To overcome this ambiguity, new clause (g) was inserted in Rule 7 to clarify that provisions of Rule 6 shall apply to the units manufacturing goods or provider of output service and not to the ISD. This amendment has ended up the long lasting dispute in the industry.

Commissioner in Revision Order has opined that as per Rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules 2004 'exempted services' means taxable services which are exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon and include services on which no service tax is leviable under Section 66 of the Finance Act. INPUT SERVICES USED FOR SELF-MANUFACTURED AS WELL AS TRADED GOODS

We are manufacturers of engineering products. We also are traders of those products, i.e., we procure these goods under our brand name and sale. We have appointed selling agents for sale of our products (both self-manufactured and traded). We pay selling commission to our indenting agents. The selling agents charge service tax on the commission. We avail Cenvat credit of service tax on selling commission paid by us on traded goods as well as self-manufactured goods, and utilise the same for payment of excise duty on our self-manufactured products. Department has issued a show-cause notice to us, informing that we are not eligible for service tax paid by us on commission attributable to traded goods. Please advise.

You are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax paid both on self-manufactured goods and traded goods, for the following reasons -

(1)Definition of ‘input service’ in rule 2(l) of the Cenvat Credit Rules is very wide. As per inclusive part of the definition, any service in relation to business of assessee is ‘input service’, since the words used are ‘such as’ and not ‘viz.’.

(2)The inclusive part of definition clearly covers ‘sales promotion’. The inclusive part of definition does not require any relation with ‘manufacture’.

(3)Cenvat Credit Rules do not require any one to one relation between input and output.

(4)Even rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not require distribution of Cenvat credit in any particular ratio. Entire credit of service tax at HO or depot or branch offices can be transferred to any unit without any restriction. The rule makes no distinction between services used for manufacture and services used for other activities like trading, financing, etc.

(5)The Finance Minister in para 148 of his Budget Speech on 8-7-2004 has stated as follows, "I propose to take a major step towards integrating tax on goods and services. Accordingly, I propose to extend credit of service tax and excise duty across goods and services".

(6)Thus, the Cenvat Credit Rules have to be interpreted keeping this goal in mind and, hence, cannot be interpreted narrowly. As per doctrine of purposive interpretation, an interpretation which advances purpose of the Statute should be preferred over an interpretation which defeats the purpose.

(7)It is clear that after introduction of the Cenvat Credit Rules, the whole company is treated as one single entity for Cenvat credit. The definition of ‘input service’ and ‘input service distributor’ has abolished distinction between ‘goods’, ‘manufacture’ and ‘services’. Entire company is treated as one unit for purpose of Cenvat credit, as is the position under ‘Goods and Service Tax’ (GST) which has been set as the goal. Even concept of ‘LTU’ (Large Taxpayer Unit) is a step in that direction.

(8)Even assuming that there is some ambiguity (though really there is none), it is well-settled principle that the benefit of doubt goes to assessee.

Thus, Cenvat credit availed by you is legally correct.

However, you must keep in mind that current decisions of Tribunal are highly conservative and, hence, ultimate result is uncertain. You should be mentally prepared to pay interest @ 13%, if final decision goes against you.

ALLOWABILITY OF INPUT CREDIT FOR TAXABLE AND EXEMPT SERVICES - OPTIONS, CONTRADICTION AND CONFUSION GALORE

Despite having various positive aspects, levying tax on the basis of value addition has its own set of problems. In cases where tax cannot be charged for various reasons, generally an issue arises, that is, how to deal with Input Credit (IC). Determination of IC attributable to taxable services is much simpler than in case of exempt services. Budget 2008 made drastic changes in this area by making amendment in rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. In the opinion of the author, this contains lot of confusion and contradictions as the terminology used is confusing and some of the provisions are contradictory to other provisions. An attempt has been made in this comprehensive article to explain the provisions of rule 6 and the terminology associated with it in detailed manner.

Introduction

1. Despite having various positive aspects, levying tax on the basis of value addition has its own set of problems. The tax structure has to take cognizance of certain special cases wherein tax cannot be charged for various reasons. An issue that arises in such cases is, how to deal with Input Credit (IC) availed in respect of such services. Since the Government is not deriving any revenue, it will be reluctant to permit IC on it. If the services dealt with are the only taxable item for the assessee, the things would have been much simpler. However, the issue arises in the case where both, i.e., taxable and exempt, services are dealt with. Determination of IC attributable to exempt services raises various issues. Ideally the assessee can be asked to maintain separate records in respect of IC as applicable to taxable and exempt services and claim IC as applicable to taxable services only. To some extent it may be possible in the case of tangible goods. However, it may not be so in the case of services which are intangible. Apart from that, in real life, it may not be possible to maintain so much of detailed records. Even if one tries to do so the cost may outweigh the benefits derived.

Scenario before Budget 2008

2. Prior to 2008 the assessees were given two options, viz., to maintain separate records with respect to inputs and Input Services (IS) for receipt and consumption, etc., and for Exempt Services (ExS). Rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 (‘the Rules’) made detailed provisions in this respect. Another option as provided under rule 6(3)(i ) was to keep the IC restricted to 20 per cent of the ST payable. Under this arrangement, the assessee, despite having substantial IC entitlement, was required to pay ST. In the case of Service Providers (SP), having substantial volume of taxable services and low volume of ExS, this was turning out to be a losing proposition as it involved cash-outflow. To some extent it was not logical in the sense that the assessee was required to pay tax while large amount of IC was forced to remain unutilised.

Post-Budget Scenario

3. Budget 2008 made drastic changes in this area. The assessee has been provided with more options. Without disturbing the provisions of rule 6(2), i.e., permitting the assessee to maintain detailed records for IC for ExS and ExG, erstwhile rule 6(3) has been replaced with new rule giving two more options to the assessee. Initially, while reading the Finance Minister’s Budget Speech one was led to believe about pragmatic approach of the revenue to the problems of the assessee. However, as it happens in the life wherein things can never be so simple, there is no reason for taxation to be the exception to the said rule. Even a cursory glance at the provisions of rule 6(3) will make the reader uncomfortable as it involves the terminology which looks the same every where. Secondly, the formula for computation which should have been put in mathematical format has been described in text format.

Understanding the basic terms

4. Before trying to understand the provisions of rule 6, it will be appropriate to have basic understanding of certain terms used most frequently. They are ‘exempt goods’, ‘exempt services’, ‘export of goods’ services’, ‘services not liable to tax’, ‘availment of Cenvat credit’ and ‘utilisation of Cenvat credit’.

The assessee, a manufacturer of excisable goods, availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on 'courier services' for the period after 1-4-2011.

It also availed cenvat credit of service tax on 'rent-a-cab service'.

NEW CENVAT CREDIT RULE 6(3) AND 6(3A) - A PANDORA’S BOX

New Cenvat credit rule 6(3) (to be effective from April 1, 2008) is correct so far as Cenvat principles are concerned. However, in practice the calculations as provided in rule 6(3) and 6(3A) are so complicated that even with help of professional chartered/cost accountant, the calculation of amount of Cenvat credit is going to be a big problem. Many issues remain unanswered in the rule and it is bound to open Pandora’s Box. In this article, the provisions of new rule are discussed and difficulties analyzed. As drafted, the new rule is incomplete and does not provide for many situations. There are some drafting mistakes also.

No Cenvat credit if final product/service exempt

1. As per the basic principle of VAT, credit of duty or tax can be availed of only for payment of duty on final product or output services. As a natural corollary, if no duty is payable on final product or output services, credit of duty/tax paid on inputs or input services cannot be availed. This principle has been embodied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

As per rule 6(1) of the Rules, Cenvat credit is not admissible on such quantity of inputs or input service which is used in manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services [The words ‘provision of’ are inserted with effect from April 1, 2008, but this is only clarificatory amendment]. Thus, if inputs and input services are partly used in exempted final product/output service, Cenvat credit of that portion of inputs/input service will not be available.

(a) Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services - Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/taxable services and partly for exempted goods/services.

In such cases, the earlier rule 6 provided two options - (a) Forget about Cenvat credit of common inputs and input services (b) Pay 10 per cent ‘amount’ on exempted goods and/or restrict Cenvat credit to 20 per cent of service tax on output services.

Now, under new rule 6, the manufacturer/service provider has following three options with effect from April 1, 2008 -

(i) Maintain separate accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services and take Cenvat credit only of inputs and input services used in dutiable goods and taxable output services - Rule 6(2) of the Cenvat Credit Rules - same as earlier rule.

(ii) Pay amount equal to 10 per cent of value of exempted goods (if he is ‘manufacturer’) and/or 8 per cent of value of exempted services (if he is service provider), if he does not maintain separate accounts of inputs and input services - Rule 6(3)(i) with effect from April 1, 2008.

(iii) Pay an ‘amount’ equal to proportionate Cenvat credit attributable to exempted final product/exempted output services, if he does not maintain separate accounts of inputs and input services - Rule 6(3)(ii) with effect from April 1, 2008.

(b) Cenvat credit on capital goods - If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and partly for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products - rule 6(4).

(c) Some services eligible even if partly used for manufacture of exempted goods/output services - Rule 6(5) provides that in case of specified 16 services, full Cenvat credit of input service is available even if these services are partly used in manufacture of exempted final product/output services. Rule 6(5) has been given overriding effect over rules 6(1), 6(2) and 6(3).

In case of these services, reversal of Cenvat or payment of ‘amount’ is not required, if these services are even partly used for providing output service or manufacture of dutiable final product. Cenvat credit will be disallowed only when these services are used exclusively in manufacture of exempted final product or exempted output service.

(viii) Can a trader avail input service tax credit? - Where the manufacturer of excisable goods has no exempted final product but has trading activity, it is worthwhile to note that rule 6 does not cover such cases specifically. The credits in respect of inputs used for manufacture can be claimed as there is manufacturing involved. In respect of input services, the assessee can examine following the procedure given below, that is, to split the input services that are common in nature into two categories. (i )16 services specified under rule 6 which would be eligible to full credits.

(ii )Those services which cannot be related to any specific activity and in such cases, the credits can be apportioned between the trading activity and the manufacturing activity on a reasonable basis. Basis could be relative turnovers or the usage of the internal resources of the organization where that would be more appropriate. This can be followed where the assessee is risk averse.

(iii )The other view could be that trading activity is distinct from manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services and, in such cases, exclude the said trading turnover from the formula explained above. This, however, could be taken up under intimation to the department to be on the safer side of the law.

(ix) Can CENVAT credit be disallowed on appeal being not filed? - Under rule 3 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, a manufacturer or producer of final product is allowed to take credit of input, input services and capital goods as per the conditions laid down therein. The CENVAT credit is a substantive benefit and cannot be denied in the absence of any legitimate reason. The similar issue was recently decided by CESTAT in Magnet Industries (Cal.) (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 12 STT 32 (CESTAT - Kolkata) wherein it was held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied merely for the reason that the same was not claimed in the appeal and that dues cannot be denied, if such dues are legitimate and patent from record. This was also in tune with Circular No. 218/52/96-CX, dated June 4, 1996. The Tribunal held that there cannot be any other conclusion, but only conclusion to be drawn is in consonance with the Circular as aforesaid to grant relief of CENVAT credit to the appellants, claiming or not claiming in appeal and to grant relief is delivers of due to the deserved on the facts and circumstances of each case. Uniformity and consistency as well as majesty being ordain of justice, the due cannot be denied, if such due is legitimate and patent from record. Therefore, the authorities below, denying CENVAT credit to the appellants and levy of penalty as well as interest had deprived the appellants from the due process of justice. Such injustice could only be ruled out setting aside the order of the authorities below to meet the ends of justice. Thus, in such cases, CENVAT credit cannot be denied.

(x) Utilization of CENVAT Credit in Capital Goods - The assessee can take full credit of duty paid on capital goods but utilize only 50 per cent thereof as provided in the CENVAT Credit Rules as per the restriction provided in rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. As such, the assessee can utilize the credit to the extent of limit of 50 per cent allowed as per law. There is no wrong utilization of the CENVAT credit nor there is any evidence of fraud or mis-statement or suppression of facts. There is no scope for levy of penalty by the department under rule 15 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. A similar view was taken by the Tribunal in CCE, Rohtak v. Surya Vinayak Industries (P.) Ltd. [(2007) (CESTAT - New Delhi)] and Delphi Automotive Systems v. CCE, Noida [2004 (163) ELT 47 (CESTAT, New Delhi)] relying upon the Apex Court judgment in P & B Pharmaceuticals (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2003 (153) ELT 14 (SC)].

(xi) Denial of CENVAT Credit when invoices issued from Unregistered Premises - A dealer has to issue a valid invoice and there is no condition in the CENVAT credit rules/excise rules that the invoices issuing office of the dealer should be registered with the department. However, the dealer must be registered with the Central Excise Department. In CCE v. Myrorn Electricials (P.) Ltd. [2007 (207) ELT 664 (Punj. & Har.)], the High Court held that CENVAT credit cannot be denied on the ground that invoices have been issued by the dealer from the premises other that for which Central Excise registration had been granted in view of Central Excise Notification No. 7/99-CE, which amended earlier rule 57G of Central Excise Rules, 1944. The Supreme Court also dismissed the departmental appeal on the same issue 2007 (215) ELT A76. Therefore, it can be said that what is important is raising of an invoice by a registered dealer and not a raising of an invoice from a registered premises.

22.6-3 Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules has been revamped w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

As per revised rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2016, the distribution should be as follows—

(a)

Credit distributed should not be more than credit of input service tax available.

(b)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly by a unit shall be distributed only to that unit.

(c)

Credit of service tax attributable to services used by more than one unit (but not to all units) shall be distributed pro rata on the basis of turnover of such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of such units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(d)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used by all the units shall be distributed pro rata on the basis of turnover of all such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of all the units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(e)

The Cenvat credit can be distributed to 'outsourced manufacturing unit'. Such 'outsourced manufacturing unit' can utilize the Cenvat credit only for purpose of payment of duty on goods manufactured for such input service distributor.

(f)

Credit of Cenvat credit as on 31-3-2016 shall not be distributed to outsourced manufacturing unit.

(g)

Provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules applies to units manufacturing excisable goods or provider of output service. It shall not apply to input service distributor. Thus, ISD should distribute on basis of total turnover of goods and services (exempted as well as taxable).

Meaning of 'unit' -'Unit' includes premises of provider of output service and the premises of a manufacturer, including the factory, whether registered or otherwise or the premises of outsourced manufacturing unit - - Explanation 1 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Meaning of total turnover - Total turnover will be calculates per provisions of rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules. Turnover of outsourced manufacturing unit will be only of goods manufactured by the outsourced manufacturing unit for the Input Service Distributor - Explanation 2 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Meaning of 'relevant period' - 'Relevant Period' means (a) if the assessee has turnover in the 'financial year' preceding to the year during which credit is to be distributed for the month or quarter, as the case may be, the said financial year or (b) If the assessee does not have turnover for some or all the units in the preceding financial year, the last quarter for which details of turnover of all the units are available, previous to the month or quarter for which credit is to be distributed - Explanation 3 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Thus, if Cenvat Credit for July 2016 is to be distributed and if all the units of assessee were working in financial year 2015-16, then distribution should be on basis of turnover of each unit during 2016-17. However, if some of the units started operations after April 2016, then turnover for April 2016 - June 2016 will have to be considered for distributing the Cenvat credit to various units.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

(v) Claiming of depreciation under CENVAT Credit Rules - As per rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, an assessee is allowed to take CENVAT credit of amount not exceeding 50 per cent of the excise duty paid on capital goods in the financial year of its receipt and the balance in the subsequent financial years. It also provides that CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods shall not be allowed on that part of its value, which the assessee includes in the value of the capital goods for the purpose of claiming depreciation under section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. These provisions do not bar the assessee from claiming depreciation of the unavailed amount of credit in the year of receipt of the capital goods in income-tax returns for the relevant assessment year. In Suprajit Engg. Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (212) ELT 394 (Trib. - Bang.), it was held that the assessee had not violated the rules for the simple reason that they had availed depreciation only in respect of that portion of duty on which they had not taken CENVAT credit. In Roots Cast (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2007 (216) ELT 448 (Chennai - CESTAT)], it has been held that depreciation of unavailed credit under the Act can be claimed in the year of receipt of goods.

(vi) Transfer of Credit - Rule 10 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 (‘Rules’ for short) deals with the transfer of credit. It provides that if a manufacturer of the final product shifts his factory to another site or the factory is transferred on account of change in ownership or on account of sale, merger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the factory to a joint venture with the specific provision for transfer of liabilities of such factory, then the manufacturer shall be allowed to transfer the CENVAT credit lying unutilized in his accounts to such transferred, sold, merged, leased or amalgamated factory.

If a provider of output service shifts or transfers his business on account of change in ownership or on account of sale, merger, amalgamation, lease or transfer of the business to a joint venture with the specific provision for transfer of liabilities of such business, then the provider of output service shall be allowed to transfer the CENVAT credit lying unutilized in his account to such transferred, sold, merged, leased or amalgamated business.

The transfer of CENVAT credit shall be allowed only if the stock of inputs as such or in process, or the capital goods, is also transferred with the factory or business premises to the new site or ownership and the inputs, or capital goods, on which credit has been availed of are duly accounted for to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise or as the case may be, the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise.

Case study - CCE v. SmithKline Beecham Consumer Health Care Ltd. - [(2008) (CESTAT - Chennai)] - The inputs, on which credit has been availed, had been duly accounted for the satisfaction of the Commissioner having jurisdiction over the old unit and, therefore, the requirement of physical transfer of stock of inputs from the old unit to the new one stood fulfilled. The department cannot any longer object to the utilization of the credit by the new unit.

Hindustan Lever Ltd. v. CCE - [(2007) - (Mum. - CESTAT] - The goods manufactured earlier remained the same even after change in management. The appellants sought the permission from the authorities well in advance and after having waited for two years, they effected transfer of credit again informing the authorities. The procedure in seeking permission was rightly followed. There being no communication from the authorities concerned either granting or refusing the permission, it shall be deemed to have been granted after a lapse of reasonable length of time.

(vii) Can credit be availed on receipt of services from abroad - Yes. Where the services received qualify as input services within the meaning of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004, the same would qualify for credit availment once the payment of service tax on such services received from abroad, has been made. In a case where these payments are substantial, the payment may be made in the last week of the month to enable early credit availment.

(viii) Can a trader avail input service tax credit? - Where the manufacturer of excisable goods has no exempted final product but has trading activity, it is worthwhile to note that rule 6 does not cover such cases specifically. The credits in respect of inputs used for manufacture can be claimed as there is manufacturing involved. In respect of input services, the assessee can examine following the procedure given below, that is, to split the input services that are common in nature into two categories.

The assessee, a service provider, had three departments. The department 'A' provided taxable service. The department 'B' provided exempted service. The department 'C' received the input service.

The assessee allocated the cenvat credit of service tax paid on input service availed by the department 'C' to the department 'A' to the extent of Rs. 1.11 crores and the department 'B' to the extent of Rs. 6.66 lakhs on the ratio of the turnover.

The Adjudicating Authority disallowed the entire cenvat credit allocated to the department 'A' on the ground that the department 'B', which provided exempted service, availed part of the cenvat credit.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal the revenue submitted that when the manufacturer or the service provider provides taxable service as well as exempted service, he comes under rule 6(2) to maintain record for verification by revenue. Once the assessee comes under rule 6(2), in that circumstance, application of rule 6(2) and rule 6(3) simultaneously is not possible. The assessee failed to comply with the condition prescribed by rule 6(3) read with rule 6(3A). Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has rightly denied the entire cenvat credit of Rs. 1.11 crores allocated to the department 'A'.

Under Rule 14 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 recovery can be made only from the person who has availed the wrong cenvat credit. In the present case, the cenvat credit has been wrongly availed by the manufacturing unit and the Revenue is asking them only to pay back the incorrectly availed cenvat credit. We therefore do not find any force in the arguments of the counsel and is therefore rejected. In our view, the letter of the Board is correct and is in order.

6. One of the contentions in the appeal filed by the appellant is that the trading is not a service or exempted service and hence provisions of Rule 6 would not be applicable. The issue whether trading is a service or exempted service was examined in the case of Mercedes Benz India (P.) Ltd. (supra) case and this Tribunal has come to same conclusion. We entirely agree with the contention of the appellant that trading is not a service or exempted service during the relevant period. We also agree that provisions of Rule 6 may not be directly applicable. However, it is to be noted that the definition of 'input service' in the Cenvat Credit Rule is 'any service' used by the provider of taxable service for providing output service or used by the manufacturer whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and clearance of final products up to the place of removal. However, inclusive part of the definition list out certain services and as held by various courts that these services have to relate with the business of manufacture or business of providing taxable service. Thus, these services cannot be in relation to the trading activity. Thus, the appellant could not have taken the entire amount of credit of input services. We also note that Revenue has denied credit of service tax in proportion of trading goods.

9.11 Provisions upto 31-3-2008

Rule 6(3) has been radically changed w.e.f. 1-4-2008. Provisions upto 31-3-2008 are summarised below.

If assessee opts not to maintain separate accounts in respect of inputs and input services utilised for exempted goods/exempted output services as required under rule 6(2), he has to pay ‘amount’ of 10% of total price (excluding taxes) of exempted final product [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

In case of output services, he could utilise credit only upto 20% of service tax on output services. [He could ‘take’ full credit of service tax on input services, but utilise only upto 20% of tax payable on output services].

The third option i.e. proportionate reversal of Cenvat credit was not available upto 31-3-2008.

Partial manufacture/provision of exempted products/services — Cenvat credit of inputs and input services is not available if final product/output service is exempt from excise duty/service tax. In case of manufacturer manufacturing both exempt and dutiable goods (or service provider providing taxable as well as exempt services), it may happen that same inputs/input services are used partly for manufacture of dutiable goods/output services and partly for exempted goods/services. In such cases, the manufacturer/service provider has two options — (a) Maintain separate inventory and accounts of receipt and use of inputs and input services used for exempted goods/exempted output services. In such cases, he should not avail Cenvat credit of the inputs and input services which are used in exempted final services at all — Rule 6(2) of Cenvat Credit Rules (b) Pay 10% ‘amount’ if he does not maintain separate inventory and records, if he is a manufacturer — Rule 6(3)(b) [If he is service provider, his credit is restricted to 20% of tax payable, as explained later] [provision upto 31-3-2008]

‘Amount’ if separate inventory and records not maintained - If the manufacturer opts not to maintain such separate accounts, he has to pay an amount equal to 10% of the ‘price’ of such exempted goods. Such payment can be made by debit to Cenvat credit account or PLA [rule 6(3)(b) as existing upto 31-3-2008].

Reversal of Cenvat credit in case of some exempted goods - In case of some specified exempted goods, the manufacturer of these final products only has to reverse Cenvat credit they had taken on inputs and input services, which were used for manufacture of exempted final product. - Rule 6(3)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Cenvat credit on capital goods — If capital goods are partly used for exempted goods and party for dutiable final products, entire Cenvat credit of duty paid on capital goods is available. Cenvat credit of duty on capital goods is not allowable only when it is exclusively used for manufacture of final products [rule 6(4)] — confirmed in Idea Cellular v. CCE (2009) 19 STT 423 = 36 VST 217 (CESTAT).

No reversal or payment of amount in certain cases — If excisable goods are removed to SEZ unit, SEZ developer, EOU, EHTP, STP, UN agencies or for exports or removal of gold or silver arising in manufacture of copper or zinc by smelting, payment of 10% ‘amount’ is not required [rule 6(6)].

Cenvat credit of service tax in case of supplies made by DTA to EOU - Supplies from DTA to EOU are entitled to Cenvat credit of service tax paid — para 6.11(v) of FTP.

Proportional Cenvat in case of general insurance companies providing taxable as well as exempt services - Rule 6(3)(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2007 provided an option to general insurance service providers providing taxable as well as exempted insurance schemes and who do not maintain separate input/input services credit accounts, to utilise Cenvat credit proportionate to the inputs and input services used in providing output services. The scheme was applicable only to general insurance services referred to in section 65(105)(d) and is optional - para 11.1 of D.O. F. No. 334/1/2007-TRU dated 28-2-2007 issued by Shri R Sekar, Joint Secretary (TRU). Now this specific provision has been deleted w.e.f. 1-4-2008.

Input credit was not reversible

• Prior to 11-5-2007, there was no embargo on availment of CENVAT credit on written-off inputs. In view of judgment in Phillips Electronics India Ltd. v. CCE 2011 (274) ELT 311 (Tri. -Mum.), wherein it was held that any CENVAT credit taken on any input written-off in financial account of the assessee prior to 11-5-2007 was not liable to be reversed, the denial of CENVAT credit was invalid. [Para 1]

CENVAT Credit on input services

• Pest control - Eligible : The claim for CENVAT credit on pest control was admissible in view of judgment in VST Industries Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (262) ELT 749 (Tri-Bang.) [Para 5]

• AMC for ST plant for sewage disposal - Eligible : The claim in respect of AMC for ST plant for sewage disposal was supported by the Tribunal's decision in Manikgarh Cement. v. CCE [Final Order No. A/84/2011-WZB/C-IV (SMB), dated 22-1-2010][Para 5]

• AMC for air conditioners for instrumentation room - Eligible : The air conditioners were installed in assessee's instrumentation room for the purpose of testing their products. Hence, there was nexus between the said service and the manufacture of excisable products by the assessee inasmuch as testing of the products in the factory is an imperative requirement pre-clearance. The requisite nexus having been established, the denial of CENVAT credit on the said service was invalid. (Para 5)

• Outdoor catering - Not eligible : In CCE v. Stanzen Toyotetsu India (P) Ltd., [2011] 32 STT 244/ 12 taxmann.com 101 (Kar.) referring to the mandatory provisions of section 46 of the Factories Act, it was held that CENVAT credit could not be denied to the assessee in respect of outdoor catering service (canteen facility) as it was their statutory liability to maintain a canteen where the number of employees was more than 250. This statutory liability under section 46 of the Factories Act does not exist in the instant case as the assessee admittedly did not have 250 or more employees/workers during the material period. Hence, in view of CCE v. GTC Industries Ltd. [2008] 17 STT 63 (Mum.-Cestat) upheld in CCE v. Ultratech Cement Ltd. [2010] 29 STT 244 (Bom.), credit was not admissible. [Para 5]

• AMC for computers - Eligible : Computers were used for manifold purposes in connection with manufacture and clearance of their products. A certain part of the CENVAT credit taken on AMC for computers was reversed by the assessee accepting the fact that this much credit was not used in connection with manufacture or clearance of their products. As regards the remaining part of the credit, as already noted, there was no rebuttal of the requisite nexus with the manufacture/clearance of excisable goods. If that be so, the credit was eligible to be taken. [Para 6]

• Air travel agent's service for employees - Not Eligible : Assessee's employees had to travel extensively in connection with the business of the assessee. However, there is no documentary evidence to show that the air travels made by the employees were in connection with the business of manufacturing and marketing of excisable products and not as part of any welfare scheme for the employees. In this scenario, the challenge against denial of CENVAT credit on air travel agent's service failed and credit was not be allowed. [Para 10]

• Online auction service - Eligible : The assessee used this service for disposal, by auction, of scrap which was generated in the course of manufacture of their final products. The scrap was also cleared on payment of duty. If that be so, online auction resorted to by the assessee was an input service used for clearance of excisable goods. A direct nexus stands established between online auction service and the clearance of excisable goods. [Para 10]

The following is a rule-wise list of the changes made in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 vide the Union Budget 2016-17 and subsequent notifications.

Unless otherwise stated, the amending notification is Notification No. 13/2016-CE(NT), dated 1-3-2016 and effective date of amendment is 1-4-2016. Note 1 — Only 2 options for reversal of CENVAT Credit specified — "Non-exempted goods removed", "exempted goods removed" and "non-exempted services" defined for rule 6(3) & 6(3A)

Rule 6(3) [old] : (3) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (1) and (2), the manufacturer of goods or the provider of output service, opting not to maintain separate accounts, shall follow any one of the following options, as applicable to him, namely:- (i) pay an amount equal to six per cent of value…..]

Rule 6(3) [new] : A manufacturer who manufactures two classes of goods, namely :- (i) non-exempted goods removed; (ii) exempted goods removed; or (b) a provider of output service who provides two classes of services, namely:- (i) non-exempted services…

Where a manufacturer deals in manufacturing of exempted goods as well as non-exempted goods, for clearance upto the place of removal or a provider of output service provides both exempted and non-exempted Services, then the assessee has option to pay (Reverse Credit) duty under two options:

i.

Pay an amount equal to 6% of value of the exempted goods and 7% value of the exempted services, subject to a maximum of the sum total of opening balance of the credit of input and input services available at the beginning of the period to which the payment relates and the credit of input and input services taken during that period, or

ii.

Pay an amount as determined under sub-rule (3A)

If any duty of excise is paid on the exempted goods, the assessee shall get the credit of the same under sub-clause (i) above. If any part of Taxable service is exempted on condition of non-allowance of CENVAT Credit of Inputs or Input Services, then also an amount equal to seven per cent of the exempted value shall be paid under sub-clause (i). The rate specified under sub-clause (i) shall be reduced to two per cent of the value of exempted services in the case of transportation of goods or passengers by rail. Once any option is availed under this sub-rule, the assessee shall have to follow the same option during the year.

Note 2 — Amendment in rule 6(3A) — Procedure for reversal payment of duty (CENVAT Reversal) under sub-clause (ii) of Rule 6(3):

No CENVAT is allowed for Inputs & Inputs Services used exclusively or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods removed or for provision of exempted services. This credit is called 'Ineligible Credit'. The whole amount of CENVAT paid on Input has to be paid/reversed. This is denoted by "A".

100% of CENVAT Credit shall be allowed for Inputs & Inputs Services used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of non-exempted goods removed or for the provision of non-exempted services. This credit is called 'Eligible Credit'. This is denoted by "B". No payment or reversal in this case.

Credit left after reducing 'A' & 'B' from the Total Credit (denoted by "T") shall be the "Common Credit" denoted by "C". C = T – (A + B)

Common Credit (C) shall be attributed towards exempted goods and exempted services by multiplying the common credit with the ratio of value of exempted goods manufactured or exempted services provided to the total value of exempted and non-exempted goods and exempted and non-exempted services in the preceding financial year.

D = (E/F) × C

Where,—

D = Ineligible Common Credit

E = Sum total of value of exempted goods manufactured or exempted services provided

F = Sum total of value of exempted and non-exempted goods and exempted and non-exempted services

A deemed rate of 50% shall be taken as "D" if there were no final products manufactured or no output service was provided during the previous Financial Year.

The remaining Common Credit (Eligible Common Credit, denoted by "G") shall be computed in following manner : G = C – D

The above-mentioned calculation shall be done on monthly provisional basis on turnover of previous year and subsequently shall be calculated on actual basis on or before 30th June of subsequent year. The differential amount, if any is to be paid along with interest.
