A Ltd. has procured convention services for its business activities. As a part of the package deal, the hotel provides to airport pick and drop facility, promotion material alongwith the conference hall. Hotel raises a single invoice for all the three activities and recovers service tax on the gross consideration. Whether A Ltd. is eligible to claim Cenvat credit of the entire service tax so paid or A Ltd. would need to proportionately reduce the Cenvat credit relating to airport transfer facility? The provision of convention services by the hotel will be considered as bundled service comprising of conference hall, promotion material and cab facility. As per section 66F of the Act, "bundled service" means a bundle of provision of various services wherein an element of provision of one service is combined with an element or elements of provision of any other service or services. If such services are bundled in the ordinary course of business, then the bundle of services is treated as consisting entirely of such service which determines the dominant nature of such a bundle. In the present case, the intention of A Ltd. is to obtain convention services and provision of cab facilities for travel to and from airport is naturally bundled with the same. Hence, A Ltd., should be eligible to claim entire Cenvat credit and there is no need to reduce the Cenvat credit in proportion to the service tax pertaining to cab services.

A Ltd. has purchased Software for provision of output services. The cost of the software is expensed off in the profit and loss account. Whether A Ltd. is eligible to claim Cenvat credit on software as 'inputs' or as 'capital goods'?

As per rule 2(a) of the Credit Rules, the term capital goods has been defined in an exhaustive manner. It includes all goods falling in specified Chapter headings which, inter alia, include Chapter 82, Chapter 84, Chapter 85, etc. Thus, the software that falls under Chapter 85 (i.e., information technology software on a media), shalls be treated as capital goods when used for providing output service. Even if the value of software has been expensed off in the profit and loss account, the same will be treated as capital goods for the Cenvat credit purposes. Treatment in the books of account will not decide the Cenvat credit eligibility. Hence, A Ltd. will be eligible to the Cenvat credit on software as 'capital goods'. Given this, the Cenvat credit will be available in two equal annual instalments. However, softwares other than those covered under Chapter 85 (i.e., softwares procured electronically) will qualify as input service if used for providing output service and CENVAT credit thereon can be claimed in one go.

Whether Cenvat credit on telephone bills addressed in the name of the company can be claimed on the basis of the electronic invoices received via e-mails or the company would require original hard copy of invoices for claiming the Cenvat credit?

In terms of rule 9(1) of the Credit Rules, the provider of output services can claim Cenvat credit on the telephone bills addressed in the name of the company on the basis of the 'invoice issued' by the provider of an output service. The eligibility of Cenvat credit is not dependent upon the mode of receipt of the invoice. Thus, so long as the invoice issued by the telecom company is addressed in the name of the recipient-company and all other conditions for claiming credit, such as nexus with the output service, are fulfilled the service recipient will be eligible to claim Cenvat credit. Receipt of invoice via e-mail will not disentitle the company from claiming the Cenvat credit.

Whether A Ltd. can claim Cenvat credit on inputs or input services or capital goods received prior to the service tax registration?

A Ltd. can claim Cenvat credit on inputs or input services or capital goods received prior to obtaining service tax registration, provided eligibility criteria/tests for qualifying as inputs, input services and capital goods are met. Reference may be drawn to the following case laws:

In J R Herbal Care India Ltd. v. CCE 2010 (253) ELT 321 (Trib.- Delhi), it was held that there is no provision, in law, that Cenvat credit is not available to unregistered manufacturer.

In Sew Construction Ltd. v. CCE [2011] 32 STT 120/12 taxmann.com 12 (CESTAT- New Delhi), demand for the period prior to registration was confirmed and it was held that the assessee would be eligible for the Cenvat credit on inputs, if that is not otherwise deniable.

In CCE v. Progressive Systems [2012] 36 STT 30/22 taxmann.com 119 (Kar.), followed in Naughty Foods v. CCE [2012] 37 STT 584/27 taxmann.com 67 (Delhi - CESTAT), it was held that an SSI unit could take the Cenvat credit of capital goods received when he was not registered. He could utilise the credit when he was registered and started payment of excise duty.

Concept of Input Service Distributor is compulsory w.e.f. 1-4-2012 if assessee has more than one factories or places of provision of service

22.6-1 As per Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as existing upto 31-3-2012, the Cenvat Credit could be distributed by Input Service Distributor in any ratio. Only restriction was that Cenvat credit distributed should not be more than available credit.

However, after 1-4-2012, the distribution is required to be on basis of turnover.

Assessee having only one factory or place of provision of service - Sometimes, an assessee has offices at various places but accounting is done centrally in the factory. Sometimes, there are various factories of assessee but accounting is done in main factory.

In such cases, in my opinion, if assessee has only one factory and/or one centralised registration of service tax, the HO or branches need not be registered and all Cenvat credit can be availed in the factory or place where centralised registration has been taken.

The reason is that Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules reads, 'The input service distributor may distribute the Cenvat credit'. 'May' cannot be read as 'must'. It is nowhere stated that the utilisation should be only through mechanism of Input Service Distributor. A facility cannot be a compulsion.

In CIT v. Mahendra Mills 2000 AIR SCW 1016 = AIR 2000 SC 1960 = 243 ITR 56 = 109 Taxman 225 (SC), it was observed, 'A privilege cannot be to a disadvantage and an option cannot become an obligation'.

In Durferrit Asea v. CCE (2010) 258 ELT 414 (CESTAT SMB), it was held that if assessee has only one manufacturing unit, HO need not be registered and Cenvat credit can be taken at factory even if invoices are with address of Head Office. Rule 7 is not compulsory if assessee is not inclined to do so.

In Manipal Advertising Services v. CCE (2010) 25 STT 30 (CESTAT), branch offices were not registered with service tax authorities. Invoices were with address of branch, but payment was made from registered premises. It was held that Cenvat credit is available at HO which had Centralised registration as it had centralised accounting system. It was held that Cenvat credit is available even if address on invoice is of branch office.

Invoice of service in name of HO is eligible. It is not necessary that HO should be registered as Input Service Distributor (when there is only one factory) - CCE v. Samita Conductors (2012) 278 ELT 492 (CESTAT SMB) * Valco Industries Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 42 GST 165 = 31 taxmann.com 360 = 286 ELT 54 (CESTAT SMB).

If assessee has only one manufacturing unit, registration as Input service Distributor is not required. Assessee can take Cenvat credit even if invoice is with address of Head Office - National Plastic Industries v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 193 = 20 taxmann.com 132 (CESTAT) * Bloom Dekor v. CCE (2013) 38 STT 336 = 29 taxmann.com 357 (CESTAT SMB).

In Doshion Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 288 ELT 291 (CESTAT), it was held that since assessee could distribute Cenvat Credit in any ratio upto 31-3-2012, the HO could distribute credit to its unit without registration as Input Service Distributor.

In WNS Global Services v. CCE (2013) 30 taxmann.com 208 (CESTAT), it was held that Cenvat credit is allowable even if assessee was not registered as Input Service Distributor.

33. Their services cannot come under the category of "Practising CA Services" since they are not registered in India. Legal consultancy is presently not taxable in India. Appellant also relied upon the judgment of CESTAT Mumbai in the case of Flat Products Equipments (I) Ltd. v. CCE 2011 (272) ELT 104 (Tri.-Mum.). None appeared on behalf of the appellant during the hearing fixed but they filed the written submission dated 28-3-2013 and relied upon TIOL news service that as per CESTAT Mumbai Bench decision in Plus Paper Foodpac Ltd. v. CCE [2013] 42 GST 217/33 taxmann.com 411 (Mum. - CESTAT) the issue is settled in their favour.

2. On the other hand ld. A.R. relied upon the following judgments in support of the fact that services in relation to trading activity are not eligible for taking Cenvat credit under Rule 4 of the Cenvat Credit Rules.

3. The issue involved in this case is admissibility of Cenvat credit on the services related to the inputs which are not used in the manufacture of goods which are exported. The inputs received by the appellants are exported as such without being used in the manufacturing activity. The point for consideration is whether the inputs which do not go in the stream of manufacture will be eligible for Cenvat credit or not. Appellant has relied upon the judgment of CESTAT Mumbai in the case of Flat Products Equipments (I) Ltd. (supra). It is observed from this judgment that the bought out items received by the appellant were used in the manufacture of excisable goods the value of which was also included in the total sale price of the goods. Similarly their reliance placed by the appellant on C.B.E. & C. Circular No. 283/117/96-CX, dated 13-12-1996 the situation covered those inputs which were also used in the manufacture of the finished goods and at times are also exported under bond for which it was clarified that such inputs can be exported under bond without any reversal of credit. However in the present case of the appellant the bought out items exported by the appellants are never used in the manufacture of the finished excisable goods as per the claim of the department. In this regard ld. A.R. has rightly relied upon the judgment of Ford India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE 2007 (214) ELT 40 (Tri.-Chennai) where the clarification dated 13-12-1996 relied upon by the appellant was also considered. After considering all the aspects of the case it was held by Chennai CESTAT Bench that credit, with respect services utilised only in the activity of trading of components, no Cenvat credit is available on such components. On the same analogy the services used with respect to traded items will not be admissible when the services are utilised only for export of such traded items which are not used in the stream of manufacture. Based on the above view, the appeal filed by the appellant is accordingly dismissed.

The 'Input Service Distributor' may distribute Cenvat Credit in respect of service tax, among its manufacturing units or providing output service. HELD (PER TECHNICAL MEMBER)

It is seen that rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Therefore, there is no authority in law for availing Cenvat credit on the quantity of inputs intended or used for the manufacture of exempted goods except in terms of rule 6(2), which allows the manufacturer to avail the Cenvat credit only in respect of that particular quantity of inputs, which is intended to be used in the manufacture of dutiable goods subject to their maintaining separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. But if separate accounts are not maintained, though Cenvat credit is availed, then sub-rule 3 of rule 6 provides for payment of amount equal to Cenvat credit on dutiable inputs for cases covered under sub-rule (3)(a ) and in respect of all other inputs, sub-rule (3)(b) of rule 6 provides for payment of an amount of 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. [Para 15]

If the interpretation put by the majority order is held to be correct, it will render the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) ibid providing for payment of an amount equal to 8 per cent or 10 per cent rather otiose. This militates against an interpretation, which renders it superfluous and is of no significance. [Para 16]

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacturer of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts had to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. There is no provision for giving retrospective effect to this amendment. It cannot be given, as the amount of reversal of credit has to be worked out in a manner prescribed in the Rules. There was no such prescription prior to the amendment. This decision of the majority will make the amendment superfluous. Such interpretation has to be avoided. [Para 23]

In the light of the aforesaid discussions, it was held that the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) are applicable when the amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to the common inputs used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted final products has been paid prior to the removal of exempted final products from the factory. [Para 26]

(i)The assessee may opt for either of the option and would have to continue with that option for the rest of the financial year.

(ii)Rule specifically disallows the credit on inputs and input services used for the manufacture of exempted goods or for the provision of exempted services.

(iii)The term ‘Value’ for the purpose of sub-rules (3) and (3A) shall have the same meaning assigned to it under section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 read with rules made thereunder or, as the case may be, the value determined under section 4 or 4A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 read with rules made thereunder.

(iv)The sub-rule also clarifies that the amount mentioned above can be paid either by utilizing Cenvat credit or by cash.

Having said this, the specific provisions in respect of each option are as follows:

u Mode of Computation : Option 1

Option 1 provides that the assessee would pay service tax at the rate of 8 per cent of value of the exempted services and 10 per cent of value of the exempted goods.

For example value of taxable services and exempt services provided by Mr. X from Delhi office is Rs. 1 lakh and Rs. 50,000, respectively. Thus, Mr. X if opting for option 1, he would pay Rs. 4,000 as service tax on exempt service and avail whole of the credit which is attributable to the taxable service or is common to both, taxable as well as exempt services.

u Mode of Computation : Option 2

If the assessee opts for option 2, he would have to pay an amount equivalent to the Cenvat credit attributable to inputs and input services used in, or in relation to, the manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services subject to the conditions and procedure specified in sub-rule (3A). Accordingly, the rule has called for the payment of Cenvat credit attributable to exempted goods/services.

If the assessee wants to opt for this option, he would have to inform his Superintendent of Central Excise with certain factual information as prescribed in rule 6(3A).

The statute has provided that the computation of the Cenvat credit would be made in accordance with rule 6(3A). Rule 6(3A) provides that the assessee would first determine the payment on account of such Cenvat credit provisionally on a monthly/quarterly basis and then would determine the final liability before 30th of succeeding year and pay accordingly.

u Mode of Provisional Payment: to be computed on monthly/quarterly basis

Provisional payment of Cenvat credit attributable to exempted goods/services = (i) + (ii), where,

‘(i )’denotes the payment of Cenvat Credit on inputs attributable to exempted services during the month and;

‘(ii )’denotes the payment of Cenvat Credit on input services attributable to exempted goods/services during the month.

Further, the rule has provided the formula for the payment of Cenvat Credit on inputs attributable to exempted services during the month which is as follows :

Total value of Cenvat credit taken on inputs less input attributable to the manufacture of exempted goods multiplied by value of exempted services provided during the preceding financial year divided by total value of dutiable goods, taxable services and exempted services provided during the last financial year.

Similarly, for the purpose of calculating the payment of Cenvat Credit on input services attributable to exempted services during the month which is as follows :

Total value of Cenvat credit taken on input services multiplied by value of all exempted goods/service produced or provided during the preceding financial year divided by Total Value of dutiable goods, taxable services and exempted goods and services provided during the last financial year.

This calculation has to be made for all the months/quarter and tax has to be paid, accordingly, before the corresponding due date.

u Mode of Final Payment: to be computed on yearly basis

For the calculation of Cenvat credit attributable to exempted goods/services for the financial year, the above formula is same only with the difference that in place of figures of preceding year, the figures of financial year for which the calculation is being done would be substituted.

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in providing the services of Maintenance and Repairs, Erection, Commissioning & Installation services, Man Power Recruitment/Supply services.

On the ground that during the period from 2003-04 to 2005-06, the assessee had collected the Service Tax from the customers but not paid the same to the Department, proceedings were initiated.

Assessee did not contest the Service Tax liability but, after issue of Show Cause Notice, filed the ST 3 returns claiming CENVAT Credit on capital goods and debited same towards payment of Service Tax and sought to carry forward balance of credit.

The Department allowed credit of capital goods received on or after 10-9-2004, but, denied credit of capital goods received prior thereto.

Commissioner (Appeals) allowed credit of capital goods received prior to 10-9-2004 as well.

Issue Involved

Whether assessee was eligible for credit ?

HELD: Capital goods was not available to service provider prior to 10-9-2004

During the relevant period i.e. prior to 10-9-2004, as per Rule 3 of the Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002, credit could have been taken on the Service Tax paid on input services which fall under the same category of taxable service as that of output service and, therefore, the CENVAT Credit of duty paid on capital goods was not available prior to 10-9-2004. Hence, credit could not be allowed in view of transitional provisions in Rule 11 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. [Paras 4 and 6]

Separate proceedings were not required for denial of credit, as it was a part of assessment :

2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service

4.15 The assessee had availed Cenvat credit on the basis of canteen bill on which service tax had been charged. Making provision for canteen services is a statutory requirement and, therefore, it was the contention of the assessee that these services had to be considered as the input services and the credit of the same was to be allowed. The case was referred to the appellate authority against the order of lower authority. The Tribunal held that a similar matter had come up before it and vide its Order Nos. A/273 to 275/08/WZB/SMB/C-I, dated 15-2-2008 it has held such credit to be admissible. Since the issue was squarely covered by the above decision, the Tribunal held that the appellants could not be denied the credit of service tax paid on the canteen bills as it had to be considered as an input service and, accordingly, set aside the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

Rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Credit of whole service tax paid on taxable services specified in rule 6(5)

4.17 The assessee was a manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods and provider of taxable and exempted services. The assessee utilized service tax credit for exempted as well as non-exempted category of services provided to it. The revenue denied credit on ground that the assessee had not maintained separate records for services received by it for exempted and for non-exempted categories and, therefore, in terms of rule 6(3)(c ), the assessee was entitled to utilize only 20 per cent of amount of credit. The revenue filed an appeal aggrieved by the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) on the ground that the Commissioner (Appeals) has not considered the provisions of the Cenvat Credit Rules 6(3) and 6(5). The adjudicating authority after examining in depth rule 6(5) has said that it is clear that a service provider, who provides taxable and exempted services, shall be allowed, credit of the whole of service tax paid on taxable services specified in the said rule 6(5) unless the said service is exclusively used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted goods or providing exempted services although no separate amounts for receipt/consumption of the input services are maintained. In rule 6(5) the important word is ‘notwithstanding’. The very use of this word means that rule 6(3) is not applicable to the input services mentioned under rule 6(5). The credit which has been taken by the party is on some of the 17 services, which are covered under rule 6(5) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004. This rule does not talk about taking or utilization, so the credit is allowed to both taken and utilized services.

The Tribunal held that impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is correct and does not suffer from any infirmity.

10.1-3 Manner of distribution of Cenvat Credit w.e.f. 1-4-2016

Rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules has been revamped w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

As per revised rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules as amended w.e.f. 1-4-2016, the distribution should be as follows —

(a)

Credit distributed should not be more than credit of input service tax available.

(b)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used wholly by a unit shall be distributed only to that unit.

(c)

Credit of service tax attributable to services used by more than one unit (but not to all units) shall be distributed pro-rata on the basis of turnover of such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of such units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(d)

Credit of service tax attributable to service used by all the units shall be distributed pro-rata on the basis of turnover of all such units during the relevant period to the total of turnover of all the units which are operational in the current year, during the 'relevant period' [i.e. on the basis of turnover ratio during the 'relevant period'. The turnover of only those units which are operational is required to be considered].

(e)

The Cenvat credit can be distributed to 'outsourced manufacturing unit'. Such 'outsourced manufacturing unit' can utilize the Cenvat credit only for purpose of payment of duty on goods manufactured for such input service distributor.

(f)

Credit of Cenvat credit as on 31-3-2016 shall not be distributed to outsourced manufacturing unit.

(g)

Provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules applies to units manufacturing excisable goods or provider of output service. It shall not apply to input service distributor. Thus, ISD should distribute on basis of total turnover of goods and services (exempted as well as taxable).

Meaning of 'unit' - 'Unit' includes premises of provider of output service and the premises of a manufacturer, including the factory, whether registered or otherwise or the premises of outsourced manufacturing unit - Explanation 1 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Meaning of total turnover - Total turnover will be calculates per provisions of rule 5 of Cenvat Credit Rules. Turnover of outsourced manufacturing unit will be only of goods manufactured by the outsourced manufacturing unit for the Input Service Distributor - Explanation 2 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Meaning of 'relevant period' - 'Relevant Period' means (a) if the assessee has turnover in the 'financial year' preceding to the year during which credit is to be distributed for the month or quarter, as the case may be, the said financial year or (b) If the assessee does not have turnover for some or all the units in the preceding financial year, the last quarter for which details of turnover of all the units are available, previous to the month or quarter for which credit is to be distributed - Explanation 3 to rule 7 of Cenvat Credit Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Thus, if Cenvat Credit for July 2016 is to be distributed and if all the units of assessee were working in financial year 2015-16, then distribution should be on basis of turnover of each unit during 2016-17. However, if some of the units started operations after April 2016, then turnover for April 2016 - June 2016 will have to be considered for distributing the Cenvat credit to various units.

Inclusive part of the definition as understood expands the scope of main definition and since main definition is restrictive, inclusive part which expands cannot be read very liberally and in such a manner that the services on which credit is allowed go beyond the scope of input service when main definition and the inclusive part are read together. In this case, the legislature has used the word premises in the case of output service provider in the place of factory for a manufacturer. Therefore, both have to be taken as place which is used for doing the work of provision of service or related to the same. The credit is also provided for service used in respect of an office relating to the premises of a service provider which would cover branches and other offices used by service provider for providing the services. Therefore, as far as the premises of the service provider or an office relating to a service provider, both have to be places from where service is provided. [Para 5.7]

In this case, assessee has taken the credit in respect of services rendered for global training centre, hostel and gym. As regards global training centre, in view of the fact that assessee was providing commercial training and coaching service and the premises of global training centre is often used for conducting commercial coaching service on which service tax is paid, credit would be admissible since it becomes a premises of the service provider for providing the service of commercial training or coaching centre. Before 1-4-2011, setting up of a premises of output service provider was also an activity for which services used were eligible for credit. Therefore, construction services used for setting up global training centre would be covered by definition of input service before 1-4-2011, since it is claimed that said services were used for setting up a global training centre. As regards hostel and gym, in respect of which various services received had been claimed to be input service, it is quite clear from the definition discussed above that both of them cannot be considered as premises from where the service is provided or an office relating to the premises from where service is provided. Therefore, the question of their necessity or essentiality is not really material once it is clear that the services are not covered by the definition itself. [Para 5.9]

(a)

Credit is admissible in respect of global training centre up to 1-4-2011;

(b)

After 1-4-2011, the services used for setting up of 'global training centre' would not be input service but services used for repairs, renovation or modernisation would be admissible;

(c)

Cenvat credit of service tax paid on services used in respect of hostel and gym whether it is setting up or repair or renovation or modernisation cannot be considered as input service. [Para 5.10]

9.4

Meaning of 'exempted services'

Rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules defines exempted service as follows.

"Exempted service" means a —

(1)

taxable service which is exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon; or

(2)

service, on which no service tax is leviable under section 66B of the Finance Act; or

(3)

taxable service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken;

but shall not include a service

(a)

which is exported in terms of rule 6A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 or

(b)

by way of transportation of goods by a vessel from customs station of clearance in India to a place outside India [The words in italics are inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2016]

Services on which no tax is payable are also 'exempt services' - For purpose of the definition of 'exempted services', services on which no service tax is leviable are also 'exempted services'. Thus, if a particular service is not taxable under present provisions of Finance Act, 1994, it will be 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

It has been clarified that export of service will not be treated as exempted service for rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules - para 6 of CBE&C Circular No. 868/6/2008-CX dated 9-5-2008.

Activity which is not 'service' is also 'exempted service' - 'Exempted service' shall include an activity which has been defined as 'not service' under section 65(44) of Finance Act, 1994, if such activity has used inputs or input services - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016 and amended w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

Meaning of 'if such activity has used inputs or input services' - In my view, activities like interest, dividend, deposits, loans etc. do not use inputs or input services in real sense of the term. Hence, these should not be treated as 'exempted service'.

Thus, trading of goods, transactions in immovable property, transaction in money and services provided by employee to employer will be 'exempted service' [The provision that service provided by employee to employer is 'exempted service for rule 6(1) does not seem to make sense, as really in that case, assessee (employer) is service receiver and not service provider at all] - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such activity shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 4 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

9.4-1 Trading of goods or securities is 'exempted service'

A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods or immovable property. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods or immovable property. The sale may be within India or outside.

For example, authorised service station of automobiles is also selling spare parts. A brand name owner manufactures some goods and also gets similar goods manufactured from ancillary units.

A Builder/Developer may also be trading in land or other immovable property.

Obviously, there will be many common input services.

As per section 66D(e) of Finance Act, 1994, trading of goods has been specified as service in negative list.

Thus, trading of goods is 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

6. Though the issues are numerous which still need clarity since the statute is still in its nascent stage, some of the identified issues are as under :

(i) Rule 6(3), Opt in - your choice, Opt out - no choice during the financial year

The sub-rule clarifies that an option would be exercisable both in the case of goods and services as manufactured or provided by the assessee. He cannot opt for Option 1 for goods and option 2 for services or vice versa. Also, exercise of such option cannot be withdrawn at any point of time during the financial year. He may change his option from the next year onwards. Thus, though the choice of opting in for the non-maintenance of separate books of account is open during the financial year, yet the option to opt out of it is unavailable to the manufacturer of service provider for that financial year.

(ii) Meaning of the term - ‘exempt’

The sub-rule does not define the term ‘exempt’ for the purpose of this sub-rule. Technically speaking, exempted goods/services are a sub-set of taxable goods/services. Exempted goods/services are specified by a notification by the Central Government and, accordingly, no duty/tax is leviable on them. However, there are other goods or services which are non-taxable and cannot be called ‘exempt’ technically. For example services of an advocate.

Having said this, the interpretation of the term ‘exempt’ is important for the calculation of duty/tax in respect of the Cenvat credit attributable towards exempted goods/services. Thus, extension of the term ‘exempt’ on non-taxable goods/services or otherwise would change the entire computation. For example when a provider of taxable services is providing exempt services and also is engaged in trading of goods (non-taxable), whether he needs to pay an amount equal to Cenvat credit attributable towards trading activity also, as he has to do in the case of exempt services. The answer is in affirmative when we equate trading to an exempt service and not otherwise.

Further, a larger question would be whether in case of an assessee engaged in the provision of taxable service and non-taxable service, would the computation under rule 6(3A) be applicable on him ? The question would be answered as ‘YES’ when non-taxable is equated as ‘exempt’ otherwise the answer is ‘NO’.

The more logical calculation would be to take out the Cenvat credit attributable towards non-taxable activities and then apply rule 6(3) on the balance Cenvat credit. Thus, the assessee should avail only the credit excluding that which is attributable towards non-taxable activities.

(iii) Choice of option - whether premises-wise or assessee-wise

Further, another point worth mentioning here is that the term used by the statute for availment of choice is manufacturer/service provider and not premises of manufacturer (factory) or service provider. Even the definition of ‘manufacturer’ under central excise uses the word ‘person’ and not ‘factory’. Accordingly, one school of thought might interpret that the availment of the options above should be same throughout all locations across India and the option cannot be availed of differently for different premises.

Expressing it with an example, Mr. X is a service provider having offices in Delhi, Mumbai and Pune, all three offices being separately registered with service tax department. Mr. X is providing taxable services under the category of ‘chartered accountant services’ and also availing the exemption provided thereunder. Thus, he is the provider of both taxable as well as exempt services. Now, the question is whether he can opt for option I for his Delhi and Mumbai offices and option II for Pune or will he have to opt for a single option for all his offices since the sub-rule uses the words ‘service provider’ when offering the choice.

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of excisable goods. During the year 2011-12, it had exported final products manufactured by itself and also exported goods imported by it. It availed cenvat credit of service tax paid on import of services received from one 'C' under reverse charge mechanism under section 66A.

The Adjudicating Authority having discovered that the assessee had availed service tax credit on marketing consultancy services for traded goods (exempted goods) rendered by 'C' opined that the assessee was eligible to take proportionate cenvat credit of service tax on manufactured goods and the cenvat credit attributable to trading of imported goods was erroneous and recoverable in terms of rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004.

Thereupon the assessee reversed the cenvat credit to the extent of service tax attributable to trading of imported goods and also paid interest. It asserted that it was eligible for the cenvat credit in respect of market consultancy services.

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the demand of service tax and interest and also imposed equal penalty on the assessee under rule 15 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with section 11AC of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Effect of rule 6 of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 :

Rule 6(1) stipulates that no Cenvat credit shall be allowed on such quantity of input or input service which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods or for provision of exempted services, save in the circumstances which are mentioned in rule 6(2).

Rule 6(2) deals with a situation where inter alia a manufacturer manufactures both dutiable final products as well as exempted goods. In such a situation, in order to avail of Cenvat credit, the manufacturer is required to maintain separate accounts for the receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs and input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products and the quantity of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of exempted goods. Rule 6(2) stipulates that a manufacturer can take Cenvat credit only on that quantity of input service which is intended for use in the manufacture of dutiable goods. In other words, Cenvat credit is not admissible on that quantity of input or input service which is not intended for use and is not used in the manufacture of dutiable goods.

Rule 6(5) confers an option to follow one of two courses of action to a manufacturer not opting to maintain separate accounts. Under rule 6(5), which has a non obstante provision overriding sub-rules (1), (2) and (3) credit of the whole of the service tax paid on taxable services of a specified description is allowable unless such a service is used exclusively in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or provision of exempted services. In other words, where a service is of the description which is specified in rule 6(5), the manufacturer is entitled to credit of the whole of the service tax unless the service is used exclusively, that is to say solely in or in relation to the manufacture of exempted goods or any provision of exempted services. [Para 13]

Services used in manufacture of exempted intermediate product are eligible for credit if such intermediate product is used in dutiable final product :

Merely because the assessee manufactures exempted goods, that would be no justification to disallow to it the benefit of availing of Cenvat credit on that quantity of input service which is utilised in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products.

The definition of the expression "input service" is cast in broad terms. The expression "input service" means any service used by the manufacture, whether directly or indirectly or in or in relation to the manufacture of final products.

It is impossible to accept the hypothesis that would assert, that input services that are utilized by the assessee in or in relation to the process of manufacture that takes place at Mumbai Offshore is not a service that is used by the manufacturer in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products. The dutiable final products that are manufactured by the assessee at its Uran plant are fundamentally premised upon the manufacturing process which commences at Mumbai Offshore.

There can be no manner of doubt that the input services which go into the process of production at Mumbai Offshore meet the description of services that are utilized by the manufacturer directly or indirectly in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products. The manufacture of the dutiable final products cannot take place without the process in question.

The words "used by the manufacturer, whether directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products" fulfil the statutory object and purpose of preventing a cascading effect and burden of duty. They must be given their plain and natural meaning.

However, it would be necessary to clarify that Cenvat credit can be availed of only on that quantity of input service which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. [Para 14]

Conclusion :

The Tribunal judgment holding that assessee was disentitled to the benefit of Cenvat credit in respect of the input services used in or in relation to the manufacture of dutiable final products on the ground that crude oil which is subject to a further process of manufacture at the Uran plant for the production of dutiable final products is exempted from central excise duty, was set aside.

ONGC admittedly also produces dutiable final products. The production of those dutiable products is possible only on the continuous supply of crude oil. However, it was clarified that as a manufacturer of both dutiable and exempted goods, the assessee would be required to comply with the discipline and rigour of rule 6 and would be entitled to take Cenvat credit only on that quantity of input service which is used in the manufacture of the ultimate dutiable product. [Para 15] This being the case, a harmonious reading of rule 3 read with rules 6 and 11 will suggest that eligibility/entitlement to credit has to be examined only at the time of receipt of input service and once it is found to be availed at a time when output service is wholly taxable and the said credit is availed legitimately, the same cannot be denied and/or recovered unless specific machinery provisions are made in this regard. As per TRU Clarification dated 28-2-2007, even if one assumed sale of immovable property after completion certificate to be 'exempt service', there is no legal requirement to reverse any credit availed on 'input services' in the past (prior to obtaining Completion Certificate) at all. [Para 16]

In the instant case, before obtaining the Completion Certificate, the service of the assessee was very much taxable during which period the assessee received input service.

From a bare reading of rule 4(7), it is clear that the assessee is not required to wait till output service is sold to the service recipient. The assessee can take the credit immediately after the day on which bill/challan of input service is received. In the instant case, there is no dispute that the assessee has availed the credit after receipt of bill, challan in respect of input service. Therefore, the assessee was legally entitled to take the credit on the date after the receipt of service bills/challans. Therefore, the availment of cenvat credit by the assessee is absolutely legal and correct in accordance with rule 4(7). At the time of taking credit, there is no existence of any exempted service. Therefore, there is no application of rule 6. The part of the service was exempted only after obtaining completion certificate. Thereafter the assessee was not required to avail the cenvat credit on the input service, if any, received after obtaining the Completion Certificate. In the instant case, the assessee has either not availed the cenvat credit in respect of the services received after obtaining the Completion Certificate in respect of exempted service or availed proportionate credit attributed to the taxable output service. For this reason also rule 6 has no application for the period after obtaining the Completion Certificate.

In case of service becomes exempted at a later stage, unlike the provision for manufactured goods provided under rule 11(1)(2) and (3), there is no such provision in respect of the service. The only provision for the service is provided under sub-rule (4) of rule 11. From a reading of sub-rule(4) of rule 11, it can be seen that even if an output service provider avail the credit and output service becomes exempted; in such case the credit only in respect of inputs lying in stock or is contained in taxable service is required to be paid, whereas there is no provision for payment of cenvat credit equivalent to the input services used in respect of exempted service. Therefore, the cenvat credit availed in respect of input service is not required to be paid back under any circumstances. [Para 18]

Therefore, the assessee was not legally required to reverse any credit which was availed by it during the period 2010 till obtaining Completion Certificate, i.e., during the period when output service was wholly taxable in its hands, merely because later on some portion of the property was converted into immovable property on account of receipt of Completion Certificate and on which no service tax would be paid in future. [Para 19]

It is the case of the revenue that by demanding 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property after obtaining Completion Certificate, the credits availed in the past are ipso facto regularized. It should, however, be appreciated that payment of 8%/10% is only an option or rather a mechanism to seek credit reversal on lump sum basis, where the assessee cannot maintain separate accounts/reverse proportionate credit on turnover basis or in cases where the assessee himself so chooses to follow such option. In other words, it is a substitute to regularise credit instead of accepting proportionate credit availed during the time when output service was exempt. Since the credits availed when output service was wholly taxable cannot be called into question, it cannot be said that such 8%/10% amount of sale of immovable property is to regularise not only credits availed after completion certificate but also availed during 2010 till the time completion certificate was obtained. In that sense, rule 6, if invoked, can deal with only prospective credits availed after output activity becoming exempt and not credits availed before the output activity become exempt. [Para 21]

4. Also it needs to be appreciated that the members of the Bench have also prescribed the way and the periodicity for reversal of credit, taking into consideration practical difficulties faced for working out the same.

This issue has been discussed and litigated over a period of time since the introduction of Cenvat credit in respect of service tax. It is high time that CBEC realizes the need for providing a clarification on this issue so as to ensure that the litigation on the same is put to rest.

I. General

In terms of rule 6 (1) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, Cenvat credit shall not be allowed on such quantity of input or input services, which is used in the manufacture of exempted goods except in these circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). In terms of sub-rule (2) of rule 6 ibid, when a manufacturer avails of Cenvat credit in respect of any input or input services and manufactures such final products which are chargeable to duty as well as the exempted goods, then the manufacturer shall either maintain separate account and inventory for the receipt, consumption of the inputs/input services meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final product and exempted final product and take Cenvat credit only in respect of inputs/input services used in or in relation to manufacture of dutiable final product, or if does not maintain such account and inventory, in accordance with the provisions of sub-rule (3) of rule 6, he shall pay an amount either equal to 10%/5% of the sale price of the exempted final product or equal to the Cenvat credit involved on the inputs/input services used in or in relation to manufacture of exempted final products to be calculated as per the provisions of this sub-rule. [Para 6.1]

In accordance with the provisions of rule 11 (3) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, a manufacturer or producer of the final product shall be required to pay an amount equivalent to Cenvat credit, if any, taken by him in respect of inputs received for use in the manufacture of final product lying in his stock or in process or contained in the final product lying in his stock, if - (i) he opts for an exemption from whole of the duty excise leviable on such excisable product manufactured by him under a notification issued under section 5A(i) of the Act or (ii) the said final product has been exempted absolutely by a notification issued under section 5A(i) of the Act and after deducting the said amount from the balance of the Cenvat credit, if any lying in his credit, the balance, if any still remaining, shall lapse and shall not be allowed to be utilized for payment of duty on any final product whether cleared for home consumption or for export. [Para 6.2]

In this case even during period w.e.f. 1-3-2008 onwards, the respondent continued to avail Cenvat credit in respect of the duty paid inputs received by them even though Menthol Crystals BP/USP and Menthol USP/BP had become fully exempt from duty and they did not pay as per the provisions of rule 11 (3), an amount equal to Cenvat Credit involved on inputs in stock, inputs in process and the inputs contained in the final products lying in stock and on 1-3-2008 and lapse the Cenvat Credit balance as on 1-3-2008, if still remaining. [Para 6.3]

II. Rule 11(3) not applicable :

In accordance with the provisions of rule 11(3), the balance credit shall lapse and cannot be utilized for any purpose whether for payment of duty on the domestic clearances or for payment of duty on the goods cleared for export. From the language of this rule, it is clear that this sub-rule is applicable only when one or more Cenvat credit availed inputs or input services have been used or in relation to manufacture of a final product which has become fully exempted under a notification issued under section 5A (1) of the Central Excise Act. If the words ''the said final product" are taken to include its plural, then also, for application of this rule, it would be necessary that all the final products become fully exempt from duty. This rule would, have no application if from common Cenvat credit availed inputs or input services more than one final product are manufactured and out of these final products, only one final product has become fully exempt and other final products have remained dutiable. In such a situation, the credit in balance can still be utilized for payment of duty on the final products which have continued to be dutiable, as in terms of rule 3 (4) (a) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, Cenvat credit can be utilized for payment of excise duty on any final product and rule 11 (3) cannot be given an interpretation which is in conflict with the provisions of rule 3 (4). Therefore, rule 11(3) does not apply to this case. [Para 8.1]

III. Rule 6(1) and Rule 6(2) not applies :

The assessee had availed Cenvat credit of service tax paid on certain services, namely, rent-a-cab service, courier service, air travel agent’s service, maintenance and repair service and telephone service. However, Cenvat credit was denied on the ground that the assessee had not submitted any evidence to show that the said services were used for the manufacture of final product. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the input service credit had been taken in or in relation to the handling of marketing of goods after place of removal on which no Cenvat credit was permissible.

This is because the definition in respect of an output service provider is more restrictive when compared to the definition in case of a manufacturer. In case of an output service provider, input service is required to be used by a service provider for providing an output service whereas in the case of a manufacturer, the words 'directly or indirectly, in or in relation to the manufacture of final products' have been used. The words 'in or in relation to' and 'directly or indirectly' have far wider connotation and coverage when compared to the words 'used for'.

While inclusive definition covers both a manufacturer and a service provider, it cannot be said that both are treated on par as far as availability of credit is concerned. Therefore, the words used in respect of input service definition for the manufacturer cannot be imported and applied to a service provider.

Moreover in the case of a manufacturer, it was held in Maruti Suzuki Ltd. (supra) that inclusive part of the definition of input service has to be read with the main part. Therefore, it becomes necessary to examine the definition of input service in respect of a service provider by looking at Rule 2(l)(i) of the Cenvat Credit Rules with inclusive part. [Para 5.4]

Again while considering the provisions of inclusive part of definition also, it has to be read in the following manner :

(a)

includes services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such factory or premises;

(b)

services used in relation to advertisement, sales promotion, market research, storage up to the place of removal, procurement of inputs;

(c)

(d)

services used in relation to inward transportation of inputs or capital goods or outward transportation up to the place of removal. [Para 5.5]

Inclusive part of the definition as understood expands the scope of main definition and since main definition is restrictive, inclusive part which expands cannot be read very liberally and in such a manner that the services on which credit is allowed go beyond the scope of input service when main definition and the inclusive part are read together. When the definition is considered in this manner, it is quite clear that the services used in relation to setting up, modernisation, renovation or repairs of a factory, premises of provider of output service or an office relating to such premises only would be considered as input service for allowing Cenvat credit. In this case, the legislature has used the word premises in the case of output service provider in the place of factory for a manufacturer. Therefore, both have to be taken as place which is used for doing the work of provision of service or related to the same. The credit is also provided for service used in respect of an office relating to the premises of a service provider which would cover branches and other offices used by service provider for providing the services. Therefore, as far as the premises of the service provider or an office relating to a service provider, both have to be places from where service is provided. [Para 5.7]

Other Issues relating to availment of Cenvat Credit

Other issues relating to availment of Cenvat credit are discussed below.

6.7-1 One to one correlation not necessary in Cenvat

Rule 3(4)(a) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that Cenvat credit may be utilised for payment of any duty of excise on any final product or service tax on output service. Thus, there is no requirement of establishing relation between inputs/input services and final product/output services. One to one relation is not required.

There is no corelation of the raw material and the final product; that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product that is manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related - CCE v. Dai Ichi Karkaria Ltd. 112 ELT 353 = AIR 1999 SC 3234 = 1999 AIR SCW 3205 = (1999) 7 SCC 448 (SC 3 member bench) - quoted with approval in CCE v. Bombay Dyeing (2007) 10 STT 286 (SC).

Cenvat rules do not provide for 'one to one' co-relation between input and output. - Kisan Products Ltd. v. CCE - (1996) 88 ELT 440 (CEGAT) * Bajaj Sevashram Ltd. v. CCE - (1996) 87 ELT 726 (CEGAT) * Nisha Conductors v. Collector and Rama Cables and Wires Ltd. v. Collector - 1993 (68) ELT 256 (CEGAT) * Pratap Steels Ltd. v. CCE 1997(95) ELT 584 (CEGAT) * Bajaj Tempo Ltd. v. CCE 2000 (117) ELT 423 (CEGAT) * HMT v. CCE (2009) 18 STT 8 = 232 ELT 217 (CESTAT 3 member bench) * CCE v. Motherson Sumi Electric Wires (2010) 252 ELT 543 (CESTAT) * Shri Dnyaneshwar SSK v. CCE (2014) 310 ELT 770 (CESTAT).

There is no one to one co-relation in Cenvat scheme - PSL Corrosion Control v. CCE (2009) 237 ELT 495 (CESTAT).

One to one corelation between credit availed on inputs and its utilisation of final products is not required under Cenvat. The rules do not provide for segregated credits, depending upon inputs and final products made from the inputs - Indian Aluminium v. CCE (2001) 137 ELT 1092 (CEGAT).

No one to one correlation is required for taking Cenvat credit - CCE v. National Trading Co. - (1996) 83 ELT 636 (CEGAT) - both members agreed on this point, though they differed on other points.

In CCE v. Bajaj Tempo Ltd. 2005 (1) STT 242 (CESTAT), it was held that credit of duty paid on inputs meant for 'matador' vehicle can be used for payment of duty on other motor vehicle 'tempo-traveller'.

CBE&C, vide para 2(viii) of circular No. 33/33/94-CX dated 4-5-1994 has confirmed that there is no 1:1 correlation between input and final product under the Cenvat scheme for utilisation of credit.

It is pertinent to note that the Government has amended rule 6 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 with effect from April, 2008. Now a manufacturer, using common inputs or input services for manufacture of dutiable as well as exempted goods and opting not to maintain separate accounts has to reverse the credit attributable to the inputs and input services used in the manufacture of exempted goods by way of formula as provided in the rule itself; or to pay 10 per cent amount of the value of the exempted goods. It is the settled law that reversal of the credit taken on the inputs is as good as non-availment of the credit on the inputs.

Under the Central Excise Act, 1944, levy is on manufacture but payment is at the time of clearance. It has been decided by the Board that credit of the duty paid on common inputs is admissible when used in the manufacturer of the final product (exempted and dutiable) provided the said credit of duty paid on inputs going into the exempted category of the final product is debited in the RG 23A-Part II account before the removal of exempted final product on actual or pro rata (estimated) basis. The facility of reversing the credit taken is neither explicitly given nor necessarily implied in the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2002. It was held in that context that the credit taken but before utilization reversed, will amount to not taking the credit and the benefit of exemption cannot be denied.

In other words, it is equivalent to reversal of credit on inputs. Therefore, according to Tribunal, the appellant had satisfied the requirement of not taking Modvat Credit on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods. Meaning of 'exempted services'

27.4 Rule 2(e) of Cenvat Credit Rules defines exempted service as follows :

"Exempted service" means a —

(1)

taxable service which is exempt from the whole of the service tax leviable thereon; or

(2)

service, on which no service tax is leviable under section 66B of the Finance Act; or

(3)

taxable service whose part of value is exempted on the condition that no credit of inputs and input services, used for providing such taxable service, shall be taken;

but shall not include a service

(a)

which is exported in terms of rule 6A of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 or

(b)

by way of transportation of goods by a vessel from customs station of clearance in India to a place outside India [The words in italics are inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2016]

Services on which no tax is payable are also 'exempt services' - For purpose of the definition of 'exempted services', services on which no service tax is leviable are also 'exempted services'. Thus, if a particular service is not taxable under present provisions of Finance Act, 1994, it will be 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

It has been clarified that export of service will not be treated as exempted service for rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules - para 6 of CBE&C Circular No. 868/6/2008-CX dated 9-5-2008.

Activity which is not 'service' is also 'exempted service' - 'Exempted service' shall include an activity which has been defined as 'not service' under section 65(44) of Finance Act, 1994, if such activity has used inputs or input services - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016 and amended w.e.f. 13-4-2016.

Meaning of 'if such activity has used inputs or input services' - In my view, activities like interest, dividend, deposits, loans etc. do not use inputs or input services in real sense of the term. Hence, these should not be treated as 'exempted service'.

Thus, trading of goods, transactions in immovable property, transaction in money and services provided by employee to employer will be 'exempted service' [The provision that service provided by employee to employer is 'exempted service' for rule 6(1) does not seem to make sense, as really in that case, assessee (employer) is service receiver and not service provider at all] - Explanation 3 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such activity shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 4 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Trading of goods or securities is 'exempted service'

27.4-1 A manufacturer and/or service provider may also be trading in goods or immovable property. The trading may be in respect of goods manufactured under his own brand name or other goods or immovable property. The sale may be within India or outside.

For example, authorised service station of automobiles is also selling spare parts. A brand name owner manufactures some goods and also gets similar goods manufactured from ancillary units.

A Builder/Developer may also be trading in land or other immovable property.

Obviously, there will be many common input services.

As per section 66D(e) of Finance Act, 1994, trading of goods has been specified as service in negative list.

Thus, trading of goods is 'exempted service' for purpose of rule 6.

In case of traded goods, the value of exempt service shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards the purchases) or ten percent of the cost of goods sold, whichever is more [Explanation I(c) after rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2011].

Thus, if the sale price is Rs. 100 and the purchase cost is Rs. 60, the difference of Rs. 40 will be considered as value of 'exempted service'. If purchase price is Rs. 95, value of exempted service will be Rs. 10 (difference or 10% whichever is more).

The service provider can avail Cenvat credit of service tax paid on input services and excise duty paid on capital goods, but not of excise duty paid on food items.

The service tax is payable on 40%/60%/70% of 'total amount'.

However, issue is whether 100% Cenvat Credit of input services is available or only proportionate Cenvat Credit of input services and input goods (other than those covered under chapter headings 1 to 22) is available, as per rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Composite contract of material plus service - The contract is composite contract of material plus services. Hence, rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules should be applicable.

Departmental clarification that food served in restaurants is 'exempted goods' - Para 8.4.3 of CBE&C's education Guide released on 20-6-2012 states that sale of food in restaurant would amount to clearance of exempt goods and thus, provisions of Rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules will be applicable.

Sale of food is deemed sale of goods, as per Constitution - Article 366(29A) of Constitution, as amended by Constitution (46th Amendment) Act, 1982, w.e.f. 2-2-1983 states as follows- 'Tax on the sale or purchase of goods' includes - - (f) a tax on supply, by way of or as part of any service or in any manner whatsoever, of goods, being food or any other article for human consumption or any drink (whether or not intoxicating), where such supply or service, is for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration - - And such transfer, delivery or supply of any goods shall be deemed to be a sale of those goods by the person making the transfer, delivery or supply and a purchase of those goods by the person to whom such transfer, delivery or supply is made.

Thus this is 'deemed sale of goods'.

Value in case of trading - As per Explanation I(c) to rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules, in case of trading, 'Value' for purpose of rule 6(3) and 6(3A) of Cenvat Credit Rules shall be the difference between the sale price and the cost of goods sold (determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles without including the expenses incurred towards their purchase) or 10% of cost of goods sold, whichever is more.

Common input services - It is a fact that common input services are used both for deemed sale of goods and provision of output (taxable) service.

How to apply rule 6 in case of common input services ? - There are three possible views :

(a)

The 60% (in case of restaurant service)/40% (in case of outdoor catering service)/30% (in case of food service with mandap/shamiana/convention service) of value (on which service tax is not paid) shall be deemed to be value of 'exempted goods' . In effect, assessee can avail only 40% (in case of restaurant service)/60% (in case of outdoor catering service)/70% (in case of food service with mandap/shamiana/convention service) of Cenvat credit of input services and balance Cenvat credit is required to be reversed.

(b)

The sale of food is to be treated as sale of goods as per Constitutional provisions. Thus, difference between sale price of goods and purchase price of inputs should be taken as value of 'exempted services' as per Explanation I(c) to rule 6(3D) of Cenvat Credit Rules. For example, in case of restaurant services, service tax is payable on 40% of value. Thus, 60% is to be taken as value of sale of food. If total value is 100 and value of purchase of goods is (say) 40, the value of 'exempted service' will be 20 (60 - 40). Thus, total value of service = taxable service + Exempt service = 40 + 20 = 60. Thus, the assessee can avail Cenvat credit of common input services in the ratio of 40/60 i.e. 66.67% of common input services and balance 33.33% should be reversed.

In terms of rule 7(b), the service tax attributable to service used in a unit 'exclusively' engaged in the manufacture of exempted goods is not available. The expression 'exclusively' appearing in the said rule relates to the unit and not to the service tax. The unit has to be exclusively engaged in the manufacture of exempted goods meaning thereby that if service tax stands utilized in a unit which is manufacturing exempted as also dutiable goods, the said rule will have no application. The expression 'exclusively' is not associated with the word 'service tax' as suggested by the assessee. It is well settled law of interpretation that where the words of a particular provision is unambiguous, no extraneous words can be introduced or taken out or can be allowed to switch places. As such, the expression 'exclusively' cannot be associated with the service tax availed by a unit manufacturing exempted goods. [Para 6]

Inasmuch as rule 7 debars taking of credit attributable to service tax used in a unit exclusively engaged in the manufacture of exempted goods and inasmuch as the 'R' unit is admittedly engaged in the manufacture of only exempted goods, the credit of service tax in respect of services used in 'R' unit is not available to the assessee.

Therefore, the order of the Adjudicating Authority disallowing proportionate credit deserved to be upheld. [Para 6]

Under the erstwhile Central Excise Rules, 1944, rule 57Q was inserted vide notification dated 1-3-1994. Sub-rule (1) of rule 57Q essentially provided the benefit of duty paid on capital goods used by the manufacturer in his factory for payment of duty of excise leviable on its final product subject to conditions contained therein. Term capital goods is defined in the definition below sub-rule (1). Sub-rule (2) of rule 57Q provided that notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1), no credit of the specified duty paid on capital goods shall be allowed if such duty has been paid on such capital goods before first day of March 1994. Thus, this rule for the first time granted the facility of utilizing the specified duty paid on capital goods used by the manufacturer in the factory discharging its duty liability but restricted the application thereof to the duty which was paid on such capital goods after 1-3-1994. [Para 7]

CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, also granted similar benefits. Term 'capital goods' was defined in rule 2A. Rule 3 of the CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, pertains to CENVAT credit. Sub-rule (1) of rule 3 provided that a manufacturer or producer of final products or a provider of output service shall be allowed to take credit to be called CENVAT credit of the various duties specified in clauses (i) to (xi) contained therein paid on any input or capital goods received in the factory of manufacture of final product or by the provider of output services on or after 10-9-2004 and any input service received by the manufacturer of the final product or by the provider of output service on or after the said date. Rule 4 of CENVAT credit Rules, 2004, prescribed conditions for allowing CENVAT Credit and essentially provided that the CENVAT credit in respect of capital goods received by the provider of output services or the manufacturer of final products can claim the credit of duty paid on such capital goods for an amount not exceeding 50 per cent of such duty in the same financial year and the balance credit may be taken in any financial year subsequent to the financial year in which the capital goods were received in the factory of the manufacturer or the premises of the goods of output services. [Para 8]

Section 2(19) of the CGST Act defines the term 'capital goods' as to mean the goods, the value of which is capitalized in the books of account of the person claiming the input tax credit and which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business. Term 'input' is defined in section 2(59) as to mean any goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used by a supplier in the course or furtherance of a business. Section 2(62) defines the term 'input tax' in relation to a registered person as to mean the Central tax, State tax, integrated tax or Union territory tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both made to him and would include several taxes specified in clauses (a) to (e) contained therein. Term 'input tax credit' is defined under section 2(63) as to mean the credit of input tax. [Para 9]

Section 16 of the CGST Act pertains to eligibility and conditions for taking input tax credit. Sub-section (1) of section 16 provides that every registered person shall subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in section 49, be entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course of furtherance of his business and said amount shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger of such person. Sub-section (3) of section 16 provides that where the registered person has claimed depreciation on the tax component of the cost of capital goods and plant and machinery under the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the input tax credit on the said tax component shall not be allowed. [Para 10]

Section 17 of CGST Act pertains to apportionment of credit and blocked credits. Sub-section (1) of section 17 provides that where the goods or services or both are utilized by the registered person partially for the purpose of any business and partially for other purposes, the amount of credit shall be restricted to so much of the input tax as is attributable to the purposes of his business. Likewise, sub-section (2) of section 17 provides that where the goods or services or both are used by the registered person partially for affecting taxable supplies including zero rated supplies and partially for exempt supplies, the amount of credit shall be restricted to so much of the input tax as is attributable to the said taxable supplies including zero rated supplies. [Para 11]

An ambiguous Explanation - An Explanation at end of Rule 3(7) of Cenvat Credit Rules states that where provisions of any other rule or notification provide for grant of partial or full exemption on condition of non-availability of credit of duty paid on any inputs or capital goods, or service tax paid on input services, provision of such other rule or notification shall prevail over provisions of these rules (i.e. Cenvat Credit Rules). - - Purpose of the Explanation is not clear and in fact, it appears to be superfluous. Probably the purpose is that if such an Exemption notification is there, it will be compulsory and full duty cannot be paid. If so, that purpose is unlikely to be achieved the way Explanation is worded. A conditional exemption is at the option of assessee. He may choose not follow the condition and then exemption will not be available. However, this Explanation seems to have lot of nuisance value.

In fact, it had created big nuisance at least in one case. In HMM Coaches Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 231 ELT 506 (CESTAT), there was an exemption notification subject to condition that assessee should not avail the Cenvat Credit. Department took a view that in view of rule 3(7), assessee cannot avail Cenvat credit i.e. in other words, he must avail the exemption notification. Luckily, Tribunal held that the exemption notification is conditional (i.e. Cenvat should not be availed). Rule 3(7) of Cenvat Credit Rules cannot be interpreted to mean that if an exemption is subject to condition that Cenvat credit should not be availed, that exemption is compulsory. Generally, exemption notification stands independently of input credit relief scheme.

On a plain reading of rule 6(1), it is obvious that if inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods, credit is not allowed except in the circumstances mentioned under sub-rule (2). A manufacturer who avails of the Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products which are chargeable to duty as also exempted goods, the manufacturer has to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of dutiable final products and the quantity of inputs used for the manufacture of exempted goods and take the Cenvat credit only on that quantity of inputs which is used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. A plain reading of this rule does not lead to any ambiguity, absurdity or defeat the provisions of the Act. Rule 6(2) and rule 6(3), read together mean that in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted products no Cenvat credit is allowed. It may, however, happen that the inputs are used in the manufacture of both exempted and dutiable goods, in which event if the register as required is maintained the credit can be taken for the quantity of inputs used in the manufacture of dutiable goods. If records are not maintained as required, the duty has to be paid in terms of rule 6(3). The presumptive tax payable in terms of rule 6(3) has been recognized and accepted by the Supreme Court in CCE v. Ballarpur Industries Ltd. 2007 (215) ELT 489. Rule 6(1) does not lead to the construction that if the manufacturer without maintaining the books, does not take credit for the duty paid on inputs for manufacture of exempted goods, rule 6(1) is satisfied. Rule 6(1) is satisfied only when the requirements of the rule 6(2) are satisfied, which requires register to be maintained for separate accounts of receipt, consumption and inventory of the inputs. Rule 6(3) provides that if separate accounts are not maintained then the amount has to be paid by a manufacturer. [Para 18]

The rule has to be read together to understand its object. Once a manufacturer manufactures from common inputs two final products, one dutiable and the other exempted, rule 6(2) would be attracted and on failure to maintain separate records, rule 6(3) would apply. Rule 6(1) in such an event would result in denying to the manufacturer Cenvat credit. Once the inputs are used in the manufacture of exempted goods irrespective of whether such inputs are used in the manufacture of dutiable goods, such manufacturer can avail of credit only in terms of rule 6(3). [Para 19]

A power to give benefit encompasses within itself the power to put conditions and restrictions under which credit is available. Power to give benefit also carries with it power to take it back or withdraw it. The rule if properly read starts with the words ‘Cenvat credit shall not be allowed’. Therefore, rule 6 makes it clear that insofar as inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods are concerned, no Cenvat credit is allowed. The rule making authority, however, noting that inputs may be used both for manufacturing final products which may be dutiable and other final products which are exempt, has provided that such manufacturer will be given credit insofar as inputs used for manufacturing of dutiable goods are concerned, if accounts are maintained in terms of the rules. Therefore, merely because the assessee contended that he was willing to forego credit on inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final product it does not warrant a departure from the requirements of rule 6(2) and 6(3). The rules contemplate that on failure to maintain accounts in terms of rule 6(2) the consequences would be in terms of rule 6(3)(a) or (b). It is not possible to read down the rule as ‘amount not exceeding’ as was sought to be contended on behalf of the assessee. [Para 24]

Rule 6(1) is clear; the Cenvat credit cannot be availed of on inputs used in the manufacturing of exempted goods. It then adds the words except in the circumstances mentioned in sub-rule (2). A Court cannot read into the said rule something different or render otiose the words. The rule mandates specifically that an assessee seeking to avail Cenvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods, the only method by which he can avail of the credit is by following sub-rule (2).
